insights.summary: The microbes living in sourdough starters don’t just appear by chance—they’re shaped by what bakers feed them. New research shows that while the same hardy yeas
insights.core: 研究发现，酸面团发酵剂中的微生物并非随机出现，而是由烘焙师的喂养方式塑造，特定耐性酵母菌种在其中起关键作用。这揭示了微生物生态与最终产品风味之间的直接关联。
insights.view: 对FMCG感官研究而言，这提示我们微生物组可作为风味的隐藏驱动因素，影响产品的一致性与差异化。CMI应超越传统配方变量，关注生产环境中的生物动态，以更全面地解释消费者感知差异，并为产品创新提供生物学层面的新视角。
insights.action: 建议启动内部研究项目，探索发酵类产品（如烘焙、饮料）中微生物谱系与感官属性的关联。与研发部门合作，收集不同批次样本进行微生物测序与感官品评，建立数据库，为产品优化和营销故事提供科学依据。

insights.title: Scientists sent viruses to space and they evolved in surprising ways
insights.summary: When scientists sent bacteria-infecting viruses to the International Space Station, the microbes did not behave the same way they do on Earth. In microgravity,
insights.core: 科学家将噬菌体送往国际空间站，发现其在微重力环境下的行为与地球不同，发生了意外进化。这表明环境变化可能触发微生物的未知变异，对生物学和未来太空探索有启示。
insights.view: 此发现提示FMCG感官研究需关注环境因素对产品微生物稳定性的影响，尤其在新型运输或保存条件下。CMI应评估极端环境对产品感官属性潜在变化，避免假设地球条件普适，为创新产品提供风险预警。
insights.action: 建议开展模拟微重力或极端环境下的产品稳定性测试，监测微生物变化对感官品质的影响。同时，跟踪相关研究，评估未来太空旅行或特殊场景下的消费品需求，为前瞻性研发储备知识。

insights.title: A once-in-a-generation discovery is transforming dairy farming
insights.summary: A Michigan dairy farm took a gamble on a new kind of soybean—and it paid off fast. After feeding high-oleic soybeans to their cows, milk quality improved within
insights.core: 密歇根一家奶牛场尝试新型高油酸大豆饲喂奶牛，结果牛奶品质在短期内显著提升。这一发现可能颠覆传统乳业生产模式，被视为“一代一遇”的行业变革机遇。
insights.view: 对FMCG感官研究而言，牛奶品质提升（如口感、风味稳定性）直接关联消费者体验。高油酸饲料可能改变乳脂组成，影响感官属性。CMI应关注这一上游创新如何传导至终端产品差异化，并预判消费者对“饲料创新”叙事的接受度。
insights.action: 建议启动乳制品感官对比测试，评估高油酸牛奶与传统牛奶在盲测中的差异。同步开展消费者概念测试，验证“可持续饲料升级”卖点对购买意愿的影响，为产品线创新提供依据。

insights.title: 17 September 2026 Departmental update Patient safety at the heart of forthcoming WHO asthma guidelines
insights.summary: The theme of World Patient Safety Day 2026 is \"Safe care for noncommunicable diseases\". For people living with long-term conditions, patient safety extends be
insights.core: WHO借2026年世界患者安全日主题，预告即将发布的哮喘指南将把患者安全置于核心，强调非传染性疾病的长期照护安全，涉及吸入给药等长期管理场景。
insights.view: 对CMI而言，这提示慢病长期管理正被纳入安全叙事，吸入类产品的感官体验（刺激感、口味、依从性）将不再只是偏好问题，而可能被重新定义为安全与疗效依从的关键变量，值得提前布局。
insights.action: 立即梳理吸入/雾化类产品感官与依从性数据，建立与安全叙事的关联框架；跟踪WHO指南发布节点，准备面向慢病管理场景的消费者洞察议题。

insights.title: How Lowe’s is building — and measuring — a full-funnel media network
insights.core: Lowe's正构建并量化一个全漏斗零售媒体网络，强调从品牌曝光到销售转化的全链路测量，而非仅关注底层转化指标。
insights.view: 对FMCG感官与CMI而言，零售媒体正从交易场转向品牌建设场。感官体验与消费者洞察需前移至媒体触达环节，用全漏斗数据验证‘感知-兴趣-购买’链路，而非孤立评估转化率。
insights.action: 梳理现有媒体投放与感官/CMI数据的断点，试点将感官偏好指标嵌入零售媒体全漏斗测量框架，优先验证上层曝光对下层转化的增益。

insights.title: Brand new bag: Chipotle, Unreal Snacks reach for fashion relevancy
insights.core: Chipotle与Unreal Snacks借时尚联名推出新品包装，试图让品牌在服饰与生活方式领域获得相关性，本质是快消品牌用跨界时尚提升年轻消费者关注度。
insights.view: 对CMI而言，这提示感官与品牌研究需从单纯口味/质地延伸至视觉、触觉及社交符号。包装与联名成为感官线索的延伸，影响消费者对品牌新鲜度与潮流度的感知。需将时尚联名纳入品牌资产与购买场景追踪。
insights.action: 建议立即开展联名包装的视觉与触觉感官测试，并追踪社交媒体声量与购买转化。将时尚联名指标纳入CMI月度品牌健康度监测，评估其对年轻客群渗透的实际贡献。

insights.title: Gen Z, Gen Alpha and the AI-ificiation of retail this holiday season
insights.core: 文章指出，Gen Z与Gen Alpha正推动零售业在假日季加速AI化，AI工具被用于个性化推荐、虚拟试穿与客服等场景，以迎合年轻消费者的数字原生习惯。
insights.view: 对FMCG感官研究与CMI而言，这意味着年轻客群的决策路径正被AI中介重塑。传统问卷与焦点小组可能无法捕捉AI推荐下的真实偏好，需将AI交互数据纳入消费者洞察体系，并关注算法对品类认知与感官期待的潜在影响。
insights.action: 建议在假日季监测AI零售触点中的消费者反馈，试点将AI对话与推荐数据接入CMI分析，评估其对品类选择与感官偏好的影响，并据此调整年轻化产品的沟通策略。

insights.title: Shoppers expect less for more this holiday season. That could mean a sales decline.
insights.core: 零售商面临假日季消费者预期转变：消费者对产品和体验的期望降低，却要求更高性价比，这种'少期待、多索取'的心态可能导致整体销售额下滑，价格敏感度显著上升。
insights.view: 对FMCG感官研究与CMI而言，这意味着消费者在预算收紧下对感官体验的容忍阈值提高，高端化叙事承压。研究需重新校准价值感知模型，识别哪些感官属性仍能支撑溢价、哪些已沦为'应有之义'，避免在降级消费中失去差异化锚点。
insights.action: 立即启动假日季价格-感官价值敏感度追踪，分层测试核心感官卖点的溢价弹性；将CMI洞察前置到产品组合与促销策略，锁定可守住的体验底线与可让渡的非核心属性。

readings.title: The one thing Anthropic could do right now to make AI safer
body: Future Perfect The one thing Anthropic could do right now to make AI safer ﻿Unless the AI company has proof that its safety strategy is working, now’s the time to quit racing. by Sigal Samuel Oct 27, 2026, 10:32 AM UTC Gift Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says his AI company can drive a “race to the top.” Where’s the evidence? Finn Gomez/Getty Images Sigal Samuel is a correspondent for Vox’s Future Perfect. She writes primarily about the future of consciousness, tracking advances in artificial intelligence and neuroscience and their staggering ethical implications. Before joining Vox, Sigal was the religion editor at the Atlantic. We’re living through an AI-fueled “ Black October ,” and things are changing fast. Hackers are using AI to breach countless companies. AI tools have uncovered security flaws that could leave 70 percent of all websites vulnerable. Governments are scrambling to secure their sites . Banks , too. And because cyberhacks can hurt supply chains, some longtime AI watchers are going full prepper , stocking up on food, cash, and more. In the center of this story is Anthropic, one of the world’s leading AI companies, which was explicitly founded on the promise that it would be a “good guy” company in a world of dubious tech giants. Anthropic says all the latest developments are very serious. Its security chief wrote last week that things are “going to get a lot worse before they get better.” Two weeks ago the company warned that AI models could soon self-replicate on the internet-connected devices in your home, like smart fridges and robot vacuums. And its co-founder now says “ the singularity ” — when AI systems speed up technical progress in a way that’s hard for humans to comprehend — “is here.” Email (required) Sign Up By submitting your email, you agree to our Terms and Privacy Notice . This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply. You might think, given its view of the risks, that Anthropic would be pumping the brakes on its cutting-edge AI progress. Just the opposite. Anthropic filed for a blockbuster initial public offering on Monday, chasing a valuation of $2 trillion even as it warns in the IPO filing that AI could “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” Every day, it is racing toward recursive self-improvement (RSI) , where AI models are smart enough to build the next, even smarter AI models by themselves. How does Anthropic justify that? As its CEO, Dario Amodei, reminded the world last week, he built the company on one big bet: that instead of driving a race to the bottom, where companies skimp on safety in their rush to beat competitors in the market, Anthropic could actually catalyze a “race to the top.” As I’ve watched Anthropic double down on its “race to the top” strategy, I’ve been uncomfortably reminded of another very risky gambit: Sam Bankman-Fried’s crypto fraud of 2022. There are important differences between the two; this is not a perfect parallel. But both involve a tiny handful of figures, strongly influenced by effective altruism, making huge bets on behalf of many, many other people. EA culture prides itself on offering a counter to commonsense morality. The community has shown a willingness to take big risks and justify them with complex calculations. Sometimes that pays off . But believing you are intelligent enough to adopt a counter-intuitive, galaxy-brained strategy and end up saving the world with it often involves some hubris. And hubris makes me nervous in a field as high-stakes as AI. The idea is that if Anthropic proves it can build AI that’s both powerful and safe, the market will expect both — so other AI companies will then feel compelled to compete on safety, too. That may sound nice in theory, but it means Anthropic has to keep building ever-more-powerful AIs. “The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier,” Amodei wrote . “And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.” In other words, Amodei is sticking to his bet. But Amodei is gambling with, by his and his company’s own telling, the future of humanity. If AI goes wrong, it could lead to our gradual disempowerment , a galling concentration of power , or even complete extinction . So there’s a very basic question that the public deserves a good answer to right at this pivotal moment: What is the evidence that Anthropic’s stated strategy — compete at the frontier so as to drive a “race to the top” — is actually successful overall? From the outside, it looks like Anthropic has done more, on balance, to drive a race to the bottom. (Disclosure: Future Perfect is funded in part by the BEMC Foundation, whose major funder was also an early investor in Anthropic; they don’t have any editorial input into our content.) In fact, part of the problem may be that Anthropic continues to treat this as a classic arms race. Specifically, the company seems to model it as a prisoner’s dilemma: If Anthropic stopped building more powerful AI, another player — whether it’s China, OpenAI, or another company — would just build it anyway. In this kind of dilemma, if the other player is going to defect, it’s rational for you to defect, even though nobody actually wants that outcome. But what if this framing misses the point? Game theory can make a huge gamble seem sophisticated, while making the obvious alternative — just don’t build a doom machine — seem naive. Yet the fact that Anthropic and others are now racing toward RSI makes it much more likely that we could lose control of AI and start to see massive damage to our world. When the cost of defecting from safety is that you create a serious risk of catastrophic harm — or of all humanity, including you, going extinct — is that still a “rational” move? Instead of telling yourself that you can galaxy-brain your way through this with fancy enough game theory, maybe you’re better off just thinking of this as something much simpler: Russian roulette. More and more leading voices in AI are starting to recognize that. “We should stop AI progress now, starting unilaterally with Anthropic and/or OpenAI stopping — and then broadening out as a second step to more AI companies and negotiations with China,” Geoffrey Irving, who was until recently the chief scientist at the UK AI Security Institute, told me. “Unilateral pauses can’t hold for long, but they are the right first step: When you’re doing a very dangerous thing, the correct action is stop, even if others are also doing dangerous things.” Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment. The 2,000-year-old debate that reveals AI’s biggest problem Let’s be clear: The question is not whether Anthropic has done anything good on the safety front. It has. Standing up to the Pentagon , temporarily holding back access to frontier models, and publicly advocating for safer AI policies are a few examples, among others . But the real question is whether the company’s “race to the top” strategy is working on balance — whether it’s net-negative or net-positive for safety. Nathan Calvin, the chief strategy officer at AI safety advocacy organization Encode, recently set off a firestorm among tech watchers, writing on X, “When I look at many notable actions that Anthropic has taken over the past year, that evidence seems most consistent to me with the view that Anthropic is primarily trying to win the race to superintelligence, and that other considerations (including safety) are fundamentally secondary.” Here’s his list of what Anthropic has done: And this is all just in the past year. If we rewind the tape further back, we see Anthropic pushing back on a landmark bill to regulate AI . Rewind even further back, and we see indications that Anthropic’s core strategy may have been flawed from the start. According to Reuters , in late 2022, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman heard rumors that Anthropic was building an AI-powered chatbot. So he ordered his employees to ship an OpenAI chatbot first. That chatbot was called ChatGPT. We all know the rest. The rivalry between OpenAI and Anthropic seems not only to have hastened the arrival of generative AI, but also to keep pushing release dates forward to this day. The two companies have been known to release new or cheaper models within hours of each other , each one keen to protect its market share. Even if you think Anthropic’s behavior was justified in 2022 because publicly demonstrating the risks of AI also demonstrates the need to regulate AI — a common claim within the company and AI discourse writ large — you have to ask: Is it still justifiable now, when AI has reached this level of power and sophistication? Anthropic has indicated that it’s getting closer and closer to achieving RSI. In January, Amodei himself wrote , “I am concerned that LLMs are approaching (or may already have reached) the knowledge needed to create and release [biological weapons] end-to-end, and that their potential for destruction is very high. Some biological agents could cause millions of deaths.” And he wrote in September, “Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it’s my worry that in 6-12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet .” But at this point, Amodei and his staffers are themselves perhaps the primary ones accelerating the rate of AI capability development. “Anthropic seems to be doing the whole RSI thing more than anyone else, other than perhaps OpenAI,” Calvin told me. “And I just think that seems insane given their publicly stated views on the risks.” “I think people at Anthropic should reckon more with the fact that it seems like the modal outcome is that the largest impact that Anthropic will have had is dramatically accelerating the race to RSI,” he continued. “On the current trajectory, everything else they will have done and thought and ideals they had will be a rounding error compared to their contribution there.” Anthropic should be willing to invite scrutiny on this point — and, if it believes it’s actually making the field safer than it otherwise would be, to show us the receipts. How? It could put before Congress a bill that actually strengthens safety, instead of weakening it. It could stick to its former Responsible Scaling Policy and get other companies to do the same, instead of jettisoning its commitments. It could influence other labs not to build RSI, instead of leading the charge. In the absence of such evidence, the “race to the top” logic just doesn’t hold water. Amodei has begun advocating for “pacing the frontier” of AI development. “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” he wrote in September. The catch is that Amodei’s plan to slow down is contingent on others agreeing to slow down too — other AI labs, to start with, and also other countries. But more experts are now saying that it would be better if a frontier company like Anthropic unilaterally stopped. “I’m glad that he proposed that we pace, but like, now we have to actually do it — and it seems like he’s saying he’s not going to do it unilaterally,” Daniel Kokotajlo, a former researcher at OpenAI who became a prominent whistleblower , told me. “That’s not very helpful, Dario! You should lead. What’s all this about ‘racing to the top’ and ‘leading by example’ if you’re just waiting?” Voluntary unilateral action by individual companies is of course no substitute for federal regulation and international treaties. But Irving argues that it’s the right first step, because if the companies wait for governments to rein them in, it may well be too late. Governments are notoriously slow. An individual company can act today. There’s a perennial objection here: “But China!” Yet the idea that we’re in a classic arms race with China has always been flawed . For starters, AI is not just one thing with one purpose, like the atomic bomb. It’s a much more general-purpose technology, like electricity. So what matters isn’t simply who gets it first, but who uses it in which ways. Besides, if the harms from AI are massive, then those harms are relevant for the other party, too. The Chinese don’t want to see catastrophic harms to all of human civilization, either. So we shouldn’t write off the possibility of coordination. Former Vox reporter Kelsey Piper recently wrote about a colloquium at Anthropic where one participant objected: A decade ago, Facebook considered acquiring the tech that would later power TikTok. But, facing pressure due to privacy and safety worries, the company passed. That didn’t end up protecting us from the scourges of a world with TikTok — all it did was hand China an early monopoly on the tech. Piper writes: Was this a policy success? Did we want to repeat it? We were obliged to grudgingly concede that it didn’t sound like a policy success. We did not want to repeat it. China might be no excuse for the U.S. labs to do reckless things, but it is a real consideration. Our next step might be bilateral talks with China, then. But by the point where you agree that Anthropic’s plans might depend on bilateral talks with China, you’ve already conceded most of the steps of Anthropic’s worldview that seemed so much like madness 10 minutes ago: continue working on AI for now, try to negotiate a slowdown, but don’t abandon work at the frontier and all the advantages that come with it. But TikTok is not a good analogy for RSI. The former may be a cesspool that rots our brains and amplifies ethnic hatred, but its dangers don’t compare to the dangers of RSI. The TikTok case may indeed be best approached as a classic prisoner’s dilemma. But with RSI, the potential downside is so catastrophic that anyone who proposes to save the world precisely by building the tech that endangers it is making a hell of a gamble on behalf of everyone else. At the very least, the burden of proof should be on them to prove their confidence is justified. AI insiders often think those outside of their industry can’t possibly understand the technical, geopolitical, and moral complexities they’re facing. But commonsense morality is commonsense for a reason: It tracks intuitions that are usually right (such as, if you don’t want a doom machine, maybe don’t build a doom machine) and trains us to be appropriately skeptical of huge, counterintuitive bets to the contrary. Precisely because the AI landscape is a complex system — there are so many actors (including different AI companies and different governments), and actions from each can trigger actions from others in ways that are hard to predict — believing you’re smart enough to take highly counterintuitive actions and end up saving the world as a result is an extremely risky gambit. Instead, maybe it’s best to just do the straightforwardly right thing: Stop. Silicon Valley’s vision for AI? It’s religion, repackaged. To be clear, “stopping” doesn’t have to mean peeling back everything that’s been done in AI so far. The powerful AI systems that are already out there can’t be put back in the box. And we may need some AI to defend from the AI that’s already out there. “I’m not saying shut down all of your data centers,” Calvin said. “But I’m saying that in particular, pushing the frontier on RSI and making it so that you’re going to be the company that is doing more fully autonomous development than anyone else in the world, does that actually make any fucking sense?” Increasingly, both AI insiders and the public are shouting no . Some insiders, perhaps aware that humanity is perfectly capable of shutting down overly dangerous tech development (we’ve done it before ), are speaking out and quitting jobs at AI companies . At public gatherings, like the recent Pro-Human Assembly in Washington, DC, and the People’s AI Assembly in New York City, people are piling on the pressure to rethink the AI race. States are drawing up their own legislation to rein in the tech . And a single X post from Calvin got so much attention that no less than Amodei himself felt compelled to respond . The AI companies are being forced to pay attention. Attention may not be all you need, but it’s a start. Anthropic眼下能做的一件事，就是让AI更安全——除非这家AI公司有证据证明其安全策略确实有效，否则现在就该退出竞赛。作者：西加尔·塞缪尔，2026年10月27日，上午10:32 UTC。礼物 Anthropic首席执行官达里奥·阿莫代伊说，他的AI公司可以推动一场“向上竞争”。证据何在？芬恩·戈麦斯/盖蒂图片社 西加尔·塞缪尔是Vox“未来完美”栏目的记者。她主要撰写关于意识未来的文章，追踪人工智能和神经科学领域的进展及其惊人的伦理影响。在加入Vox之前，西加尔是《大西洋月刊》的宗教编辑。我们正经历一个由AI助燃的“黑色十月”，事态变化飞快。黑客正利用AI入侵无数公司。AI工具发现了可能让70%的网站变得脆弱的安防漏洞。各国政府正手忙脚乱地加固自己的网站。银行也是如此。而且，由于网络黑客可能伤及供应链，一些长期关注AI的人正彻底变成末日准备者，囤积食品、现金等物资。这个故事的中心是Anthropic，全球领先的AI公司之一，它明确以这样的承诺创立：在一个充满可疑科技巨头的世界里，做一家“好人”公司。Anthropic说，所有最新进展都非常严重。其安全主管上周写道，情况“在好转之前会变得糟糕得多”。两周前，该公司警告说，AI模型可能很快在你家中联网的设备上自我复制，比如智能冰箱和机器人吸尘器。其联合创始人现在说，“奇点”——即AI系统以人类难以理解的方式加速技术进展——已经到来。邮箱（必填） 注册 提交你的邮箱，即表示你同意我们的条款和隐私声明。本网站受reCAPTCHA保护，并适用谷歌隐私政策和 terms of service。你可能会想，鉴于其对风险的看法，Anthropic应该会踩下刹车，放慢其前沿AI的进展。恰恰相反。Anthropic周一申请了重磅IPO，寻求2万亿美元估值，即便它在IPO文件中警告AI可能“对人类构成灾难性或生存性风险”。每一天，它都在奔向递归自我改进（RSI），即AI模型聪明到足以自行构建下一个更聪明的AI模型。Anthropic如何为此辩解？正如其首席执行官达里奥·阿莫代伊上周提醒世界的那样，他创建这家公司基于一个重大赌注：Anthropic实际上可以催化一场“向上竞争”，而不是推动一场“向下竞争”——在后者中，公司为了在市场上击败竞争对手而匆忙行事、在安全上偷工减料。在我观察Anthropic加码其“向上竞争”之际——

在讨论“p”策略时，我不由得不安地想起了另一个极其冒险的赌局：2022年萨姆·班克曼-弗里德的加密货币欺诈案。两者之间存在重要差异，并非完美的类比。但两者都涉及极少数人物，深受有效利他主义影响，代表许许多多其他人做出巨大赌注。EA文化以提供常识道德的替代方案而自豪。这个社群表现出愿意承担巨大风险并用复杂计算为其辩护的倾向。有时这确实奏效。但相信自己足够聪明，能够采取一种反直觉的、银河级大脑的策略并最终以此拯救世界，往往涉及某种傲慢。而在AI这样一个高风险领域，傲慢让我感到紧张。其理念是，如果Anthropic证明它能够构建既强大又安全的AI，市场就会同时期待这两者——于是其他AI公司也会感到有压力，在安全性上展开竞争。这在理论上听起来不错，但这意味着Anthropic必须不断构建越来越强大的AI。“如果实践这些力量的公司处于前沿，那么驱动‘向顶竞争’的力量就会有效得多，”阿莫代伊写道。“纵观这一策略的整体，我为我们的过往记录感到自豪，并坚持这一路线。”换句话说，阿莫代伊在坚持他的赌注。但根据阿莫代伊及其公司自己的说法，他是在拿人类的未来赌博。如果AI出问题，可能导致我们逐渐失去权力、权力令人恼怒地集中，甚至完全灭绝。因此，在这个关键时刻，公众理应得到一个好的答案，一个非常基本的问题：有什么证据表明Anthropic所宣称的策略——在前沿竞争以推动“向顶竞争”——整体上实际上是成功的？从外部来看，总体而言，Anthropic所做的更像是推动了一场“向底竞争”。（披露：Future Perfect部分由BEMC基金会资助，该基金会的主要资助者也是Anthropic的早期投资者；他们对我们的内容没有任何编辑输入。）事实上，部分问题可能在于Anthropic继续将此视为经典的军备竞赛。具体而言，该公司似乎将其建模为囚徒困境：如果Anthropic停止构建更强大的AI，另一个参与者——无论是中国、OpenAI还是其他公司——无论如何都会构建它。在这种困境中，如果另一方要背叛，你选择背叛是理性的，尽管没有人真正想要那种结果。但如果这种框架错过了重点呢？博弈论可以让一个巨大的赌注显得精密复杂，同时让显而易见的替代方案——就是不建造末日机器——显得天真。然而，Anthropic和其他公司现在正竞相迈向RSI，这使得情况更加

##段落
我们很可能失去对AI的控制，并开始看到我们的世界遭受大规模破坏。当背离安全的代价是你制造了灾难性伤害的严重风险——或者包括你自己在内的全人类灭绝的风险——这还能算是“理性”之举吗？与其告诉自己你可以用足够花哨的博弈论像银河级大脑一样想通这件事，也许你不如把它想成一件简单得多的事：俄罗斯轮盘赌。越来越多AI领域的领军声音开始认识到这一点。“我们现在就应该停止AI的进展，首先由Anthropic和/或OpenAI单方面停止——然后作为第二步扩大到更多AI公司并与中国谈判，”直到最近还担任英国AI安全研究所首席科学家的杰弗里·欧文告诉我。“单方面暂停无法持久，但它们是正确的第一步：当你在做一件非常危险的事情时，正确的行动就是停下来，即使别人也在做危险的事情。”Anthropic未回应置评请求。一场延续2000年的辩论揭示了AI最大的问题。让我们明确一点：问题不在于Anthropic在安全方面是否做过任何好事。它做过。挺身对抗五角大楼、暂时限制前沿模型的访问、公开倡导更安全的AI政策，这些只是其中几个例子。但真正的问题是，该公司的“向上竞赛”战略总体而言是否奏效——对安全而言是净负面还是净正面。AI安全倡导组织Encode的首席战略官内森·卡尔文最近在X上发文，在科技观察人士中引发了一场风暴：“当我审视Anthropic过去一年采取的许多值得注意的行动时，这些证据在我看来最一致的解读是，Anthropic主要是在试图赢得超级智能的竞赛，而其他考量（包括安全）从根本上说是次要的。”以下是他列出的Anthropic所做之事：而这一切都仅仅发生在过去一年里。如果我们把录像带倒回更早，会看到Anthropic曾抵制一项监管AI的里程碑式法案。再往前倒，我们会看到有迹象表明Anthropic的核心战略可能从一开始就有缺陷。据路透社报道，2022年底，OpenAI首席执行官萨姆·奥尔特曼听到传言称Anthropic正在构建一个AI驱动的聊天机器人。于是他命令员工抢先发布一个OpenAI聊天机器人。那个聊天机器人叫ChatGPT。后面的故事我们都知道了。OpenAI与Anthropic之间的竞争似乎不仅加速了生成式AI的到来，而且至今仍在不断把发布时间往前推。众所周知，这两家公司曾在数小时内相继发布新的或更便宜的模型，每一家都急于

##段落
为了保护其市场份额。即使你认为Anthropic在2022年的行为是合理的，因为公开演示AI的风险也同时证明了监管AI的必要性——这是公司内部以及整个AI讨论中常见的主张——你也必须问：在AI已经达到如此强大和复杂程度的今天，这种行为还站得住脚吗？Anthropic已表示其正越来越接近实现递归自我改进（RSI）。今年1月，阿莫代伊本人写道：“我担心大语言模型正在接近（或可能已经达到）端到端创建和释放[生物武器]所需的知识水平，且其毁灭潜力极高。某些生物制剂可能导致数百万人死亡。”他在9月还写道：“鉴于AI能力发展的加速趋势，我担心在6到12个月内，这样的集群就能凭借持久性僵尸网络接管整个互联网。”但到了这一步，阿莫代伊及其团队成员本身或许正是加速AI能力发展的主要推手。“除了OpenAI，Anthropic似乎在RSI这件事上比任何人都做得更多，”卡尔文告诉我。“鉴于他们公开表达的风险观点，我只是觉得这近乎疯狂。”“我认为Anthropic的人应该更认真地面对一个事实：最可能的结果是，Anthropic最大的影响将是急剧加速RSI的竞赛，”他继续说道。“按照当前轨迹，他们所做的一切、所思考的一切以及所抱有的理想，与他们在这一方面的贡献相比，都将只是一个舍入误差。”Anthropic应当愿意在这一点上接受审视——并且，如果它真相信自己正在让这个领域变得比原本更安全，那就拿出证据来。怎么做？它可以向国会提交一项真正加强而非削弱安全的法案。它可以坚守其此前的《负责任扩展政策》，并推动其他公司效仿，而不是抛弃自己的承诺。它可以影响其他实验室不去构建RSI，而不是带头冲锋。在缺乏此类证据的情况下，“向上竞争”的逻辑根本站不住脚。阿莫代伊已开始倡导为AI发展“设定前沿节奏”。“我们必须放慢提升AI模型能力的步伐，”他在9月写道。问题在于，阿莫代伊的放缓计划取决于其他人也同意放缓——首先是其他AI实验室，还包括其他国家。但越来越多的专家现在表示，像Anthropic这样的前沿公司单方面停止会更好。“我很高兴他提议我们应设定节奏，但问题是，现在我们必须真正去做——而看起来他是在说自己不会单方面去做。

“单方面行动，”曾是OpenAI研究员、后来成为知名举报者的丹尼尔·科科塔伊洛对我说，“这不太有帮助，达里奥！你应该带头。如果你只是在等待，那‘竞相向上’和‘以身作则’这些说法又有什么意义？”个别公司的自愿单边行动当然不能替代联邦监管和国际条约。但欧文认为，这是正确的第一步，因为如果公司等待政府来约束它们，可能就太晚了。政府以行动缓慢著称。个别公司今天就可以行动。这里有一个常被提出的反对意见：“那中国呢？”然而，认为我们与中国处于经典军备竞赛中的想法一直是有缺陷的。首先，人工智能不像原子弹那样只是具有单一用途的单一事物。它是一种通用性 much 更强的技术，就像电力一样。所以重要的不仅仅是谁先获得它，而是谁以何种方式使用它。此外，如果人工智能的危害是巨大的，那么这些危害对另一方也同样相关。中国人也不想看到全人类文明遭受灾难性伤害。所以我们不应该排除协调的可能性。前Vox记者凯尔西·派珀最近写到Anthropic的一次研讨会，其中一位参与者提出异议：十年前，Facebook曾考虑收购后来为TikTok提供动力的技术。但由于隐私和安全担忧面临压力，该公司放弃了。这最终并没有保护我们免受TikTok世界的祸害——它只是把这项技术的早期垄断权拱手让给了中国。派珀写道：这是政策成功吗？我们想重蹈覆辙吗？我们不得不勉强承认，这听起来不像是政策成功。我们不想重蹈覆辙。中国可能不是美国实验室做鲁莽事情的借口，但它是一个真实的考量。那么我们的下一步可能是与中国进行双边会谈。但当你同意Anthropic的计划可能取决于与中国的双边会谈时，你已经接受了Anthropic世界观的大部分步骤，而这些步骤在10分钟前看起来还像是疯狂之举：目前继续研究人工智能，尝试谈判放缓，但不要放弃前沿工作及其带来的所有优势。但TikTok并不是递归自我改进的好类比。前者可能是一个腐蚀我们大脑、放大种族仇恨的污水池，但其危险无法与递归自我改进的危险相比。TikTok案例可能确实最好作为经典的囚徒困境来处理。但对于递归自我改进，潜在的下行风险是如此灾难性，以至于任何提议通过构建危及世界的技术来拯救世界的人，都是在代表所有其他人进行一场巨大的赌博。至少，举证责任应该在他们身上。

##段落
以证明他们的信心是有根据的。AI圈内人常常认为，行业外的人不可能理解他们面临的技术、地缘政治和道德层面的复杂性。但常识道德之所以是常识，是有原因的：它追踪的直觉通常是对的（比如，如果你不想要一个末日机器，也许就别造末日机器），并训练我们对那些与之相反的、巨大且反直觉的赌注保持适当的怀疑。恰恰因为AI格局是一个复杂系统——参与者如此之多（包括不同的AI公司和不同的政府），每一方的行动都可能以难以预测的方式触发其他方的行动——相信自己足够聪明，能够采取高度反直觉的行动并最终拯救世界，是一种极其冒险的赌注。相反，也许最好的做法就是做直截了当正确的事：停下来。硅谷对AI的愿景？那是宗教，换了层包装而已。需要明确的是，“停下来”并不一定意味着撤销迄今为止在AI领域所做的一切。已经存在的强大AI系统无法被收回盒中。而且我们可能需要一些AI来防御已经存在于世的AI。“我不是说关掉你所有的数据中心，”卡尔文说，“但我是说，特别是，在递归自我改进（RSI）上推进前沿，让自己成为世界上比任何人都更多地进行完全自主开发的公司，这到底他妈的有意义吗？”越来越多的AI圈内人和公众都在大声说“不”。一些圈内人——也许意识到人类完全有能力叫停过于危险的技术开发（我们以前就这么做过）——正在公开发声并从AI公司辞职。在公众集会上，比如最近在华盛顿特区举行的“亲人类大会”和在纽约市举行的“人民AI大会”，人们正在施加压力，要求重新思考AI竞赛。各州正在起草自己的立法来约束这项技术。而卡尔文的一条X帖子引发了极大关注，以至于阿莫代伊本人都觉得不得不做出回应。AI公司正被迫予以关注。关注可能不是你所需要的一切，但它是一个开始。查看更多：人工智能 未来完美 创新 科技 用最新的Vox填字游戏让大脑休息一下 极右翼刚刚输了。两次。最高法院准备让纳税人资助反LGBTQ歧视 特朗普在密歇根州的恶毒收官信息 Z世代对特朗普产生了买家懊悔 邮箱（必填） 注册 提交你的邮箱即表示你同意我们的条款和隐私声明。本网站受reCAPTCHA和谷歌隐私政策及服务条款保护。广告商内容来自 这是……的标题

readings.title: 6 ways to give that aren’t about money
body: Good news: You can be a generous person without writing a bunch of checks. In fact, many of the most awe-inspiring and effective examples of generosity are gifts of time and energy, talent and love, custom-fitted to a specific need. This type of giving is open to everyone.
Many of the most awe-inspiring and effective examples of generosity are gifts of time and energy, talent and love, custom-fitted to a specific need.

Not sure where to begin? Here are six gifts of time and attention that have the strong potential to spark ripple effects that affect millions, from head of TED Chris Anderson’s new book, Infectious Generosity .

Zen master Thich Nhat Hanh taught that attention is the most precious gift we can give someone. This is where generosity starts — with a willingness to stop focusing on ourselves and to instead pay attention to someone else and their needs. From that act of connection, anything can happen.

Truth is, it can be difficult. We spend much of our time lost in our own worlds. We are often reluctant to focus on the issues that others are dealing with. So we put up shields. And that means that many of the people who could really use our attention never feel seen by us. The generosity of attention is therefore the generosity of being willing to be a little uncomfortable, to take down those shields, to give up some time, to risk coming to care about someone else.
Whether you stop and have a meaningful connection with a person in need or spend 30 minutes researching a cause you think might matter, you have already begun your generosity journey.

In our connected era, there’s a type of generosity that matters more than ever: a willingness to reach out to those with whom we disagree with. Many disputes today play out in public online. Huge audiences can become glued to online feuds. What if we could bring a satisfying resolution to more of these conflicts?

It’s hard to reach out to our critics. This is a particularly challenging form of the generosity mindset. You are sacrificing your personal comfort for the greater good of bringing people together. But if you’re successful, there’s a powerful knock-on benefit: You are helping change the tone of public discussion today. That’s a gift to all of us.
The single greatest gift we can give is knowledge — knowledge that solves a problem, fills a need or opens a pathway forward.
In countless circumstances, the single greatest gift we can give is knowledge — knowledge that solves a problem, fills a need or opens a pathway forward.

Our single biggest piece of advice to someone coming to speak on the TED stage is to think of their talk not as an opportunity to pitch something (like a business or a cause) but rather as a gift. It is a chance to freely share valuable ideas with the audience. And those ideas have the potential to impact a listener’s life for years to come.

If you possess knowledge that others may benefit from, consider how you could share it to create ripple effects. What may take you a few hours to prepare and act on could light up someone’s life — and that could just be the beginning.

In our connected age, the networks we have access to matter more than ever. Therefore, one of the most important forms of viral generosity is to help people connect with others. The simplest way to do this is to make an introduction.

As psychologist and TED speaker Adam Grant has argued, an introduction can be fairly easy to give — and unbelievably valuable to receive. Ask many people how they met their partner, got their dream job or found the perfect collaborator for their creative project, and the answer will often be the same: someone — a friend, a neighbor, a colleague — introduced them to the right person. What you’re effectively doing is giving someone else access to your network of resources. And those introductions can have exponential consequences.

In his remarkable book Human Universals , anthropologist Donald Brown documented how hospitality is one of hundreds of human behaviors that have been observed in every single culture ever studied. But if hospitality is so ubiquitous (and so pleasant), is it really a form of generosity? Well, yes. Quite apart from any costs involved, it takes effort to invite someone over, whether friends or possible future friends. It’s easier just to watch the next episode of the TV series you’re into.
So how can hospitality contribute to infectious generosity? Hospitality taps into our deepest instincts for connection to one another. And each experience of it evokes a desire to reciprocate.
People need money, food, shelter and healthcare, to be sure. But we also yearn for beauty, wonder, laughter, transcendence — all elements of enchantment.

Pioneering artist Lily Yeh was approached by the dancer and choreographer Arthur L. Hall to undertake a community art project in a derelict, abandoned plot in her home city of Philadelphia. “I was interested but totally scared,” Yeh recalled. “I had little resources and no experience in working outdoors in a community setting. I wanted to run away, but I did not want to see a coward in the mirror. So I stepped into the project.”

The community project became the Village of Arts and Humanities, an art park full of trees, sculptures and mosaics created by local adults and children in collaboration with Yeh. Yeh’s work led her to a profound realization: that creating beauty in public spaces is profoundly healing and transformative for communities.

People need money, food, shelter and healthcare, to be sure. But we also yearn for beauty, wonder, laughter, transcendence — all elements of enchantment. Those who can enchant can offer a gift of immense value.

好消息：你不必开一堆支票也能成为一个慷慨的人。事实上，许多最令人惊叹、最有效的慷慨范例，都是时间与精力、才华与爱心的馈赠，是为特定需求量身定制的。这种付出对每个人都是敞开的。
##段落
许多最令人惊叹、最有效的慷慨范例，都是时间与精力、才华与爱心的馈赠，是为特定需求量身定制的。
##段落
不知道从哪里开始？以下是六种时间与关注的馈赠，它们极有可能引发波及数百万人的涟漪效应，出自TED负责人克里斯·安德森的新书《传染性慷慨》。
##段落
1. 转移注意力
禅宗大师一行禅师教导说，注意力是我们能给予他人最珍贵的礼物。慷慨正是从这里开始——愿意停止关注自己，转而关注他人及其需求。从这一联结的行为出发，一切皆有可能。
##段落
事实是，这并不容易。我们把大量时间耗费在自己的世界里。我们常常不愿去关注他人正在面对的问题。于是我们竖起盾牌。而这意味着，许多真正需要你关注的人，从未感到被我们看见。因此，注意力的慷慨，就是愿意让自己稍微不舒服、放下那些盾牌、付出一些时间、冒险去关心他人的慷慨。
##段落
无论你是停下来与一个有需要的人建立有意义的联结，还是花30分钟研究一个你认为可能重要的议题，你都已经踏上了自己的慷慨之旅。
##段落
2. 搭建桥梁
在我们这个互联的时代，有一种慷慨比以往任何时候都更重要：愿意主动接触那些与我们意见相左的人。如今许多争端都在网上公开上演。庞大的受众会紧盯着网络骂战。如果我们能为更多这类冲突带来令人满意的化解，会怎样？
##段落
主动接触批评我们的人很难。这是一种尤其具有挑战性的慷慨心态。你是在牺牲个人的舒适，换取把人们聚在一起的更大善果。但如果你成功了，就会有一个强大的连锁好处：你在帮助改变当今公共讨论的基调。那是给我们所有人的礼物。
##段落
我们能给予的唯一最大礼物是知识——解决问题的知识、满足需求的知识，或开辟前路的知识。
##段落
3. 分享知识
在无数情形下，我们能给予的唯一最大礼物是知识——解决问题的知识、满足需求的知识，或开辟前路的知识。
##段落
我们对某人最重要的建议

##段落
站上TED舞台演讲，意味着演讲者不应将其视为推销某样东西（比如一项业务或一个事业）的机会，而是把它当作一份礼物。这是一个自由地与观众分享宝贵想法的机会。而这些想法有可能在未来数年里持续影响听众的生活。

##段落
如果你拥有能让他人受益的知识，想一想你可以如何分享它，从而产生涟漪效应。你花几个小时准备和行动的事情，或许能点亮某人的生活——而这可能仅仅是个开始。

##段落
4. 促成连接

在这个互联的时代，我们能够触及的人脉网络比以往任何时候都更加重要。因此，最具感染力的慷慨行为之一，就是帮助人们与他人建立连接。最简单的方式就是做一次引荐。

##段落
正如心理学家、TED演讲者亚当·格兰特所言，引荐这件事给出时相当容易——收到时却价值不可估量。问问许多人他们是如何遇见伴侣、获得梦想工作、或为创意项目找到完美合作者的，答案往往如出一辙：某个人——一位朋友、邻居、同事——把他们介绍给了对的人。你实际上在做的是，让别人得以接入你的人脉资源网络。而这些引荐可能产生指数级的连锁效应。

##段落
5. 延伸款待

人类学家唐纳德·布朗在其杰出著作《人类共性》中记载，款待行为是被研究过的每一种文化中都观察到的数百种人类行为之一。但既然款待如此普遍（又如此令人愉悦），它还算是慷慨的一种形式吗？答案是肯定的。撇开任何花费不谈，邀请某人来家里——无论是朋友还是可能成为朋友的人——本身就需要付出心力。只管看你正在追的那部剧的下一集，显然要轻松得多。

##段落
那么，款待如何能促成有感染力的慷慨？款待触动了我们内心深处对彼此连接的本能渴望。而每一次被款待的体验，都会唤起一种想要回报的愿望。

##段落
人们固然需要金钱、食物、住所和医疗保健。但我们也渴望美、惊奇、欢笑、超越——这些都是魅力的要素。

##段落
6. 创造魅力

先驱艺术家莉莉·叶受邀于舞者兼编舞家亚瑟·L·霍尔，在她家乡费城一块荒废废弃的地块上开展一个社区艺术项目。“我很感兴趣，但完全吓坏了，”叶回忆道。“我资源匮乏，也没有在社区环境中户外工作的经验。我想逃跑，但我不想在镜子里看到一个懦夫。于是我踏入了这个项目。”

##段落
这个社区项目后来成为了“艺术与人文村”，一座满是树木、雕塑和马赛克的艺术公园，全部由当地成年人创作。

##段落
她与Yeh合作，为老年人和儿童创作。Yeh的工作让她深刻意识到：在公共空间创造美，对社区具有深远的疗愈与转化力量。
##段落
人们当然需要金钱、食物、住所和医疗。但我们也渴望美、惊奇、欢笑与超越——这些都是“魅力”的要素。能够赋予魅力的人，赠予的是一份无价之礼。
##段落

readings.title: How we can exercise more without even trying
body: 10 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Melissa Hogenboom Incidental activity can reduce our risk of cardiovascular disease and even death. You can try some simple forms of it in a meeting, on a flight or while reading this article. It can be easy to spend an entire day sitting. First at your desk at work, then perhaps in your car, followed by a couple of hours on the sofa. Before you know it, you're having dinner and realise you haven't exercised all day. Many global studies have found that a sedentary lifestyle can increase the risk of serious health conditions . Everything we can do to decrease sedentary time therefore benefits our overall health. But it can be challenging to find the time. That's where incidental exercise comes in. This is the moving around we do outside of deliberate exercise. It's also known as "non-exercise activity thermogenesis", or NEAT. This refers to any energy we use for movement that isn't sleeping, eating or deliberate exercise, says Anantha Narayanan, a research fellow at the Auckland University of Technology in New Zealand. Incidental exercise can be as simple as tapping your leg when you are sitting down or doing the washing up. "Smaller movements like shifting posture, rolling the shoulders or flexing the feet count too," says Narayanan. Incidental exercise is emerging as a surprisingly powerful tool for protecting our health, helping us to burn more calories, reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease, and even lower our risk of death.   Once we're aware of this "incidental activity", we can build more of it into our everyday routine with a few simple lifestyle tweaks. Here are some you might want to try. Take, for instance, leg fidgeting. Growing up, we're encouraged not to fidget, which is seen as a sign of boredom and not paying attention. There are many reasons to ignore this advice.  During prolonged periods of sitting, muscles in our legs are relatively inactive. This reduces the regular muscle contractions that help to clear glucose from the bloodstream and support healthy blood circulation, says Narayanan. But fidgeting increases muscle activity and therefore helps us to burn more calories compared with when we are sitting still, a recent study has found. "Some earlier research suggests that leg fidgeting may help maintain blood vessel function and improve blood sugar control," says Narayanan. Standing as you do this may enhance these benefits. (Read more from the BBC about when you do and don't need to worry about blood sugar spikes .) Similarly, a small study found that habitual leg shaking , a form of fidgeting, burns about 16% more energy compared with sitting still. The researchers found that higher levels of incidental activity could offset the health risks associated with sitting for more than 11 hours a day Unlike structured activity, incidental movement does not require a gym membership or for us to carve out specific time to move. We often forget that everyday household activities can decrease sedentary time. Cooking, gardening and vacuuming are also forms of incidental exercise. We don't need to spend hours moving to gain health benefits. Just four minutes per day of brief, incidental bursts of activity that last less than a minute can help to offset the increased risk of cardiovascular diseases from sedentary time, a large 2024 study found . In the study, researchers analysed data from over 22,000 UK participants wearing a tracking device which captured how much they moved throughout the day. The sample was limited to individuals who did not regularly take part in purposeful exercise. The participants were followed for eight years. The researchers found that higher levels of incidental activity could offset the health risks associated with sitting for more than 11 hours a day. Follow-up research has found that incidental activity is also linked to a lower risk of premature death . Nicholas Koemel, senior research fellow at Monash University in Australia, who led the research, says the type of activities we could include are climbing flights of stairs, carrying heavy shopping bags or playing with children. By paying attention to opportunities that help us increase our movement throughout the day, people may be able to increase the intensity of these activities, says Koemel. This could include walking faster than your normal pace to get to your destination or parking further away when going to the shops. While you're there, consider using a basket instead of a trolley. Before you realise it, you may well have strengthened your muscles by carrying a few kilos of shopping around. Large fitness goals can feel overwhelming, so another strategy to introduce movement throughout the day could involve "piggybacking" on activities you are already doing, says Amanda Daley, professor of behavioural medicine at Loughborough University in the UK. This simply involves adding some movement to an activity you are already doing. You could try doing a calf raise while brushing your teeth, a leg raise under your desk, or going for a walk while on a call instead of sitting down. Daley says that in her household there's a rule that any packages ordered online must be delivered to a nearby locker instead of to her house. "If we want something we have to pick it up. This can also be a great way to get teenagers out of their rooms to get some walking into their day." We can build new habits into the working day too. In one study, Daley and colleagues provided doctors with standing desks. This helped them reduce the time they would otherwise have been sitting by about two hours per day. This also encouraged more conversations with their patients about the benefits of reducing sedentary time, the team found. More like this: • Five minutes of exercise a day could help millions of people live longer • Three enjoyable ways to slow your brain's ageing • What I learned when I gave up sugar for six weeks "Incidental activity can also be a time-efficient way to be physically active because you don't always need to put a lot of time aside." says Daley. "It's important to find approaches that are less daunting and feel more manageable to achieve." Best of all, the more incidental activity you do throughout the day, the more purposeful it can become over time. This could be motivating, says Koemel. "When something becomes ingrained in your lifestyle, incidentally, it has inherently become your lifestyle." With that in mind, I'm going to start unashamedly tapping my legs during meetings. I might get some funny looks, but I'll know that I'm benefitting my health.  * Melissa Hogenboom is a senior health correspondent at the BBC. She is melissa_hogenboom on Instagram.  -- For trusted insights on health and wellbeing, sign up to the Health Fix newsletter by senior health correspondent Melissa Hogenboom who also writes the Live Well For Longer and Six Steps to Calm courses.  For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on Facebook and Instagram . ##段落
10小时前 分享 保存 添加为Google首选 梅丽莎·霍根布姆 偶然活动可以降低我们患心血管疾病甚至死亡的风险。你可以在开会时、在飞机上或阅读本文时尝试一些简单的形式。很容易一整天都坐着。先是在工作的办公桌前，然后也许在车里，接着在沙发上待上几个小时。不知不觉中，你正在吃晚饭，才意识到自己一整天都没有锻炼。许多全球研究发现，久坐不动的生活方式会增加严重健康问题的风险。因此，我们能为减少久坐时间所做的一切都有益于我们的整体健康。但找到时间可能很有挑战性。这就是偶然运动的用武之地。这是我们在刻意锻炼之外所做的活动。它也被称为“非运动性活动产热”，简称NEAT。新西兰奥克兰理工大学研究员阿南塔·纳拉扬说，这指的是我们用于运动的任何能量，不包括睡眠、进食或刻意锻炼。偶然运动可以简单到坐着时抖腿或洗碗。“像变换姿势、转动肩膀或绷脚这样的小动作也算，”纳拉扬说。偶然运动正逐渐成为一种出人意料地强大的保护健康的工具，帮助我们燃烧更多卡路里、降低心血管疾病风险，甚至降低死亡风险。

##段落
一旦我们意识到这种“偶然活动”，我们就可以通过一些简单的生活方式调整，将更多此类活动融入日常。以下是一些你可以尝试的方法。以抖腿为例。从小到大，我们被教导不要坐立不安，因为这被视为无聊和不专心的表现。有很多理由可以忽略这个建议。纳拉扬说，在长时间坐着期间，腿部肌肉相对不活跃。这会减少有助于清除血液中葡萄糖和维持健康血液循环的规律肌肉收缩。但最近一项研究发现，与静止坐着相比，抖腿能增加肌肉活动，从而帮助我们燃烧更多卡路里。“一些早期研究表明，抖腿可能有助于维持血管功能和改善血糖控制，”纳拉扬说。在做这个动作时站立可能会增强这些益处。（阅读更多BBC关于何时需要以及何时不需要担心血糖飙升的内容。）同样，一项小型研究发现，习惯性抖腿——一种坐立不安的形式——比静止坐着多燃烧约16%的能量。研究人员发现，更高水平的偶然活动可以抵消与久坐超过

##段落
每天超过11小时。与结构化活动不同，偶然性运动不需要健身房会员资格，也不需要我们专门腾出时间来活动。我们常常忘记，日常家务活动也能减少久坐时间。做饭、园艺和吸尘也是偶然性运动的形式。我们不需要花几个小时运动才能获得健康益处。2024年一项大型研究发现，每天只需四分钟、每次持续不到一分钟的短暂偶然性活动爆发，就有助于抵消久坐时间带来的心血管疾病风险增加。在这项研究中，研究人员分析了超过22,000名英国参与者的数据，这些参与者佩戴了追踪设备，记录了他们一天中活动的量。样本仅限于不经常参加有目的性锻炼的人群。参与者被随访了八年。研究人员发现，较高水平的偶然性活动可以抵消每天坐着超过11小时所带来的健康风险。后续研究发现，偶然性活动还与较低的过早死亡风险相关。领导这项研究的澳大利亚莫纳什大学高级研究员尼古拉斯·科梅尔表示，我们可以纳入的活动类型包括爬楼梯、提沉重的购物袋或与孩子玩耍。科梅尔说，通过留意那些有助于我们在一天中增加运动量的机会，人们或许能够提高这些活动的强度。这可能包括以比平时更快的步伐走向目的地，或者去商店时把车停得更远。到了那里，考虑使用购物篮而不是购物车。不知不觉中，你可能已经通过提着几公斤购物袋走来走去而锻炼了肌肉。宏大的健身目标可能让人感到不堪重负，因此，另一种在一天中引入运动的方法可以是“搭便车”式地依附于你已经在做的活动，英国拉夫堡大学行为医学教授阿曼达·戴利说。这 simply 意味着在你已经在做的活动中加入一些运动。你可以尝试在刷牙时做提踵，在办公桌下做抬腿，或者打电话时去散步而不是坐着。戴利说，在她家里有一条规矩：任何网上订购的包裹都必须送到附近的储物柜，而不是送到她家。“如果我们想要什么东西，就必须自己去取。这也是让青少年走出房间、在日常中增加步行的好方法。”我们也可以把新习惯融入工作日。在一项研究中，戴利和同事为医生提供了站立式办公桌。这帮助他们减少了原本会坐着的时间。

##段落
每天大约两小时。研究团队还发现，这也促进了他们与患者之间关于减少久坐时间益处的更多交流。更多类似内容：• 每天锻炼五分钟可能帮助数百万人活得更久 • 三种令人愉快的方法延缓大脑衰老 • 我戒糖六周的体会 “顺便活动也是一种省时的身体活动方式，因为你不必总是专门腾出大量时间。”戴利说。“找到不那么令人生畏、感觉更容易实现的方法很重要。”最重要的是，你一天中进行的顺便活动越多，随着时间推移，它就越能变得有目的性。科梅尔说，这可以成为一种动力。“当某件事不知不觉地融入你的生活方式时，它本质上就已经成为你的生活方式。”想到这一点，我打算开始在开会时毫不掩饰地抖腿。我可能会招来一些奇怪的目光，但我知道这对我的健康有好处。* 梅丽莎·霍根布姆是BBC资深健康记者。她的Instagram账号是melissa_hogenboom。-- 如需值得信赖的健康与福祉洞察，请订阅资深健康记者梅丽莎·霍根布姆主笔的Health Fix新闻简报，她还撰写了Live Well For Longer和Six Steps to Calm课程。如需更多来自BBC的科学、技术、环境与健康报道，请在Facebook和Instagram上关注我们。健康 锻炼 长寿 专题

readings.title: Why are more Americans moving to Ireland?
body: 15 April 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Anne Cassidy In a historic reversal, the number of Americans moving to Ireland last year was higher than the number of Irish people migrating to the US. Was this just a blip or the start of a more profound trend? Michael Sable is an American stand-up comedian and communications manager who moved from Washington DC to Dublin in 2016.  Sable, who draws on his experience of being an American living in the Republic of Ireland in his stand-up routine, says that, when he first arrived, many Irish people he met were surprised he'd made the move, but now they don't question it.  "I've noticed that, as the years go on, people have been less and less incredulous when hearing that an American moved to Ireland," he says.  Sable is one of a rising number of people who have moved to Ireland from the US, with the latest data showing the figure nearly doubling from  4,900 to 9,600 between 2024 and 2025 ,  exceeding the number of Irish people headed in the opposite direction.   It comes as the US saw more people leave than arrive last year, according to a report from US think tank the  Brookings Institution . It said this was the first time that this had been the case "in at least half a century".  The think tank highlighted "dramatic changes in immigration policy" under the second administration of President Trump, including more removals of undocumented foreign workers, and the White House "all but suspend[ing]" the US programme for accepting refugees.    Separately, more American citizens are choosing to move abroad than ever before, says the  Wall Street Journal.  It calculated that "at least 180,000 Americans" voluntarily left the US in 2025, which it said was a record high.   The reversal in the flow of migration between Ireland and the US marks a historic turning point in the shared history of the two countries, which have deep-rooted ties.  For centuries, millions of Irish people emigrated to the US in search of work or a better life, making Irish Americans one of the country's largest ethnic groups. There have been several US presidents with Irish ancestry, including John F Kennedy and Joe Biden, whose visits to Ireland were  celebrated more like homecomings  than diplomatic missions.   Irish writer Colm Tóibín has frequently explored the relationship between Ireland and the US in his work, particularly in his novels, Brooklyn and Long Island, which follow the story of an Irish girl who emigrates to America in the 1950s.  Tóibín, who lives in the US, says the relationship between the US and Ireland has changed. "A myth was created that America was a great place of opportunity and wealth," he says. "It was built into the [Irish] culture that if there's any trouble, you go to England, if there's any ambition or spark you go to America." "The flow of young people [from Ireland to the US] looking for work just hasn't continued. So, that is going to be a big change in the future, because you're not going to get the same easy connection between Ireland and America," he adds.  The trend partly reflects political shifts in both countries. As well as developing into a high-tech, export-driven knowledge economy, Ireland has undergone a social transformation in recent decades, moving from a deeply conservative society to a liberal, progressive nation, following referendums on divorce, abortion and gay marriage.    Tóibín, who was a prominent campaigner for the "yes" vote in Ireland’s same-sex marriage referendum, says: "Everyone became more aware that Ireland was a more liberal, cosmopolitan, open society, and that it would be a good place to live." By contrast, the US has moved to the political right under President Trump, who, since returning to office, has launched a major crackdown on illegal immigration.   Tóibín revisits the Irish-American immigrant experience in his latest short story collection, The News from Dublin. In one story in the collection, Five Bridges, the protagonist is an undocumented Irish immigrant preparing to leave America before US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, known as Ice, come looking for him. The number of Irish citizens deported from the US  rose by more than 50%  in 2025.  "There are large numbers of Irish people in America who are official in every way – they pay taxes, own their own house, have kids in school, but they came in on a tourist visa," says Tóibín. "If Ice found them, Ice would detain them. That's really frightening." Expatsi, a firm that helps US citizens to move abroad,  reported it experienced a month's worth of traffic  in the hours after President Trump's election in 2024. Expatsi co-founder Jen Barnett says the reasons Americans cite for leaving are wide-ranging. "[Factors include] what's going on politically in the US, and has been for 10 years, the cost of living, and then safety. Gun violence is so prevalent," she says.  Politics was also a driving factor for Kevin Wozniak, an American lecturer living in Ireland. He and his husband left Boston in 2023 after he got a post at Maynooth University, 23km (14 miles) west of Dublin.  "My motivation to look at opportunities abroad was deep fears about the trajectory of the country in the era of Donald Trump," Wozniak says. "Ireland has liberalised very significantly and has moved in exactly the opposite direction that the US is moving." Natalia Lange, a migrant support worker based in Crosshaven, county Cork, moved there from Michigan with her husband after the 2024 US election. Lange, who is half-Hungarian and has an EU passport, dreamed of living in Ireland since visiting on a school trip. "Politically, Ireland aligns much more with how we think," she says. "The US has the infrastructure to take in a lot more people, but it's a lot less inviting." Lauren Udoh, from Houston, Texas, moved to Claregalway, in county Galway, in 2021 after marrying her Irish husband. Udoh, who has two young children, works as an executive assistant and documents expat life on social media under the moniker TheGalwayGal.  "One of the biggest benefits is safety. I feel a lot safer here," she says. "With kids going to school, you don’t have to worry about school shootings." Emigration from Ireland has fallen, with 65,600 people leaving in the year to April 2025, a  6% decrease on 2024 , according to the Irish Central Statistics Office (CSO). For those wanting to live abroad, Australia is the most popular destination.  The CSO said 13,500 people left Ireland for Australia in the year to April 2025, the highest level since 2013. This is more than double the estimated 6,100 people who left Ireland for the US, which was, however, still up 22% on the previous year.   Restrictions around J1 visas, which allow Irish university students to work and travel in the US, has caused many  Irish students to rethink studying in the US.    Karen McHugh, CEO at Safe Home Ireland, an organisation supporting Irish-born emigrants wishing to return to Ireland, says: "We've certainly noticed an increase in queries about returning [from the US to Ireland]," she says. "Australia and Canada are two major countries where people are now going to from Ireland, and that's ease of getting a visa." Irish student Jamie McElhinney is currently on a work placement in Portugal as part of his hospitality management course. McElhinney, who studies at Dundalk Institute of Technology, says current immigration controls put him off seeking a work placement in the US. "I was going to go to Boston, and then all of the news about Ice started coming out. It’s a deterrent from going over there," he says.  While there are opportunities in Ireland, with  employment at 74.4%,  there is also a growing housing crisis, with recent  protests  over the shortage of affordable housing.  Barnett says the housing shortage is something the Americans her company helps to relocate are mindful of, adding: "They don't want to add to [the housing crisis], so one of the things we talk to them about is staying out of city centres." Sable, whose Irish grandparents emigrated to the US in 1939, is one of many Americans whose ancestry enabled them to get an Irish passport. Applications for Irish passports in the US rose by 10% in 2024 , the Irish Department of Foreign Affairs reported.  Sable now thinks of Ireland as home. "Culturally, I identify a lot more with Irish people," he says. "It's a very collective society, not huge on individualism like in the US." More like this:  •  Why Ireland's film industry is booming    •  Is New York's cannabis business flying high?   •  The 'brutal' toll of war on Dubai’s tourist trade Bill Hillyard, another American with Irish roots, relocated to Ireland for the cooler climate. He and his wife Anne left California following wildfires in 2019. "My wife said we need to move somewhere where it rains." They now run a pub called The Algiers in Baltimore, Co Cork.  Hillyard says he now tries to avoid turbulent events in the US. "I tried not to follow the news because I'm here now," he says. "But I'm reminded every day, because everyone asks me about Trump and what's going on there… I'm West Cork's ambassador to the US at this point." -- For global insights and expert analysis for the boardroom and beyond, sign up to the  World of Business newsletter , while  The Essential List  delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights. ##段落
2026年4月15日 分享 收藏 在Google上设为首选 安妮·卡西迪 在一次历史性的逆转中，去年移居爱尔兰的美国人数量超过了移居美国的爱尔兰人数量。这只是一时的反常现象，还是一个更深刻趋势的开端？迈克尔·塞布尔是一位美国单口喜剧演员兼传播经理，2016年从华盛顿特区搬到都柏林。塞布尔在脱口秀中融入自己作为生活在爱尔兰共和国的美国人的经历。他说，初到之时，许多他遇到的爱尔兰人都对他做出这一决定感到惊讶，但如今他们已不再质疑。“我注意到，随着时间推移，人们听到美国人移居爱尔兰时越来越不觉得难以置信了，”他说。塞布尔是从美国移居爱尔兰的人数不断上升的一个缩影，最新数据显示，这一数字在2024年至2025年间从4900人几乎翻倍至9600人，超过了反向前往美国的爱尔兰人数量。

##段落
与此同时，根据美国智库布鲁金斯学会的一份报告，去年离开美国的人数多于流入美国的人数。报告称，这是“至少半个世纪以来”首次出现这种情况。该智库强调了特朗普总统第二任期内“移民政策的剧烈变化”，包括加大驱逐无证外籍劳工的力度，以及白宫“几乎暂停”了美国接收难民的计划。另据《华尔街日报》报道，越来越多的美国公民选择移居海外。该报测算，“至少18万美国人”在2025年自愿离开了美国，称这是历史新高。

##段落
爱尔兰与美国之间移民流向的逆转，标志着这两个有着深厚渊源的国家共同历史上的一个历史性转折点。几个世纪以来，数百万爱尔兰人移居美国寻求工作或更好的生活，使爱尔兰裔美国人成为美国最大的族裔群体之一。美国有多位总统具有爱尔兰血统，包括约翰·F·肯尼迪和乔·拜登，他们对爱尔兰的访问被当作归乡而非外交使命来庆祝。爱尔兰作家科尔姆·托宾在其作品中频繁探讨爱尔兰与美国的关系，尤其是在他的小说《布鲁克林》和《长岛》中，讲述了一位爱尔兰女孩在20世纪50年代移居美国的故事。现居美国的托宾表示，美国与爱尔兰之间的关系已经改变。“人们创造了一个神话，认为美国是一个充满机遇和财富的伟大地方，”他说。“这已融入[爱尔兰]文化之中——如果有麻烦，就去英国；如果有野心

##段落
“否则你就去美国。”他补充道：“年轻人（从爱尔兰到美国）找工作的潮流并没有延续下去。因此，这将是未来的一个重大变化，因为爱尔兰和美国之间那种轻而易举的联系将不复存在。”

##段落
这一趋势部分反映了两国政治格局的转变。爱尔兰不仅发展成为一个高科技、出口导向的知识经济体，近几十年来还经历了社会转型——在离婚、堕胎和同性婚姻公投之后，从一个极度保守的社会转变为一个自由、进步的国家。

##段落
托宾曾是爱尔兰同性婚姻公投中“赞成”票的著名推动者，他说：“每个人都越来越意识到，爱尔兰是一个更自由、更国际化、更开放的社会，是一个宜居的好地方。”相比之下，美国在特朗普总统的领导下转向了政治右翼，特朗普自重返白宫以来，已对非法移民展开了大规模打击。

##段落
托宾在其最新短篇小说集《都柏林消息》中重新审视了爱尔兰裔美国移民的经历。其中一篇名为《五座桥》的故事中，主人公是一名无证爱尔兰移民，在美国移民和海关执法局（ICE）来找他之前准备离开美国。2025年，被美国驱逐出境的爱尔兰公民人数上升了50%以上。

##段落
“美国有大量爱尔兰人在各方面都是合法的——他们纳税、拥有自己的房子、孩子在上学，但他们是持旅游签证入境的，”托宾说，“如果ICE找到他们，ICE就会拘留他们。这真的很可怕。”

##段落
Expatsi是一家帮助美国公民移居海外的公司，据其报告，2024年特朗普当选后的几小时内，其网站流量相当于平时一个月的总量。Expatsi联合创始人珍·巴内特表示，美国人给出的离开理由多种多样。“（因素包括）美国政治正在发生的变化——而且这种变化已经持续了10年——生活成本，还有安全。枪支暴力太普遍了，”她说。

##段落
政治也是凯文·沃兹尼亚克的驱动因素，他是一位居住在爱尔兰的美国讲师。2023年，他在都柏林以西23公里（14英里）的梅努斯大学获得职位后，与丈夫离开了波士顿。

##段落
“我寻找海外机会的动机是对唐纳德·特朗普时代美国发展轨迹的深切担忧，”沃兹尼亚克说，“爱尔兰已经非常显著地自由化了，其发展方向与美国恰恰相反。”娜塔莉亚·兰格是科克郡克罗斯黑文的一名移民支持工作者，在2024年美国大选后与丈夫从密歇根搬到了那里。兰格有一半匈牙利血统，持有欧盟护照，她梦想住在爱尔兰，于——

##段落
一次学校旅行时来过这里。“在政治上，爱尔兰与我们的想法更加一致，”她说。“美国有接纳更多人的基础设施，但远没有那么友好。”来自得克萨斯州休斯敦的劳伦·乌多（Lauren Udoh）在嫁给爱尔兰丈夫后，于2021年搬到了戈尔韦郡的克莱尔戈尔韦。乌多有两个年幼的孩子，是一名行政助理，并以TheGalwayGal的网名在社交媒体上记录外派生活。“最大的好处之一是安全。我在这里感觉安全多了，”她说。“孩子上学，你不用担心中枪击事件。”根据爱尔兰中央统计局（CSO）的数据，爱尔兰的移出人数有所下降，截至2025年4月的一年中有65,600人离开，较2024年下降6%。对于想移居国外的人来说，澳大利亚是最受欢迎的目的地。CSO表示，截至2025年4月的一年中，有13,500人离开爱尔兰前往澳大利亚，为2013年以来的最高水平。这比估计前往美国的6,100人多出一倍以上，不过前往美国的人数仍比上年增长22%。J1签证（允许爱尔兰大学生在美国工作和旅行）的限制，已促使许多爱尔兰学生重新考虑赴美留学。Safe Home Ireland是一家为希望返回爱尔兰的爱尔兰裔移民提供支持的组织，其首席执行官凯伦·麦休（Karen McHugh）表示：“我们确实注意到，关于（从美国返回爱尔兰）的咨询有所增加，”她说。“澳大利亚和加拿大是人们现在从爱尔兰前往的两个主要国家，原因是签证容易获得。”爱尔兰学生杰米·麦克尔希尼（Jamie McElhinney）目前正在葡萄牙进行工作实习，这是他酒店管理课程的一部分。就读于邓多克理工学院的麦克尔希尼表示，当前的移民管制让他不愿寻求赴美工作实习。“我原本打算去波士顿，后来所有关于Ice的新闻开始出现。这让人不敢去那边，”他说。虽然爱尔兰有机会，就业率达到74.4%，但也存在日益严重的住房危机，近期还因经济适用房短缺而出现抗议。巴尼特表示，她公司帮助搬迁的美国人会注意到住房短缺问题，并补充说：“他们不想加剧（住房危机），所以我们与他们谈论的一件事就是不要住在市中心。”萨布尔的外祖父母于1939年移居美国，他是众多因血统而获得爱尔兰护照的美国人之一。爱尔兰外交部报告称，2024年美国爱尔兰护照申请量增长了10%。萨布尔现在把爱尔兰视为家。“在文化上，我更认同爱尔兰人，”他说。“这是一个非常……

##段落
“集体社会，不像美国那样崇尚个人主义。”更多类似内容：• 爱尔兰电影产业为何蓬勃发展 • 纽约的大麻生意是否蒸蒸日上？• 战争对迪拜旅游业的“残酷”冲击

##段落
另一位有爱尔兰血统的美国人比尔·希利亚德为了更凉爽的气候移居爱尔兰。2019年野火之后，他和妻子安妮离开了加利福尼亚。“我妻子说我们需要搬到一个下雨的地方。”他们现在在科克郡巴尔的摩经营一家名为The Algiers的酒吧。

##段落
希利亚德说，他现在尽量回避美国发生的动荡事件。“我尽量不关注新闻，因为我现在在这里，”他说。“但我每天都会被提醒，因为每个人都会问我特朗普的事以及那边的情况……我现在都成了西科克驻美国大使了。”
