ELLSWORTH, Kansas — David Rankin has never been one for putting up campaign lawn signs. As a lifelong Republican in a town of 3,000 — where Donald Trump has won by 50-point margins since 2016 — he’s never seen a reason to put a candidate’s name in his yard. But recently, Rankin and his wife Dina did something new. Frustrated with their senators in Washington, DC, they went out to their front lawn and hammered in a sign in support of the Rev. Adam Hamilton, a Methodist megachurch pastor running for US Senate — and a Democrat. As signs of a midterm blue wave rise around the country, perhaps no state has been more surprising to watch than Kansas, a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years. A string of polls now show the incumbent GOP Sen. Roger Marshall locked in a tight race for survival, buffeted by low approval ratings, a string of personal controversies, poor campaigning, and Trump’s unpopularity over healthcare cuts, fuel costs, beef prices , and tariffs. Kansas is now a toss-up, attracting both national attention and last-minute cash investments from the national parties. Pundits have pointed to a range of reasons: the national backlash against the president; the unusual weakness of Marshall’s candidacy; the persistence of pocketbook issues for Kansas voters. But there’s also something more interesting afoot, a difference that may have its own national repercussions. Hamilton’s campaign is a rare instance of a Democrat deliberately rallying people of faith, boldly proclaiming the Gospels, openly talking about Jesus Christ, and asking voters to find — and embrace — a profoundly Democratic message in the beliefs they profess every Sunday. “Our faith is respectful…it reflects the ideas of justice and fairness, things that are just fundamental to the Bible,” Hamilton told me in early October. “Two thousand verses in the Bible talk about poverty and taking care of the poor. That’s not what you hear from Christian nationalists.” That was part of the draw for the Rankins. They had known about Hamilton for a while. Friends had been to his church, and David — a retired choir director — told me that his own Presbyterian congregation had used Hamilton’s books and various sermon series as part of their Bible study. So when they found out Hamilton had decided to run earlier this year — as a Democrat, no less — they prepared themselves for the possibility that they might have to break with their political party this year. Adam Hamilton speaks to a crowd gathered at Red Fern Booksellers in Salina, Kansas. Christian Paz/Vox “Things are not right right now. They’re not right in Washington and we have to do better,” Rankin told me. “His faith is just going to make him better as he serves us.” If Hamilton, and a handful of other candidates of faith in nearby Iowa and Texas, win, it could signal a shift in US politics — or at least a tremor in one of its most rock-solid certainties. One of the defining stories of the last century has been the realignment of religion, religious life, and religious voters on the political spectrum — and the complete shift of evangelicals toward the GOP. From the 1960s to the 1980s , Democrats could routinely count on majority support among white evangelical Protestants in congressional elections, and at least substantial support from them at the presidential level. But by the 1990s — with Americans becoming more evangelical and evangelicals becoming more Republican — the GOP had effectively locked in a permanent voting bloc, especially powerful in the heartland and the South. Meanwhile the opposite has been true for the Democratic Party: Rapid liberalization and secularization has moved nonreligious and anti-religious voters toward the Democrats, while religious Democratic voters tend to come from smaller progressive churches. The shift has only accelerated in recent years, as Trump has consolidated evangelical voters, while white college-educated voters — who are largely secular — moved left. And when blue-state Democrats try to deploy faith-based messages, they get derided or dismissed as awkward, disingenuous, or off-brand. The result: In recent years, Democrats have mostly ceded religious voters, outreach, and messaging to Republicans. That has made it almost impossible for the party to compete in red and rural states, where white evangelical voters make up a substantial share of the electorate. In turn, Democrats have faced increasingly long odds to win those Senate seats, or expand the electoral map in presidential contests. Whether he wins or loses in Kansas, Hamilton’s overperforming campaign poses a high-stakes question for Democrats nationally: Can a true moderate, a self-described radical centrist, and an openly religious person offer a road map for reclaiming Christianity and winning back religious voters? Maybe Hamilton does represent such a playbook. But to watch him on the trail, you find another fact that makes his path look much harder for other Democrats to walk. Hamilton greets attendees during a campaign event in Lenexa, Kansas, on October 4, 2026. Arin Yoon/Bloomberg via Getty Images Hamilton is a Methodist megachurch pastor running for US Senate, and a Democrat. Arin Yoon/Bloomberg via Getty Images It’s not just that Hamilton is a religious Democrat, or even that he’s mastered a message for religious swing voters hoping to reconcile their faith with a Democratic candidate. He’s also a deeply talented public speaker, well-connected community leader, and authoritative religious voice willing — unlike most pastors — to wade directly into electoral politics. He is, in other words, a unicorn. He’s the leader of a very unique church — not just a politician “affiliated” with Christianity or training to join the clergy, but an established figure in an established institutional denomination that insulates him against attacks on his faith and character. (One of those came from no less than Vice President JD Vance, who attacked Hamilton in September as “dressed in the skin suit of our religion.”) The skills that come with leading a megachurch also lend themselves easily to campaigning — but might not be replicable for others, at least not to this extent. And Hamilton has managed to ease concerns from secular or nonreligious liberals, without compromising his centrist, at times heterodox, religious and political beliefs. His campaign could change control of Congress. But beyond that, it also offers a new, possibly more effective, political language for Democrats in a post-Trump world. On a recent Thursday in Hutchinson, Kansas, Adam Hamilton found himself therapizing a crowd of several hundred. “Republicans for Hamilton” pins floated in the audience at this downtown theater in the middle of the state, as he diagnosed the problems in Washington that have bled into Kansas. Members of the US Senate, Hamilton said gently, had become like Dorothy’s traveling companions in The Wizard of Oz : They’d lost their minds, their hearts, and their courage. The historic Fox Theatre in downtown Hutchinson, Kansas. Christian Paz/Vox Along the way, he said, they, and President Donald Trump, had torn apart the fabric of the community, turning neighbors into suspicious strangers. Heads nodded in agreement; those closest to me sighed and lowered their heads. Hamilton recounted something a mother once asked him: to be “somebody who’s going to help me not hate my neighbors with the red caps anymore.” “And she wasn’t talking about Chiefs fans,” he quipped. Laughter broke the silence. To see Hamilton in action feels like being thrown back to a forgotten era of politics: His tone is conciliatory. He’s eager to dispense with the “extremes.” He slips into preaching about “radical love,” and he’s comfortable quoting scripture and referencing Christian teachings when answering policy questions. Time permitting, he shakes hands and greets everyone in a room. His public persona is built far less on his political experience — this is his first race — than on his three decades of experience leading a megachurch. In his own telling, tending to the middle has been a defining part of his life’s work. His faith journey started in high school. Raised nominally Catholic, he embraced atheism as he watched his parents go through a divorce and after his grandmother died by suicide. After a late night of smoking weed with a friend, he heard a knock at the door: a Pentecostal missionary was inviting him to church. Though not necessarily sold on this movement, he did meet his wife LaVon at church — and they married a week after graduating. Yet around this time, he says he felt a stirring to become a pastor. He enrolled at the evangelical Oral Roberts University to train as a preacher, but was thrown into despair, disillusionment, and doubt when his two best friends died in an accident. Seeking counsel and comfort from Pentecostal pastors and leaders, he was met with platitudes (“Everything happens for a reason”) and unanswered questions — and so began a journey that led him to John Wesley, the English theologian, and the movement he founded, Methodism. Hamilton speaks inside of the Fox Theatre to a few hundred people in Hutchinson. Christian Paz/Vox “I carry my pocket testament with me everywhere,” Hamilton told me, pulling out his copy of the Gospels and the epistles of John, as he tends to do on the trail. “This is my defining story. This book and its story define how I understand what it means to be human and is at the center of my life.” He was just 25 when he founded the Church of the Resurrection, commissioned by his bishops in the United Methodist Church to start a church “for thinking people.” The point was to “use your intellect and not check your brain at the door,” he says on the stump. “And have a heart. Focus on both a spiritual life, but also on living out faith and justice in the world. These things go hand in hand.” A view of the main sanctuary of the United Methodist Church of the Resurrection in Leawood, Kansas. The modern building is one of three main buildings on the church campus. Christian Paz/Vox And so it came to pass that a congregation that started off meeting in the chapel of a funeral home in the 1990s grew into Kansas’s largest church, and the largest Methodist congregation in the country. The church now has nine locations across two states counting about 24,000 members between them, anchored by a spaceship-looking complex in Leawood, a Kansas City suburb. Hamilton, and members of the church, are quick to point out the radical centrism of the church: It’s split roughly evenly between Republicans, Democrats, and independents. Hamilton himself is a former Republican. The Leawood location features both a 3,500-capacity sanctuary, with a full orchestra and 80-person choir for traditional services, a smaller space for modern, nondenominational-inspired worship, and a chapel. And though the spotlight of the campaign has brought scrutiny, media visits, and broadsides from out of state, it’s also Hamilton’s experience in the church, combined with an unpopular and inexperienced GOP incumbent, that have made the race competitive. The light pouring through the Swedish chapel’s windows in Lindsborg seemed to amplify the hundreds of singing voices. Hamilton, stumping at the front of the room, had broken out into song — “All Creatures of Our God and King” a hymn based on St. Francis of Assisi’s 800-year-old prayer — and the crowd at this Lutheran college quickly joined in. I’d had my eye on Adam Hamilton for a few months. I was hoping to cover his primary campaign, but given his religious and politically moderate background, it wasn’t clear that he would win. When he did, I saw a chance to explore a question central to my beat: How does politics influence American religion, and how can religion influence the two major parties — especially today’s Democrats? I reported this story from Kansas — flying into Kansas City and driving nearly 200 miles to a bookstore in Salina, where Hamilton was scheduled to speak and meet supporters. I spent the rest of the day following his campaign to Lindsborg (about 45 minutes away) and Hutchinson (another 30 minutes away). The next day, I was off to Garden City in the far west of the state for another campaign stop (another 200 miles away), stopping for a meal in Hanston on my way back to Ellsworth in central Kansas for another event. I spent the following day in Salina and stopped in Topeka, before heading to Overland Park, where I attended a Sunday service at Hamilton’s church before returning to DC in the evening. In all, I covered about 900 miles of roads in four days, crisscrossing the state of Dorothy and Toto and talking to dozens of voters. “You just got to take the time to do that,” he said after the final alleluia. Before the song, he had been speaking about the Christian roots of his campaign: the Biblical call to do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly, all for the sake of God’s creation. Oftentimes life, and especially politics, make it hard to see the beauty in nature, he was saying, and the complexity in everything. Hamilton’s popularity in both his church and among Kansas voters owes a great deal to the fact that he’s a moderate. Coming from the coasts, that word, used around Hamilton, doesn’t quite mean what I expected. A “moderate” in American Democratic politics usually describes a longtime Democrat who carves out a middle lane on very specific issues — usually defense or reducing the deficit. But Hamilton has no trouble with complicated, unfixed, occasionally heterodox views, including on hot-button social issues. Take a question a woman in the chapel asked him about abortion: What does he think about reproductive rights in a state like Kansas? He’s spent the last two decades writing and talking about his evolving thoughts on abortion . He calls himself “pro-life with a heavy heart,” telling the woman that, as a pastor, he feels “personally moral tension when it comes to abortion.” Worshippers chat and socialize inside the main sanctuary at the Church of the Resurrection after a Sunday service. The day’s sermon was centered on the Parable of the Good Samaritan. Christian Paz/Vox But he would be taking on a different role as a US senator, Hamilton said. Crisis pregnancies “lead me to have compassion, and say there needs to be legal and safe access to abortion,” he said. On this issue, politicians are usually pressured to take absolutist positions to satisfy their party’s base, but Hamilton sees his own view as representing what most Kansans actually want. People here have already voted multiple times to preserve abortion access, he said, and when an effort to undo abortion rights protections in the state constitution was on the ballot in 2022, it lost by nearly 20 points. He said he believed at the time that the legislature should not “be making that decision for women who are facing really difficult situations.” This particular tension comes from his mother’s own experience: Worried she wouldn’t be able to support or raise a child at 17, her father, a TWA pilot, had encouraged her to travel to Switzerland for an abortion when she got pregnant. She considered it, but ultimately refused, leading to her being kicked out of her home and moving in with Hamilton’s 16-year-old father. Even today she tells Hamilton to remember her story — “I just can’t imagine how much poorer the world would be if I had gotten on that airplane and you had never been born.” “There are things that are clearly black and white, but there’s a lot where there’s room; I may not ever get to where you are, but I can see where you’re coming from and I can respect you for that,” Hamilton said to me and other reporters after the chapel event. “People on the extremes on either end, they don’t want me telling the story about my mom. … But in the broad center, the folks who are on the left say, ‘You know what? That’s real. I know that you’re going to solidly make sure that there’s abortion rights.’ And on the right, people say, ‘I appreciate the fact that you understand the moral tension.’” He applies a similar mindset to LGBTQ issues. His own church welcomes gay and lesbian people, even as he accepts that individual Methodist congregations can choose their own approach (he advocated for that middle ground while trying to prevent a schism between the mainstream UMC and a traditionalist and conservative offshoot that broke off in 2023). On the trail, Hamilton hews to the middle on other policy issues as well, raising concerns about the national debt, endorsing border security and ICE’s “original” purpose, letting local communities decide on AI data centers, and critiquing “far-left climate” activism. He’s running ads condemning socialism and the extremes of both sides. And he peppers his speeches with the phrase “independent-minded Democrat.” Hamilton leans down to listen to a child’s questions during a campaign stop at a garden and nursery store in Garden City, Kansas. Christian Paz/Vox In the same way, Hamilton is not afraid to evangelize. He’s both eager and willing to talk about his faith, to preach the Gospel, and to share his personal journey to God, while also reassuring liberal, nonreligious people, and Democrats broadly that he believes in the separation of church and state. He isn’t one of those Christians, he seems to suggest, but he is still uncompromisingly Christian. “We’re not running to force our religion on other people, but we are running as people who say our Gospel calls us to something different,” he said. When comparing the core priorities of the GOP — fiscal responsibility, limited government, personal civil liberties, and a strong defense — with the core priorities of Democrats — social safety nets, education, the elderly, making sure that vulnerable people are cared for — the space to be a gospel-reading Democrat is quite obvious, he said. “Jesus never talked about civil liberties,” Hamilton said. “He never talked about fiscal responsibility, a strong defense or limited government. But he did talk about, ‘I was hungry and you gave me something to eat. I was thirsty and you gave me something to drink.’ … Which of these two sounds more like Jesus in the Gospels?” Which is where the lessons for other Democrats appear plainly. Hamilton thinks the party he joined earlier this year could learn a few things from his campaign, and those of other people of faith running as Democrats across the country. “Sometimes they have inadvertently alienated religious voters who are just right of center who would easily have come on board if they felt like they were welcomed,” he said. “The Democratic Party would be far stronger and wiser if they were openly willing to say, ‘Of course we embrace people of faith and we need them.’” And it’s that ability, to combine faith with moderation and openness, that is compelling to the voters across the political spectrum I talked with. “I’m a Christian and I feel that in Christianity we feed the hungry, clothe the poor, all those things that I read in the New Testament. And I feel that he gets that,” Susan Combs, a 73-year-old registered Republican, told me. “This Christian nationalism that is going on is not really, to me personally, it’s not what Christianity is about.” She and others pointed to Hamilton and Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian , as examples of a kind of Christian political revival. Both of them, plus a handful of other Democrats running on openly faith-based messages, present case studies for strategists, scholars, and others who are watching the campaign for political lessons. When Talarico and Hamilton use religious language, “it really stands out, even though it’s really more of a return to what we’ve seen in the past,” Dave Campbell, a religion and politics scholar at the University of Notre Dame, said. “The trick with religious language is that people from within a religious community, they pick up on the subtleties. Do they really speak the way I do? Do they really understand the world the way I do? And if you don’t really understand those nuances, your rhetoric can come off as not only inauthentic, but even offensive.” The former Baptist pastor, religious researcher, and professor Ryan Burge noted that Democrats will likely not be able to pull many white evangelical Christians into their coalition. But his own examination of the data shows that there’s ample room for Democrats to grow their margins among white Catholics and mainline Protestant voters — those who belong to old non-evangelical institutional churches like the Presbyterian, Episcopalian, Lutheran, and Methodist churches. The Wesley Chapel on the campus of the Church of the Resurrection in Leawood. The ceiling is meant to evoke an old fishing boat leading to Christ, in the center of the stained glass windows. Christian Paz/Vox These voters will remain up for grabs in future elections — though outreach may only work in certain states that still have strong mainline traditions. “You can’t win in a place like Arizona — that’s not where your base is,” Burge said. But traditional denominations are still strong in the heartland and farm country. “A place like Kansas, Iowa, Nebraska, even Missouri to some extent, Wisconsin — those are the kind of places I think that message would do well,” Burge said. “It wouldn’t do well nationwide, though.” Burge told me the key for Democrats to be competitive in religious spaces again will be to win over old mainliners “who used to be a Bill Clinton voter, even an early Obama voter, who got lost by the progressivism of the Democratic Party on social issues. That’s the kind of voter that you can win back, the 75-year-old Lutheran, Presbyterian.” The bigger question, Burge told me, is an uncomfortable one Democrats as a party must face: that the secular far left is loud, but not large. “A lot of those people [who are religiously unaffiliated] are actually open to the idea of religion,” he said. Even among those who don’t identify with any particular organized religion, atheists only make up less than one in five . “A lot of [religiously unaffiliated people] do believe in something. Those people are not going to be turned off by some religious talk,” Burge said. “At some point you’ve got to say to the loud secular left, ‘Hey, we appreciate you and we want your votes, of course, but you’re going to vote for us anyway. We need the votes of Catholics and mainline Protestants and those kinds of people. They’re the ones we’re going for.” At a rally in the Kansas City suburbs in September, Vice President JD Vance unintentionally delivered an in-kind donation to Hamilton’s campaign. He leveled an attack liberal and mainline Protestant Christians have long fielded from the religious right: that Hamilton’s faith was just “left-wing radicalism dressed in the skin suit of our religion.” “That is not Christianity,” Vance, a Catholic convert who grew up in evangelical, Pentecostal, and nondenominational faith traditions, said of Hamilton , also calling him “a guy who would insult your faith and spit on your religion to accrue donations to himself.” By contrast, he described Marshall as “a proud Christian” with “real faith and real principles.” Marshall also attends a mainline Christian church. More than 100 Methodist clergy came to Hamilton’s defense in the wake of the broadside, urging Marshall, and Vance, to be more careful on the campaign. “When you attack Adam’s pastoral ministry, his home congregation, and our denomination as a whole, you sow seeds of division and dissent,” they wrote . “You tear at the fabric that is the body of Christ.” The pastor of Marshall’s old church called Hamilton “a middle-of-the-road pastor” who is “pretty good at loving his enemies.” Trump himself recently called him “a Radical Left LUNATIC Dumocrat,” who is “is not one us [evangelicals].” But the personal attacks on his faith, and the defenses, may have only underscored one of Hamilton’s perceived advantages. In Kansas, at least, moral character has become one of the defining stories of the race. It’s no coincidence that Hamilton’s big break came in September, when a major New York Times investigation upended the race by reporting that Marshall — a former OB-GYN — had sued more than 700 former patients, some of them new mothers, for unpaid medical bills. Many were charged 18 percent interest, and 81 were arrested in debt-collection cases. Campaign ads interviewing doctors who said Marshall’s practices were unusual and Marshall’s former patients soon inundated Kansas airwaves. “It is ridiculous to suggest that Dr. Marshall ever arrested patients,” Abbi Enders, Marshall’s campaign press secretary, wrote in response to a question from Vox about the article. “The Kansas Bill of Rights states, ‘No person shall be imprisoned for debt,’ proving this to be a blatant lie.” Many of the arrests in the cases of Marshall’s former patients were due to missed court dates. That story broke right before Hamilton trounced Marshall during a debate at the Kansas state fair. Videos of Marshall being drowned out by booing crowds spread quickly — while competing clips of Hamilton talking about being both liberal and conservative also went viral during this window. Hamilton’s favorability has become a prominent example of another shift in Trump-era American politics: the sense that Republicans are now losing the character war, nominating deeply flawed candidates who project strength and bluster at the expense of integrity, decency, and other qualities people trust. Across red states like Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, and Texas, Democrats have held an edge in polling when voters were asked which party’s candidate has better moral character. In Kansas, more stories would soon drip out, contributing to the deteriorating public image of Marshall: reports that Marshall’s primary residence was in Florida , not Kansas; an unpaid cookie bill from a 2020 campaign event; allegations of inappropriate usage of officials funds or taxpayer money for campaign purposes . The result: Hamilton leading the field of key toss-up Senate races with the highest net favorability ratings in a CNN average of polls from September and October. Hamilton during a campaign event in Lenexa, Kansas, on October 4, 2026. Arin Yoon/Bloomberg via Getty Images Republicans have fired back, going after his religion and church. Vance and Marshall attacked his church’s participation in a Pride festival. Marshall campaign ads have criticized the church’s handling of decades-old child sexual abuse allegations against a former volunteer at a church camp, alleging that Hamilton “protected a pedophile.” Trump, at his rally in Wichita last week, delivered his own spin on these accusations, saying Hamilton “used church dollars to fund anti-religious transgender activity,” and “shielded a child sexual predator at his church.” Marshall has continued calling Hamilton a far-left, “woke megachurch CEO,” and went after his church again at a debate last week, asking if he was “leading from the middle when one in four churches left his denomination? Is that what you call leading from the middle when you split the Methodist church?” “People know what I’ve stood for — they know I’m not some woke, far left, whatever,” Hamilton said in an interview. “And I feel at peace about it.” Still, “that’s 24,000 other people in my church that you’re attacking and you’re attacking every other mainline Christian across the state of Kansas as you’re doing that.” When asked about this charge in an email, Marshall’s press secretary did not respond. When Hamilton discusses religious liberty and the separation of church and state, he makes something clear: “I’m not running to be the chaplain of the Senate.” Over the days that I followed him, he repeated this line, usually in response to liberal-leaning voters curious or skeptical about endorsing someone so vocally religious. “If anything, that might have been a negative,” Sally Gillihan, a Democrat, told me in Hutchinson. “I was really worried that that’s what he was relying on, that’s what he was going to go to bat for.” After hearing him talk about policy, religious freedom, and restoring normalcy, those fears went away. Others, including Sam Buttram, a 2020 Marshall voter who works in the cattle industry, told me that Hamilton’s religiosity wasn’t a selling point for him, but that it’s “a lot of what makes him who he is,” which makes him trust his character. “I just wish more politicians were like him…independent-minded, wanting to do the right thing for the people instead of worried about staying in office or agreeing with some other politician.” Ultimately, Hamilton’s unexpected campaign success so far might be due to the combination of all this — not only his faith, but the impression that many voters have that he is guided not by right or left but his own values, as evidenced by his heterodox views and moderate temperament. In his case, those values are informed by his faith, but for other Democrats in other red states, they might not need to be. Still, that might not make it any easier for Democrats trying to emulate the Hamilton playbook. Much of Hamilton’s success, Burge told me, is due to his unique position. “People don’t realize how good megachurch pastors are at stuff like [campaigning]. When you’re used to talking to 2,000, 3,000 people every weekend, you are a politician,” he said. “It’s a superpower though. … You’ve got to be a one in a million kind of person.” See More : Culture Life Midterm Elections 2026 Politics Religion Take a mental break with the newest Vox crossword Gen Z has buyer’s remorse on Trump How a megachurch pastor gave Democrats a prayer in Kansas What do you do when your love and your life are in two different places? 他急于摒弃那些“极端”。他不知不觉地开始宣讲“激进的爱”，在回答政策问题时，他乐于引用经文和基督教教义。如果时间允许，他会与房间里的每个人握手问候。他的公众形象远非建立在政治经验之上——这是他第一次参选——而是建立在他领导大型教会三十年的经验之上。用他自己的话说，走中间路线一直是他毕生事业的定义性部分。他的信仰之旅始于高中。他名义上是天主教徒，但在目睹父母离婚、祖母自杀身亡后，他转向了无神论。在一次深夜与朋友抽大麻后，他听到敲门声：一位五旬节派传教士邀请他去教堂。虽然他对这一运动未必完全信服，但他确实在教堂遇到了妻子拉冯——他们在毕业后一周就结婚了。然而大约在这段时间，他说自己感到一种成为牧师的召唤。他进入福音派的奥罗尔·罗伯茨大学接受传道人培训，但当他最好的两个朋友在一场事故中去世时，他陷入了绝望、幻灭和怀疑之中。他向五旬节派的牧师和领袖寻求建议和安慰，却只得到陈词滥调（“凡事皆有因”）和无解的疑问——于是一段旅程开始了，引领他走向英国神学家约翰·卫斯理及其创立的循道宗运动。汉密尔顿在哈钦森的福克斯剧院内向几百人发表讲话。Christian Paz/Vox “我随身携带我的袖珍圣约书，”汉密尔顿告诉我，拿出他那本福音书和约翰书信的副本，这是他在竞选途中常做的事。“这是我的定义性故事。这本书及其故事定义了我对人之为人意义的理解，是我生活的中心。”他创立复活教会时年仅25岁，由联合卫理公会的主教们委任，创办一间“为思考者而设”的教会。要点是“运用你的才智，不要在门口把脑子寄存掉，”他在竞选演讲中说。“同时要有一颗心。既关注灵性生活，也关注在世间践行信仰与正义。这些事情相辅相成。”堪萨斯州利伍德联合卫理公会复活教会主圣所一景。这座现代建筑是教堂园区三座主要建筑之一。Christian Paz/Vox 于是，一个始于1990年代在殡仪馆小教堂聚会的会众，发展成为堪萨斯州最大的教会，也是全国最大的循道宗教会。该教会现已在两个州拥有九个聚会点，合计约24000名成员，以利伍德一座形似飞船的建筑群为核心。

堪萨斯城的一个郊区。汉密尔顿和教会成员都急于指出教会的激进中间主义：共和党人、民主党人和独立人士大致各占三分之一。汉密尔顿本人曾是共和党人。利伍德场地既有可容纳3500人的圣所——配有完整管弦乐队和80人合唱团用于传统礼拜——也有一个较小的空间用于现代、受非宗派启发的敬拜，还有一个小教堂。尽管竞选活动的聚光灯带来了审视、媒体来访和来自外州的猛烈抨击，但正是汉密尔顿在教会中的经历，加上一位不受欢迎且缺乏经验的共和党现任议员，才使这场选战具有竞争力。在林兹堡的瑞典小教堂里，倾泻而下的阳光透过窗户，似乎放大了数百人的歌声。汉密尔顿在房间前方竞选演说时突然唱起歌来——《万物的主宰与君王》，这首赞美诗改编自圣方济各800年前的祈祷文——这所路德会学院的人群很快加入其中。我关注亚当·汉密尔顿已有几个月了。我原本希望报道他的初选竞选，但鉴于他的宗教背景和政治温和立场，他能否获胜并不明朗。当他获胜后，我看到了一个探索我报道领域核心问题的机会：政治如何影响美国宗教，宗教又如何影响两大政党——尤其是今天的民主党？我从堪萨斯州发回这篇报道——飞抵堪萨斯城，驱车近200英里到萨利纳的一家书店，汉密尔顿计划在那里演讲并会见支持者。当天余下时间，我跟随他的竞选活动前往林兹堡（约45分钟车程）和哈钦森（再30分钟车程）。第二天，我前往该州最西部的加登城参加另一场竞选活动（又是200英里外），在返回途中于汉斯顿吃饭，然后到堪萨斯州中部的埃尔斯沃思参加另一场活动。接下来的一天我在萨利纳度过，并在托皮卡停留，然后前往欧弗兰帕克，在那里参加了汉密尔顿教会的周日礼拜，傍晚返回华盛顿。四天里，我总共走了约900英里的路，纵横穿越多萝西和托托的家乡，与数十位选民交谈。“你就是得花时间去做这件事，”他在最后的哈利路亚之后说。在唱歌之前，他一直在谈论他竞选活动的基督教根源：圣经的呼召——行公义、好怜悯、存谦卑的心，一切为了上帝的创造。他当时说，生活，尤其是政治，常常让人难以看到自然之美，也难以看到万物的复杂性。汉密尔顿在教会和堪萨斯选民中的受欢迎程度，很大程度上归功于他是一个温和派。来自

“我欣赏你理解这种道德张力这一点。”他在LGBTQ议题上也采取类似心态。他自己的教会欢迎男女同性恋者，尽管他也接受各个卫理公会堂会可以自行选择做法（他曾倡导这一中间立场，同时试图阻止主流联合卫理公会与2023年分裂出去的传统主义保守派分支之间发生分裂）。在竞选活动中，汉密尔顿在其他政策议题上也走中间路线，提出对国家债务的担忧，支持边境安全和移民及海关执法局的“最初”宗旨，主张由当地社区决定人工智能数据中心事宜，并批评“极左气候”行动主义。他投放广告谴责社会主义以及两端的极端立场。他还在演讲中反复使用“有独立思想的民主党人”这一说法。汉密尔顿在堪萨斯州加登城一家园艺苗圃商店的竞选停留活动中俯身倾听一个孩子的问题。Christian Paz/Vox 同样，汉密尔顿不怕传福音。他既渴望也愿意谈论自己的信仰、宣讲福音、分享自己走向上帝的个人历程，同时也向自由派、非宗教人士以及广大民主党人保证，他相信政教分离。他似乎想表明，他不是那类基督徒，但他仍然毫不妥协地是基督徒。“我们竞选不是为了把宗教强加给别人，但我们是以这样的人身份竞选：我们说福音召唤我们去做不同的事，”他说。他说，将共和党的核心优先事项——财政责任、有限政府、个人公民自由和强大国防——与民主党的核心优先事项——社会安全网、教育、老年人、确保弱势群体得到照顾——相比较，作为一个读福音书的民主党人，其空间相当明显。“耶稣从未谈论公民自由，”汉密尔顿说。“他从未谈论财政责任、强大国防或有限政府。但他确实谈到，‘我饿了，你们给我吃；我渴了，你们给我喝。’……这两者中哪一个听起来更像福音书中的耶稣？”这正是对其他民主党人的启示显而易见之处。汉密尔顿认为，他今年早些时候加入的政党可以从他的竞选以及全国其他以民主党人身份参选的信仰人士的竞选中学到一些东西。“有时他们无意中疏远了那些只是略微偏右的宗教选民，而这些人如果感到自己受到欢迎，本来很容易加入进来，”他说。“如果民主党人公开愿意说，‘我们当然拥抱信仰人士，我们需要他们’，民主党会强大得多、明智得多。”而正是这种能力，将信仰

##段落
他带着节制与开放的态度，这在我交谈过的各政治光谱选民中都颇具吸引力。“我是基督徒，我觉得在基督教中，我们给饥饿者食物、给穷人衣穿，这些都是我在新约中读到的。我觉得他懂这一点，”73岁的注册共和党人苏珊·科姆斯告诉我。“正在发生的这种基督教民族主义，对我个人而言，并不是基督教的真义。”她和其他人指出，汉密尔顿和得克萨斯州民主党参议员候选人、长老会神学院学生詹姆斯·塔拉里科，是某种基督教政治复兴的典范。他们两人，再加上其他几位以公开信仰信息竞选的民主党人，为策略师、学者以及其他观察这场竞选以汲取政治教训的人提供了案例研究。当塔拉里科和汉密尔顿使用宗教语言时，“它确实很突出，尽管它实际上更像是回归我们过去所见的方式，”圣母大学宗教与政治学者戴夫·坎贝尔说。“宗教语言的诀窍在于，宗教社群内部的人能捕捉到那些微妙之处。他们真的像我这样说话吗？他们真的像我这样理解世界吗？如果你并不真正理解那些细微差别，你的言辞不仅会显得不真诚，甚至可能冒犯他人。”前浸信会牧师、宗教研究员兼教授瑞安·伯奇指出，民主党人可能无法将许多白人福音派基督徒拉入他们的联盟。但他自己对数据的审视显示，民主党人在白人工天主教徒和主流新教选民中仍有充足空间来扩大优势——这些人属于长老会、圣公会、路德会和卫理公会等古老的非福音派建制教会。位于利伍德的复活教会校园内的卫斯理教堂。天花板意在唤起一艘引领人归向基督的旧渔船，位于彩色玻璃窗的中央。克里斯蒂安·帕斯/Vox这些选民在未来的选举中仍将摇摆不定——尽管外联可能只在某些仍保有强大主流传统的州奏效。“你在亚利桑那这样的地方赢不了——那不是你的基础所在，”伯奇说。但传统教派在腹地和农业地区仍然强大。“堪萨斯、爱荷华、内布拉斯加，甚至某种程度上密苏里、威斯康星——这些是我认为那类信息会奏效的地方，”伯奇说。“不过，它不会在全国范围内奏效。”伯奇告诉我，民主党人要在宗教空间重新具备竞争力的关键，将是赢回那些老主流派——“他们曾是比尔·克林顿的选民，甚至是早期的奥巴马选民，却被进步主义所迷失——”

##段落
在社会议题上，民主党面临的最大问题是一个令人不安的现实：世俗极左翼声音很大，但人数并不多。伯奇告诉我，很多“宗教上无归属”的人其实对宗教持开放态度。即使在那些不认同任何特定组织化宗教的人当中，无神论者也不到五分之一。“很多（宗教上无归属的人）确实相信某种东西。这些人不会因为一些宗教话语就反感，”伯奇说。“到了某个时候，你必须对喧嚣的世俗左翼说：‘嘿，我们感谢你们，当然也想要你们的选票，但你们反正都会投给我们。我们需要天主教徒和主流新教徒这些人的选票。他们才是我们要争取的对象。’”

##段落
九月份在堪萨斯城郊区的一次集会上，副总统JD·万斯无意中给汉密尔顿的竞选送上了一份大礼。他抛出了自由派和主流新教基督徒长期以来从宗教右翼那里听到的攻击：汉密尔顿的信仰不过是“披着我们宗教外衣的左翼激进主义”。“那不是基督教，”万斯——一个在福音派、五旬节派和非宗派信仰传统中长大、后皈依天主教的信徒——这样评价汉密尔顿，还称他是“一个为了给自己筹款而侮辱你的信仰、唾弃你的宗教的人”。相比之下，他称马歇尔是“一位自豪的基督徒”，拥有“真正的信仰和真正的原则”。马歇尔同样参加主流基督教会的礼拜。在这番猛烈攻击之后，一百多位卫理公会神职人员站出来为汉密尔顿辩护，敦促马歇尔和万斯在竞选中更加谨慎。“当你攻击亚当的牧职事工、他的家庭教会以及我们整个教派时，你就是在播撒分裂和异议的种子，”他们写道。“你们在撕裂基督身体这块织物。”马歇尔原先所在教会的牧师称汉密尔顿是“一位中间路线的牧师”，“相当擅长爱他的仇敌”。特朗普本人最近称他为“激进左翼疯癫民主党员”，“不是我们（福音派）中的一员”。但这些针对他信仰的人身攻击以及随之而来的辩护，可能恰恰凸显了汉密尔顿的一项公认优势。至少在堪萨斯，道德品格已成为这场竞选的决定性叙事之一。汉密尔顿的重大转机出现在九月并非巧合——当时《纽约时报》的一项重大调查颠覆了选情，报道称马歇尔——一名前妇产科医生——曾起诉七百多名前患者追讨未付医疗账单，其中一些是刚生产的母亲。许多人被收取了18%的利息，一项——

##段落
在讨债案件中，有81人被捕。竞选广告采访了多位医生，他们表示马歇尔的执业方式异乎寻常；马歇尔昔日的患者很快便充斥了堪萨斯的广播和电视。马歇尔竞选团队的新闻秘书阿比·恩德斯在回应Vox就上述文章提出的问题时写道：“暗示马歇尔医生曾经逮捕过患者，这实在荒谬。《堪萨斯权利法案》规定，‘任何人不得因债务而被监禁’，这证明该说法是彻头彻尾的谎言。”在马歇尔昔日患者的案件中，许多逮捕是因当事人未按时出庭所致。这篇报道曝出的时机，恰在汉密尔顿于堪萨斯州博览会的一场辩论中大败马歇尔之前。马歇尔被嘘声淹没的视频迅速传播开来——与此同时，汉密尔顿谈论自己兼具自由派与保守派立场的片段也在同一时间段内疯传。汉密尔顿的良好好感度已成为特朗普时代美国政治另一转变的突出例证：人们感到共和党人如今正在品格之战中落败，他们提名那些缺陷深重的候选人，这些人以牺牲正直、体面以及其他人们所信赖的品质为代价，来展现强硬与虚张声势。在阿拉斯加、艾奥瓦、堪萨斯、俄亥俄和得克萨斯等红州，当选民被问及哪个政党的候选人品格更好时，民主党人在民调中一直占据优势。在堪萨斯，很快还会有更多报道陆续流出，进一步损害马歇尔的公众形象：有报道称马歇尔的主要住所位于佛罗里达而非堪萨斯；2020年一场竞选活动留下一笔未付的饼干账单；还有指控称其不当使用官员经费或纳税人的钱用于竞选目的。结果是：在CNN于9月和10月汇总的民调中，汉密尔顿在关键摇摆参议院选战中领先群雄，净好感度评分最高。2026年10月4日，汉密尔顿在堪萨斯州莱内克萨的一场竞选活动上。Arin Yoon/Bloomberg via Getty Images
##段落
共和党人已发起反击，攻击他的宗教和教会。万斯和马歇尔抨击他所在教会参与骄傲节活动。马歇尔的竞选广告批评该教会在处理一起针对教会营地前志愿者的数十年前儿童性侵指控时的做法，声称汉密尔顿“保护了一名恋童癖者”。特朗普上周在威奇托的集会上对这些指控作出自己的演绎，称汉密尔顿“用教会的钱资助反宗教的跨性别活动”，并且“在自己的教会里庇护了一名儿童性侵犯者”。马歇尔继续称汉密尔顿为极左的“觉醒巨型教会CEO”，并在上周的一场辩论中再次攻击他的教会，质问他是否“在四分之一教会脱离其教派时还算是在从中道领导？当卫理公会分裂时，这就是你所谓的从中道领导吗？”

##段落
“教会？”汉密尔顿在一次采访中说，“人们知道我主张什么——他们知道我不是什么觉醒派、极左派之类的。”“对此我心安理得。”不过，“你这么做，是在攻击我教会里的另外两万四千人，也是在攻击堪萨斯州各地的每一位主流基督徒。”当被问及这一指控时，马歇尔的新闻秘书在邮件中未作回应。当汉密尔顿谈及宗教自由与政教分离时，他把一件事说得很清楚：“我竞选不是为了当参议院的牧师。”在我跟随他的那些天里，他反复提到这句话，通常是在回应那些倾向自由派、对他如此高调宣扬宗教感到好奇或怀疑的选民。“要说有什么影响，那可能反而是个减分项，”民主党人萨莉·吉利汉在哈钦森告诉我，“我原本真的很担心，他靠的就是这个，他要为之站台的就是这个。”在听了他谈论政策、宗教自由和回归常态之后，这些担忧便消散了。其他人，包括2020年投票给马歇尔、从事养牛业的萨姆·巴特拉姆，告诉我汉密尔顿的虔诚对他来说并不是卖点，但这“很大程度上造就了他这个人”，让他信任他的人品。“我只希望有更多政客像他一样……有独立思想，想为民众做正确的事，而不是操心如何保住职位，或者附和某个别的政客。”归根结底，汉密尔顿迄今出人意料的竞选成功，或许正是这一切的综合结果——不仅是他的信仰，还有许多选民的一种印象：指引他的不是左右之分，而是他自己的价值观，他那非正统的观点和温和的性情便是明证。就他而言，这些价值观受其信仰塑造，但对其他红州的民主党人来说，未必需要如此。不过，这或许并不能让试图效仿汉密尔顿套路的民主党人轻松多少。伯奇告诉我，汉密尔顿的成功很大程度上归功于他独特的处境。“人们没有意识到大型教会的牧师有多擅长[竞选]这类事。当你习惯了每个周末对着两千、三千人讲话，你就是个政客了，”他说，“不过这是一种超能力。……你得是万里挑一的那种人。”查看更多：文化 生活 2026年中期选举 政治 宗教 用最新的Vox填字游戏让大脑休息一下 Z世代对特朗普心生悔意 一位大型教会牧师如何为堪萨斯的民主党人带来祈祷 当你的爱与你的生活身处两地，你该怎么办？ 特朗普正试图推翻一场尚未发生的选举 邮箱（必填） 注册 提交你的邮箱，即表示你同意我们的条款与隐私声明。本网站受re保护

readings.title: How solar became bigger than nuclear
body: 9 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Jocelyn Timperley After defying projections, solar's dramatic growth means it is now overtaking nuclear as a global power source. Here are seven reasons for solar's success, and where it might go from here. The world's solar power is crossing a threshold. A decade ago, it barely registered on a global scale, providing just 1% of the world's power. In 2026, it will almost certainly increase to 10% of power, and overtake nuclear, a mainstay of electricity since the late 1970s. Globally, solar electricity generation quietly overtook nuclear power (just) in 2025, according to statistics from UK-based energy think tank Ember . And BBC analysis of Ember data over  the past 12 months up to September 2026 shows it clearly outstripping nuclear, producing 13% more power. "[Solar] generating more electricity than all the world's nuclear power plants is a pretty insane stat, for sure," says Dave Jones, co-founder of Ember.  From China's vast arrays to a recent solar upsurge driven by escalating oil prices, the incredible rise of solar power has defied all projections. Here are seven ways it has become an apparently "unstoppable force" – and what the future looks like from here.   "Solar is now the engine of the power transition," says Jan Rosenow, a professor of energy and climate policy at the University of Oxford in the UK. Solar has become the fastest-growing source of new electricity in history , and by far the largest source of new electricity globally. In 2025, it met three-quarters of the growth in the world's demand for electricity, overtaking wind power generation (wind power is also growing, just a little more slowly). That's where solar's going, to not just be king of electricity, but king of energy – Dave Jones "It wasn't expected," says Rosenow. Mainstream projections, he says, have underestimated solar year after year . Outlooks such as those from the International Energy Agency (IEA), an influential intergovernmental organisation based in Paris, "assumed linear growth and slowly falling costs, and got both wrong". Over 2026, multiple sources indicate solar electricity generation will almost certainly far exceed nuclear globally. Nuclear's electricity generation has remained more or less constant since 2000, while solar's has increased some 2,700-fold. Solar, a mature technology for some 15 years now, became the cheapest electricity in history in 2020. Since then, solar has scaled, efficiency has risen, and the amount of silicon and silver used in panels has gone down, leading prices to fall yet further , says Jones.  "Massive Chinese manufacturing scale and current overcapacity have pushed module prices to record lows," says Rosenow.  In particular, a large fall in the price of panels in 2023-24 pushed us into the current era of what Jones calls "offensively cheap" solar. "A panel in itself is just so unbelievably cheap," he says. "It's well under $100 (£75)… and that's going to keep you generating electricity for 30, 40 years without any input at all." Of course, it's not just in purely economic terms that solar is bringing down costs. Researchers have calculated the US's rising wind and solar generation brought it $249bn (£186bn) in climate and health benefits between 2019 and 2022 . China is still the world's biggest solar power by far but is by no means the only player. Despite the US imposing a variety of tariffs on solar , it remains the second country when it comes to installations, which are still skyrocketing – especially in states won by President Trump in 2024 . In fact, the US now has enough solar to power more than one-third of its households . "Tariffs and other federal policies that constrain renewable energy growth are certainly expected to raise costs and slow expansion relative to what we otherwise would have seen," says Alicia Zhao, an expert in US mitigation pathways at the University of Maryland.  "However, economics are a key part of why solar has been able to grow so quickly. Even with rising costs, solar is still one of the cheapest sources of new power in the US. And it is getting built regardless of political lines ." India, meanwhile, is moving away from fossil fuels far faster than China did, and new solar has met 60% of its rise in power demand in the past two years. In Australia, over four million homes now have rooftop solar: well over a third of all households. Countries like Pakistan and Lebanon have also begun installing solar at breakneck speeds , while across Africa countries are installing some 100,000 solar panels  per day. In many places, escalating diesel prices, driven by the Russia-Ukraine conflict and US-Israel war with Iran , has swung the cost needle yet further in solar's favour. This is especially the case in many African countries where home diesel generators are a mainstay due to unreliable grids. Rooftop solar panels, nearly all of them imported from China, have now taken off as an alternative. Ethiopia has even banned the import of petrol and diesel cars in a bid to tackle oil dependency and pollution, says Jones. Solar is also rapidly providing new electricity where fossil-based grids can't keep up with demand. Pakistan, for example, has become a surprising poster child for the solar revolution due to its extraordinarily rapid rise in installations . In 2019, solar provided less than 2% of its electricity; now it's 24%, driven by costly, unreliable grid electricity combined and cheap solar imports from China. "What's really incredible in Pakistan is… generally most of the solar boom has been out of people's pockets," says Jones. "People can afford it, without needing to take out loans." A similar story has been seen in several other "sun belt" countries, from Lebanon to Nigeria . "[Solar] lets households act without waiting for governments or utilities," says Rosenow. "In uncertain times, that speed and independence is extremely valuable." Solar power, of course, can only be produced during the day when the sun is shining. To turn it into electricity that can be dispatched at any time, it needs to be paired with batteries. Fortunately, batteries have been having their own cost revolution , transforming their ability to support the solar rollout. "Solar plus storage is now routinely cheaper than new fossil plants in sunny regions," says Rosenow. "Batteries have largely solved the daily problem of shifting midday sun into the evening." In California, for example, solar and batteries met on average over a quarter of electricity demand from 19:00-21:00 (the evening peak) over the first half of 2026. US states such as Vermont are now rolling out grid-integrated systems of home batteries, often paired with solar. Barriers still remain for longer-term storage of solar across seasons, cloudy periods and monsoon seasons, though, both Rosenow and Jones say. It means the integration of solar into the wider electricity system still matters, says Rosenow. Solar is seen as a key part of the push towards electrification , reducing fossil fuel use in areas that previously didn't use electricity, such as via electric cars. Electrification has been chosen as a major theme at this year's UN climate talks in Turkey . "That's where solar's going, to not just be king of electricity, but king of energy," says Jones.  Still, it all requires a plan, Julia Souder, chief executive of the Long Duration Energy Storage Council, a global executive-led non-profit established at COP26, warned recently . "There is an inherent danger in uncontrolled electrification, and adding massive new loads without built-in flexibility creates a fragile system," she wrote in a blog for international policy network Ren21. "Electrification is not automatically resilient."  The limits on solar are now grids, storage and how fast we electrify demand, says Rosenow – not panels or cost. "The bigger question is no longer whether solar grows but whether our power systems and institutions can keep up." In the US, data centres and electrification mean power demand is growing for the first time in decades, says Zhao, with energy security a national priority .  "Renewables already make up over 90% of new capacity in the US," she says. "This need for secure, quickly deployable electricity could create a critical opportunity for [further] renewable energy growth even without support from the current federal government." In the past few years, plug-in panels (or "balcony solar"), have started spreading rapidly in Germany . These generate less electricity than rooftop panels but feed it directly into homes via a standard socket. They have now been approved in several other countries and US states including California . Meanwhile, agrivoltaics, which combines food production and solar panels, is being touted as a solution to concerns in some areas about the land use of solar. Other technologies from floating and "mirror" solar plants to perovskite panels and solar windows could all see growth in coming years. In 2026, the world's solar capacity will go on rising, but the rate of expansion may slow down for the first time ever, says Jones. This is down to China: last summer, it changed its regime for managing and supporting new solar installations , leading to a burst of installations in 2025 to fall under the old price regime. Elsewhere, it's a different picture. "If you exclude China, there's more panels being installed this year than last year," says Jones. By 2030, the IEA thinks solar power generation will have reached double that of 2025's levels, with solar overtaking hydro to become the world's third-largest electricity source . "Wherever grid power is costly and unreliable, the economics keep pulling people towards solar," says Rosenow. "There is one caveat: if Chinese solar panels are difficult to import this will not happen at speed."  More like this: • The US state replacing power plants with home batteries •  The dream of beaming solar energy from orbit • Perovskite: The 'wonder material' that could transform solar   There has been a lot of bad news about the climate recently. It's now incredibly likely the 1.5C global limit set in Paris in 2015 will be breached, the world is seeing rising climate impacts and is edging towards several climate tipping points this century. But the solar success story shows we are also making progress in ways that were never anticipated. A decade ago, "no one was getting close to expecting that to happen", says Jones, noting that the growth in clean electricity has directly translated to fewer coal plants being built.  "Now, worst cases [of climate change] are somewhere between 2-3C of warming, rather than 4C of warming."  -- For essential climate news and hopeful developments to your inbox, sign up to the Future Earth newsletter, while The Essential List delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights twice a week. 9小时前 分享 收藏 在Google上设为首选 Jocelyn Timperley 在一次次超出预期之后，太阳能的迅猛增长意味着它如今正超越核能，成为全球性电力来源。以下是太阳能成功的七个原因，以及它未来可能的走向。全球太阳能发电正在跨越一个门槛。十年前，它在全球范围内几乎无足轻重，仅提供世界1%的电力。到2026年，这一比例几乎可以肯定将升至10%，并超越自20世纪70年代末以来一直是电力支柱的核能。

##段落
根据英国能源智库Ember的统计数据，2025年全球太阳能发电量（勉强）悄然超过了核能。而BBC对截至2026年9月的过去12个月Ember数据的分析显示，太阳能已明显超越核能，发电量高出13%。"太阳能发电量超过全球所有核电站的总和，这确实是个相当惊人的数字，"Ember联合创始人戴夫·琼斯说。从中国庞大的光伏阵列，到近期油价上涨推动的太阳能热潮，太阳能的惊人崛起超出了所有预测。以下是它成为看似"不可阻挡的力量"的七个方面——以及未来从这里走向何方。

##段落
"太阳能如今是能源转型的引擎，"英国牛津大学能源与气候政策教授扬·罗森诺说。太阳能已成为历史上增长最快的新增电力来源，也是迄今为止全球最大的新增电力来源。2025年，它满足了全球电力需求增长的四分之三，超过了风力发电（风电也在增长，只是稍慢一些）。"这就是太阳能的走向——不仅要做电力之王，还要做能源之王，"戴夫·琼斯说。

##段落
"这出乎意料，"罗森诺说。他表示，主流预测年复一年地低估了太阳能。国际能源署（IEA）等机构——这家总部位于巴黎、颇具影响力的政府间组织——的展望"假设了线性增长和成本缓慢下降，结果两者都判断错了"。2026年全年，多方信息表明全球太阳能发电量几乎必将远超核能。自2000年以来，核能发电量基本保持恒定，而太阳能发电量增长了约2700倍。太阳能作为一种成熟技术已有约15年，并在2020年成为历史上最便宜的电力。琼斯说，自那以后，太阳能规模扩大、效率提升，电池板中使用的硅和银用量减少，价格进一步下降。"中国庞大的制造规模和当前的产能过剩已将组件价格推至历史低点，"罗森诺说。尤其是2023至2024年间组件价格的大幅下跌，推……

##段落
这把我们带入了琼斯所称的“便宜得离谱”的太阳能时代。“一块光伏板本身就便宜得令人难以置信，”他说，“远低于100美元（75英镑）……而且它能为你发电30、40年，完全不需要任何投入。”当然，太阳能降低成本并不只是纯粹经济意义上的。研究人员计算得出，美国不断增长的风能和太阳能发电在2019年至2022年间带来了2490亿美元（1860亿英镑）的气候与健康效益。中国仍是迄今为止全球最大的太阳能发电国，但绝非唯一的参与者。尽管美国对太阳能施加了各种关税，它仍然是装机量第二的国家，而且装机量仍在飙升——尤其是在2024年特朗普总统赢下的那些州。事实上，美国现在的太阳能发电量足以满足超过三分之一家庭的用电需求。“限制可再生能源增长的关税和其他联邦政策，确实会相对我们本可看到的局面抬高成本、放缓扩张，”马里兰大学美国减排路径专家艾丽西亚·赵说，“然而，经济性是太阳能得以如此快速发展的关键原因之一。即便成本上升，太阳能仍是美国新增电力中最便宜的来源之一。而且无论政治立场如何，它都在被建设。”与此同时，印度摆脱化石燃料的速度远比中国当年快得多，过去两年新增太阳能满足了其电力需求增长的60%。在澳大利亚，如今有超过400万户家庭安装了屋顶太阳能：远超全部家庭的三分之一。巴基斯坦和黎巴嫩等国也已开始以极快的速度安装太阳能，而非洲各国每天安装约10万块太阳能板。在许多地方，俄乌冲突和美以对伊战争推动柴油价格不断上涨，使成本天平进一步向太阳能倾斜。在許多非洲国家尤其如此，由于电网不可靠，家用柴油发电机是主要依靠。屋顶太阳能板——几乎全部进口自中国——如今已作为替代方案迅速普及。琼斯说，埃塞俄比亚甚至禁止进口汽油和柴油汽车，以应对石油依赖和污染问题。在化石燃料电网无法满足需求的地方，太阳能也在迅速提供新的电力。例如，巴基斯坦因其装机量的超高速增长，已成为太阳能革命出人意料的典范。2019年，太阳能提供的电力不足其总量的2%；如今这一比例已达24%，驱动力来自昂贵且不可靠的电网电力，以及来自中国的廉价太阳能进口产品。“巴基斯坦真正令人惊叹的是……总体而言，大部分太阳能热潮一直是

##段落
“这不需要人们掏空钱包，”琼斯说，“人们负担得起，无需贷款。”从黎巴嫩到尼日利亚，其他几个“阳光地带”国家也出现了类似情况。“（太阳能）让家庭无需等待政府或公用事业公司就能行动，”罗森诺说，“在不确定的时期，这种速度和独立性极具价值。”当然，太阳能只能在白天阳光照射时产生。要将其转化为可随时调度的电力，就需要与电池配套。幸运的是，电池自身也经历了一场成本革命，改变了其支持太阳能推广的能力。“在阳光充足的地区，太阳能加储能现在的成本通常低于新建化石燃料电厂，”罗森诺说，“电池已在很大程度上解决了将正午阳光转移到傍晚的日常难题。”例如在加利福尼亚，2026年上半年，太阳能和电池在19：00至21：00（傍晚高峰）平均满足了超过四分之一的电力需求。佛蒙特等美国州份正在推广家庭电池与电网整合的系统，通常与太阳能配套使用。不过，罗森诺和琼斯都表示，太阳能在跨季节、阴天和季风季节的长期储存方面仍存在障碍。罗森诺说，这意味着太阳能融入更广泛的电力系统仍然很重要。太阳能被视为推动电气化的关键一环，可减少此前不使用电力的领域（如电动汽车）的化石燃料使用。电气化已被选为今年在土耳其举行的联合国气候谈判的主要主题。“这就是太阳能的走向——不仅成为电力之王，还要成为能源之王，”琼斯说。尽管如此，这一切都需要规划，长时储能理事会首席执行官朱莉娅·苏德近日警告说。该理事会是一家在COP26上成立的全球性高管主导的非营利组织。“不受控制的电气化存在固有危险，在没有内置灵活性的情况下增加大量新负荷会造就一个脆弱的系统，”她在为国际政策网络Ren21撰写的博客中写道，“电气化并不会自动具备韧性。”罗森诺说，太阳能目前的限制在于电网、储能以及我们电气化需求的速度——而非组件或成本。“更大的问题不再是太阳能是否会增长，而是我们的电力系统和机构能否跟上。”赵表示，在美国，数据中心和电气化意味着电力需求几十年来首次增长，能源安全成为国家优先事项。“可再生能源已占美国新增装机容量的90%以上，”她说，“这种对安全、可快速部署电力的需求，可能为（进一步的）可再生能源增长创造关键机遇，即使没有当前……的支持。”

##段落
联邦政府。”过去几年，即插即用式光伏板（或称“阳台光伏”）在德国开始迅速普及。这些设备发的电比屋顶光伏板少，但可通过标准插座直接为家庭供电。目前，它已在其他多个国家和美国多个州（包括加利福尼亚州）获批。与此同时，将农业生产与光伏板相结合的“农光互补”模式，正被推崇为解决部分地区光伏用地担忧的方案。从漂浮式光伏和“镜面”光伏电站，到钙钛矿光伏板和光伏窗户，其他技术在未来几年都可能迎来增长。琼斯表示，2026年全球光伏装机容量将继续增长，但扩张速度可能首次放缓。这主要归因于中国：去年夏天，中国调整了新建光伏设施的管理和支持机制，导致2025年出现一波抢装潮，以赶上旧的价格机制。在其他地区，情况则不同。琼斯说：“如果把中国排除在外，今年安装的光伏板比去年更多。”国际能源署认为，到2030年，光伏发电量将达到2025年水平的两倍，光伏将超越水电，成为世界第三大电力来源。罗森诺表示：“在电网电力昂贵且不可靠的地方，经济因素会持续推动人们转向光伏。但有一个前提：如果中国光伏板难以进口，这一进程就不会快速实现。”更多类似内容：• 美国这个州正用家庭电池取代发电厂 • 从轨道传输太阳能的梦想 • 钙钛矿：可能改变光伏格局的“神奇材料”近期关于气候的坏消息很多。2015年巴黎协定设定的1.5摄氏度全球升温上限如今极有可能被突破，世界正目睹气候影响加剧，并正滑向本世纪多个气候临界点。但光伏的成功故事表明，我们也在以从未预料到的方式取得进展。琼斯说，十年前，“没有人接近预料到这种情况会发生”，并指出清洁电力的增长已直接转化为燃煤电厂建设的减少。“如今，气候变化的最坏情况大约在升温2至3摄氏度之间，而不是4摄氏度。”——欲获取重要气候新闻和令人鼓舞的进展，请订阅“未来地球”新闻简报；而“精选清单”每周两次为您送上精心挑选的特稿与洞见。欲了解更多BBC的科学、技术、环境与健康报道，请在脸书和Instagram上关注我们。地球 太阳能 可再生能源 技术 可持续性 能源 电力 中国 专题报道

readings.title: A smart way to handle anxiety — courtesy of soccer great Lionel Messi
body: A smart way to handle anxiety — courtesy of soccer great Lionel Messi
What separates the very best in the world from the remaining 7 billion of us?

Exceptional talent often looks like an act of revolution — a person doing something in a way no one has ever done it before — but many revolutionary talents are actually built on a foundation of evolutionary tweaks. These tweaks develop over time, often compensating for weaknesses and anxieties that might derail a lesser talent.
For all his brilliance, though, Messi is famously anxious. For several years, he habitually vomited on the field before big matches.

Take the world’s best soccer player, an Argentinean named Lionel Messi. Messi has won more Ballon d’Or trophies, awarded to the best soccer player of the year, than any other player. He has scored more goals in a calendar year than any other living player, is the top all-time scorer in Spain’s La Liga, and has the highest goal ratio in the sport today, scoring almost once every match.

For all his brilliance, though, he’s famously anxious. For several years, Messi habitually vomited on the field before big matches. After a string of disappointing national-team losses, another former Argentinean giant of the game, the late Diego Maradona, uncharitably criticized Messi by suggesting that it was “useless trying to make a leader out of a man who goes to the toilet twenty times before a game.”

Being incredibly talented doesn’t immunize you against anxiety, and many of the world’s best grapple with anxiety precisely because they expect so much from themselves. But Messi hasn’t allowed his anxiety to diminish his brilliance because he’s mastered a coping mechanism that also doubles as the secret behind his tactical brilliance.
Messi does two things during these first few minutes. First, he calms himself. Second, he scopes out the opposition.

A soccer match runs for 90 minutes (plus a few minutes for “injury time”), and most players are active in the game from the first minute. As soon as the whistle blows, they implore their teammates to pass the ball and pursue the tactics their coaches laid out before the game.

But Messi is famous for not playing the game during its opening minutes. This is his evolutionary tweak, which developed as he played the game at progressively higher levels. For the opening minutes, Messi ambles back and forth near the middle of the field and almost never engages with his teammates. Whereas other players run and sometimes sprint, Messi spends much of his time walking, rarely breaking into more than a slow jog.

Messi does two things during these first few minutes. First, he calms himself. Easing into the game is Messi’s way of ensuring he’s fully engaged for the remainder of the game. His on-field vomiting has resolved itself, in part perhaps because he’s found a more effective way to calm his nerves. Second, he spends this time scoping out the opposition. His legs move slowly, but his eyes dart from player to player, assessing his opponents’ strengths, weaknesses, and tactics, and monitoring his own team’s movement with and around the ball. Messi is less valuable to his team early in the game, but this tactical pause elevates his value for the remaining 95 percent of the game.

If you split soccer game play into “preparatory” and “engaged” components, Messi leans heavily on preparation. During one classic game between Messi’s Barcelona and archrivals Real Madrid, in 2017, Messi ran for just four minutes and walked for more than eighty of the game’s ninety minutes. When he was engaged, though, he was dynamic, creating nine chances, scoring one goal, and feeding the ball to a teammate who scored another goal.
As you might imagine, pausing is harder than it sounds. In the face of silence and anxiety, our instinct is to act.

That pattern isn’t unusual for Messi, and it’s often in the biggest games that he accentuates his in-game preparation. That preparation also explains his ability to find himself in the right place at the right time, over and over. Though his positional play appears otherworldly, it isn’t a miracle; it’s that he’s learned, minute by minute, that a particular defender leaves a particular square of pitch uncovered or that two midfielders leave a small corner of the pitch open when they gravitate to the middle of the field.
The lesson for the rest of us is clear: When you’re anxious, whether in athletics or in life more broadly, pause. Slow down . Prepare.

As you might imagine, pausing is harder than it sounds. In the face of silence and anxiety, our instinct is to act. Judson Brewer, a psychiatrist and neuroscientist, has spent much of his career thinking about how to do nothing.
About fifteen years ago, Brewer developed a mindfulness-based treatment for addiction.
His approach instructs addicts to resist the waves of anxiety during moments of craving by following the four steps of an approach that goes by the acronym RAIN:
I nvestigate your emotions and thoughts (e.g., “What is happening in my body now?”)
N ote what is happening from moment to moment.

Brewer has said that his approach was inspired by clinical psychologist Tara Brach’s . To test the approach, Brewer worked with smokers who were struggling to quit. Nicotine addiction is notoriously stubborn — more so than many harder drugs that produce stronger immediate responses in users.

Before unleashing the program on smokers, Brewer wanted to test the system on himself. The problem was “I was a nonsmoker,” Brewer wrote, “who needed to be able to relate to patients who felt as though their heads were going to explode unless they smoked.”

Nicotine has a half-life of around two hours, so to begin, smokers need to resist the urge to light up for two hours at a time. Brewer reasoned that smokers who could last two hours without a cigarette would cultivate new nonsmoking habits, extending those stretches till they no longer felt the urge to smoke at all.

He simulated these periods of resistance by learning to meditate for two-hour stretches without moving. During moments of restlessness, he followed the RAIN steps — recognize, allow, investigate, note — and if he moved his body, the clock would reset, and he’d have to start again.

This might sound easy, but two hours is a long time to sit still without entertainment. “Surprisingly it wasn’t the physical pain of not shifting for a long time that got me,” Brewer wrote. “It was the restlessness … Those cravings shouted, ‘Get up!’ ”
Months later, when most of the patients on other treatment plans had relapsed, his mindfulness group stayed clean.

For many months, Brewer would get close, then restlessness would defeat him. “Then one day,” he wrote, “I did it. I sat for the full two hours … Each subsequent sit got easier and easier because I had the confidence that it could be done. And I knew that my patients could quit smoking. They simply needed the proper tools.”

Brewer was right. His patients had been stuck, incapable of quitting one of the most addictive substances on earth. But when he ran study after study, pitting his RAIN mindfulness method against the most effective addiction treatment approaches of the day, his approach was more than twice as effective.

Months later, when most of the patients on other treatment plans had relapsed, his mindfulness group stayed clean. They were more than five times as likely to have shaken their addictions using an approach that essentially taught them to pause at the moment their bodies were most urgently driving them to act.

Of the four steps in Brewer’s RAIN approach, the second — allowing — is perhaps the most critical. Allowing an experience to wash over you sounds disarmingly easy because it doesn’t require you to do anything. But that’s exactly the point. It’s difficult because you’re forced to do nothing despite the urge to act.

是什么将世界上最顶尖的人与我们其余70亿人区分开来？
非凡的天赋往往看起来像一场革命——一个人以从未有人用过的方式去做某件事——但许多革命性的天赋实际上建立在渐进式微调的基础之上。这些微调随时间逐步发展，常常是为了弥补那些可能让稍逊一筹的天才偏离正轨的弱点和焦虑。
然而，尽管才华横溢，梅西却以焦虑著称。有几年时间，他习惯性地在大赛前于球场上呕吐。
以世界上最优秀的足球运动员、阿根廷人莱昂内尔·梅西为例。梅西获得的颁发给年度最佳足球运动员的金球奖奖杯数量超过任何其他球员。他在一个自然年内的进球数超过任何其他在世球员，是西班牙甲级联赛的历史最佳射手，并且拥有当今足坛最高的进球率——几乎每场比赛都能攻入一球。
然而，尽管才华横溢，他却以焦虑著称。有几年时间，梅西习惯性地在大赛前于球场上呕吐。在一连串令人失望的国家队失利之后，另一位阿根廷足球传奇人物、已故的迭戈·马拉多纳毫不留情地批评梅西，暗示“试图把一个赛前要上二十次厕所的人培养成领袖是徒劳的”。
才华横溢并不能让你对焦虑免疫，世界上许多最优秀的人恰恰因为对自己期望太高而与焦虑搏斗。但梅西没有让焦虑削弱他的光芒，因为他掌握了一种应对机制，而这种机制同时也是他战术天赋背后的秘密。
在这开场几分钟里，梅西做了两件事。第一，他让自己平静下来。第二，他观察对手。
一场足球比赛持续90分钟（加上几分钟的“伤停补时”），大多数球员从第一分钟起就积极参与比赛。哨声一响，他们就催促队友传球，执行教练赛前布置的战术。
但梅西以在开场几分钟内不参与比赛而闻名。这就是他的渐进式微调，是随着他在越来越高的水平上踢球而逐渐发展出来的。在开场几分钟里，梅西在球场中部附近来回踱步，几乎从不与队友互动。其他球员奔跑、有时冲刺，而梅西大部分时间都在走路，很少加速到超过慢跑的节奏。

##段落
这是ssi确保自己在比赛剩余时间里全情投入的方式。他在场上呕吐的问题已经自行缓解，部分原因也许是他找到了更有效的镇定神经的办法。其次，他利用这段时间摸清对手的底细。他的双腿缓慢移动，但目光却在球员之间来回扫视，评估对手的强弱与战术，同时观察本队围绕球的跑动与配合。比赛初期，梅西对球队的价值相对较低，但这段战术性的暂停提升了他在剩余95%比赛时间里的价值。

##段落
如果把足球比赛拆分为“准备”和“投入”两个部分，梅西严重偏向准备。2017年梅西所在的巴塞罗那与宿敌皇家马德里之间的一场经典比赛中，梅西只跑了四分钟，而在九十分钟的比赛里走了八十多分钟。然而当他投入时，他极具爆发力——创造了九次机会，打入一球，还助攻队友再进一球。

##段落
可以想见，暂停比听起来要难。面对沉默与焦虑，我们的本能是行动。

##段落
这种模式对梅西来说并不罕见，而且往往是在最重大的比赛中，他更加突出自己赛中的准备工作。这种准备也解释了他为何能一次又一次地出现在正确的位置、正确的时间。尽管他的位置感看似超凡脱俗，但这并非奇迹；而是他逐分钟地摸清了某位后卫会漏掉哪块草皮，或者哪两名中场在向中路靠拢时会留出球场哪个小角落的空当。

##段落
给我们其他人的启示很清楚：当你焦虑时，无论是在竞技体育还是更广泛的生活中，暂停。放慢。准备。

##段落
可以想见，暂停比听起来要难。面对沉默与焦虑，我们的本能是行动。精神病学家兼神经科学家贾德森·布鲁尔职业生涯的大部分时间都在思考如何“什么都不做”。

##段落
大约十五年前，布鲁尔开发了一种基于正念的成瘾治疗方法。

##段落
他的方法指导成瘾者在渴求发作时，通过遵循一个缩写为RAIN的四步法来抵御焦虑的浪潮：

##段落
Recognize what is arising.（识别正在升起的东西。）

##段落
Allow it to be there.（允许它存在。）

##段落
Investigate your emotions and thoughts (e.g., "What is happening in my body now?")（探究你的情绪与想法，例如“我身体里现在发生了什么？”）

##段落
Note what is happening from moment to moment.（逐刻留意正在发生的事。）

##段落
布鲁尔曾表示，他的方法受到临床心理学家塔拉·布拉赫的启发。为检验该方法，布鲁尔与正在努力戒烟的吸烟者合作。尼古丁成瘾以顽固著称——比许多能对使用者产生更强即时反应的硬性毒品更难戒断。

##段落
在全面推行该方案之前

##段落
布鲁尔想在自己身上测试这套方法，对象是吸烟者。问题在于，“我是一个不吸烟的人，”布鲁尔写道，“却需要能够理解那些觉得除非抽烟否则脑袋就要炸开的患者。”

##段落
尼古丁的半衰期约为两小时，因此一开始，吸烟者需要一次抵抗两小时不点烟的冲动。布鲁尔推断，能坚持两小时不抽烟的吸烟者会培养出新的不吸烟习惯，逐渐延长这些时段，直到完全不再有抽烟的冲动。

##段落
他通过练习冥想、连续两小时不动来模拟这些抵抗期。在躁动不安的时刻，他遵循RAIN步骤——识别、允许、探究、标注——如果他动了身体，计时就会重置，他必须重新开始。

##段落
这听起来可能很简单，但两个小时不动、没有任何消遣，是一段很长的时间。“出乎意料的是，让我难受的并不是长时间不挪动的身体疼痛，”布鲁尔写道，“而是那种躁动不安……那些渴望在喊：‘起来！’”

##段落
几个月后，当其他治疗方案的大多数患者已经复吸时，他的正念小组依然保持戒断。

##段落
有好几个月，布鲁尔总是接近成功，然后躁动不安击败了他。“然后有一天，”他写道，“我做到了。我坐满了整整两个小时……之后每一次静坐都变得越来越容易，因为我有信心这件事可以做到。而且我知道我的患者能够戒烟。他们只是需要合适的工具。”

##段落
布鲁尔是对的。他的患者一直困在原地，无法戒掉地球上最容易上瘾的物质之一。但当他开展一项又一项研究，将自己的RAIN正念方法与当时最有效的成瘾治疗方法进行对比时，他的方法效果高出一倍多。

##段落
几个月后，当其他治疗方案的大多数患者已经复吸时，他的正念小组依然保持戒断。他们用这种本质上教会他们在身体最迫切驱使自己去行动的瞬间暂停下来的方法，成功戒除成瘾的可能性高出五倍多。

##段落
在布鲁尔RAIN方法的四个步骤中，第二步——允许——或许是最关键的。让一种体验冲刷而过，听起来容易得令人放下戒备，因为它不需要你做任何事情。但这恰恰是关键所在。它之所以困难，是因为你被迫在冲动面前什么都不做。

##段落
然而，尽管暂停和准备有诸多好处，有时候正事并不会按计划进行。梅西输掉了无数场比赛，布鲁尔实验结束后，也并非所有尼古丁成瘾者都在数周或数月后仍保持戒断。掌握这些失败之后的焦虑和不适至关重要，而这也是最

readings.title: Is Italy the new tax haven for the global rich?
body: 22 April 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google John Laurenson Italy has already been attacked by the French Government for using tax incentives to lure wealthy French and other international residents away, but with the war in the Middle East hurting the Gulf states, Italy has become an even more attractive location for the rich. Tax wasn't the main reason for leaving France, Robert insists over a café crème at Charles de Gaulle airport. It was the beauty of Italy, the bella vita  (the beautiful/good life), the art and the music. But for the Frenchman, buying a house in Rome and becoming an Italian tax resident was a very nice part of the package offered by the country, where high net worth individuals can pay a fixed annual tax on all foreign income – regardless of amount – and enjoy a series of other exemptions.  Robert, who describes himself as only "moderately wealthy", moved to Italy eight years ago after a career in computers which ended with him selling his company. Robert, not his real name, may not be among the French billionaires who have fled the French taxman for Italy, but the advantages to him are clear.   If he'd been buying a house in France, he would have had to pay what the French call frais de notaire (solicitor's fees) most of which goes to the government (much like Stamp Duty in the UK or Real Estate Transfer Taxes in the US). In Italy there's an exemption for the prima casa , the first house you buy. In France, President Macron transformed France's Impot sur la Fortune  (wealth tax) into an Impot sur la Fortune Immobilière  (real estate wealth tax) so stock market investments, for example, are no longer affected but "if you have ten million dollars' worth of property, this tax is very painful indeed," says Robert. Again, there's nothing like that in Italy.  In France you also have to pay a property tax ( taxe foncière or land tax). "We don't have that here for the prima casa (first home)," says Robert, although he notes "there is a high charge for refuse collection". The best thing as far as he is concerned is that there is no inheritance tax on property you own in Italy up to €1 million ($1.1 million) and it's only 4% beyond that threshold. In France the tax-free limit is much lower – €100,000 ($110,000) – and beyond that it's a sliding scale up to a top rate of 45%. But it's for the seriously rich that Italy starts to look like a fiscal paradise. "I have friends who have moved here for tax reasons and others who are thinking about it," Robert tells me. "For people who really pay a lot of tax, Italy is very attractive because of it's "flat tax". In Italy, the taxman fixes an upper limit of tax that can be levied on income. However much you earn, you never pay more than that. The upper limit is now €300,000 ($353,000). Although not long ago it was €100,000 before rising to €200,000. If you're paying a million euros of income tax a year in France, Italy is very tempting. As for US citizens, Americans are always taxable on worldwide income, so moving to Italy would not help their tax bill. Even at €300,000, Italy's flat tax is still low for anyone making over €1m per year compared to anywhere else in Europe – Peter Ferrigno Robert tells me that he has two rich French friends who have moved to Italy in the past few months, but they came from the UK. They were both working in finance in the City of London and were keen to move to a place where the fiscal regime was as sympathetic to them as the one Britain had before it changed the rules for wealthy foreign residents.  "Even at €300,000, Italy's flat tax is still low for anyone making over €1m per year compared to anywhere else in Europe. And it means you get tax certainty and clarity, within the heart of Europe, rather than having to go a long way," says Peter Ferrigno, director of tax services at wealth migration specialists Henley & Partners. "We have meetings with people every week who would like to leave France," says Paris-based tax lawyer Jerome Barre. "They are unhappy about the tax situation now and they are worried that it will become harsher in the future. People are not confident with the political climate. Taxes are changing a lot, almost every year. People are frightened that after the election of the new president in 2027, things could become harder than today," he says. At this stage though it's more "questions from entrepreneurs and wealthy people who are wondering if they would like to move or not move rather than people actually moving," Jerome Barre explains. "Relocation requires full commitment and careful structuring," he stresses. He adds that for business-owners  " they need to change the seat of the company. They are subject in France to an exit tax." If many wealthy French people are at the "thinking-about-moving" stage, the question is being felt even more acutely in the United Arab Emirates. It's inevitable that many people will reconsider UAE – Peter Ferrigno But giving up on Dubai's zero-tax regime will be very difficult for many. "When you are in a country where you do not pay any tax, it's very difficult to come back to a country where you have to pay a lot. Especially for those used to spending a lot of money. The net in your pocket is very different, says Barre. And, he adds, people who have grown used to the zero-tax life "are not used to administrative formalities anymore – tax returns, documents – so it's not easy." More like this: • Dubai's tourism industry reels from 'brutal' impact of war • Why more Americans are now moving to Ireland • Is New York's cannabis business really flying high? "It's inevitable that many people will reconsider UAE," says Henley & Partners' Peter Ferrigno. "But I think it's far too early for people to wholesale uproot their life when it involves work, family, etc. The vast majority of people in the UAE are still regular people doing regular jobs, even most of the millionaires are millionaires because they are doing well paid jobs rather than being asset owners. If the war is relatively short, they will remain. If it drags on, then people will inevitably look elsewhere, or relocate the family and work remotely until it's safer. If you're in the UAE for work, there aren't likely to be that many equivalent roles in Italy," he says. However, it is likely that the war in the Middle East will dissuade many rich Europeans who would have otherwise moved there from re-locating to the UAE. Last year, Dubai was the number one destination by far for migrating millionaires, according to Henley & Partners. That number is bound to tumble in 2026, and with its attractive offer for the very wealthy, as well as its reputation for  la dolce vita  of course, it may well be Italy that benefits. -- For global insights and expert analysis for the boardroom and beyond, sign up to the  World of Business newsletter , while  The Essential List  delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights.  For more on business and beyond, follow us on  LinkedIn . ##段落
2026年4月22日 分享 收藏 在Google上设为首选 约翰·劳伦森 意大利此前已因利用税收优惠吸引富裕的法国人及其他国际居民迁入，而遭到法国政府的抨击；但随着中东战争冲击海湾国家，意大利对富人而言已成为更具吸引力的地方。罗伯特在戴高乐机场一边喝着咖啡奶油，一边坚称，离开法国的主要原因并不是税收。真正的原因是意大利的美、美好生活（bella vita）、艺术和音乐。但对这位法国人来说，在罗马买房并成为意大利税务居民，是这个国家所提供的一揽子条件中非常美好的一部分——在意大利，高净值人士可以就全部海外收入缴纳固定的年度税额，无论金额多少，还可享受一系列其他豁免。罗伯特自称只是“中等富裕”，八年前在结束计算机行业的职业生涯并卖掉公司后移居意大利。罗伯特（化名）或许不属于那些为躲避法国税务部门而逃往意大利的法国亿万富翁之列，但对他来说，好处显而易见。如果他是在法国买房，就必须支付法国人所说的公证费（frais de notaire），其中大部分归政府所有（很像英国的印花税或美国的房地产转让税）。在意大利，购买首套房（prima casa）可享受豁免。在法国，马克龙总统将法国的财富税（Impot sur la Fortune）改为房地产财富税（Impot sur la Fortune Immobilière），因此股票市场投资等不再受影响，但罗伯特说，“如果你拥有价值一千万美元的房产，这项税确实非常沉重”。而在意大利，根本没有类似税种。在法国，你还必须缴纳房产税（taxe foncière，即土地税）。“我们这里首套房不用交，”罗伯特说，不过他提到“垃圾收集费很高”。在他看来，最好的一点是，你在意大利拥有的房产价值不超过100万欧元（110万美元）时无需缴纳遗产税，超过该门槛也仅需缴纳4%。在法国，免税上限要低得多——10万欧元（11万美元）——超过部分按累进税率征收，最高可达45%。但正是对真正的富豪来说，意大利才开始显得像避税天堂。罗伯特告诉我：“我有朋友因税务原因搬到这里，还有其他人在考虑这么做。”“对于真正缴纳大量税款的人来说，意大利因其‘单一税’而非常有吸引力。”在意大利，税务部门对可征收的收入设定了一个上限。无论你赚多少，缴税都不会超过这个上限。目前的上限是30万欧元（35.3万美元）。尽管

##段落
尽管不久前还是10万欧元，后来涨到了20万欧元。如果你在法国每年缴纳100万欧元的所得税，意大利就非常有吸引力了。至于美国公民，美国人始终需要就其全球收入纳税，所以搬到意大利并不会减轻他们的税负。即便税率是30万欧元，对于年收入超过100万欧元的人来说，意大利的单一税率相比欧洲其他地方仍然很低——彼得·费里尼奥告诉我，他有两位富有的法国朋友在过去几个月搬到了意大利，但他们是从英国搬来的。这两人此前都在伦敦金融城从事金融工作，并且都渴望搬到一个税收制度对他们同样友好的地方，就像英国在修改针对富裕外国居民的规则之前那样。

##段落
“即便税率是30万欧元，对于年收入超过100万欧元的人来说，意大利的单一税率相比欧洲其他地方仍然很低。而且这意味着你能在欧洲腹地获得税收的确定性和清晰度，而不必远走他乡，”财富移民专业机构Henley & Partners的税务服务总监彼得·费里尼奥表示。“我们每周都会与想要离开法国的人会面，”驻巴黎的税务律师杰罗姆·巴雷说。“他们对当前的税收状况不满，并且担心未来会变得更加严苛。人们对政治气候缺乏信心。税收变化很大，几乎每年都在变。人们害怕在2027年新总统选举之后，情况可能会比现在更艰难，”他说。不过，巴雷解释说，现阶段更多的是“企业家和富人在提出问题，他们在想自己要不要搬走，而不是人们真的在搬迁”。“搬迁需要全身心的投入和精心的规划，”他强调说。他补充说，对于企业主而言，“他们需要更换公司的注册地。他们在法国需要缴纳退出税。”如果许多富裕的法国人正处于“考虑搬迁”的阶段，那么这个问题在阿联酋的感受甚至更为强烈。彼得·费里尼奥说，很多人重新考虑阿联酋是不可避免的。但对许多人来说，放弃迪拜的零税制将非常困难。“当你身处一个不用缴任何税的国家，要回到一个需要缴纳大量税款的国家是非常困难的。尤其是对于那些习惯了大手大脚花钱的人来说。你口袋里的净收入差别很大，”巴雷说。他还补充说，那些已经习惯了零税生活的人“不再习惯行政手续——纳税申报、文件——所以这并不容易。”更多类似内容：• 迪拜旅游业因战争的“残酷”冲击而震荡 • 为什么越来越多的美国人现在搬到爱尔兰 • 纽约的大麻生意真的在腾飞吗

igh？“很多人重新考虑阿联酋是不可避免的，”Henley & Partners的彼得·费里尼奥表示。“但我认为，现在让人们因为工作、家庭等因素而彻底连根拔起还为时过早。阿联酋的绝大多数人仍然是从事普通工作的普通人，甚至大多数百万富翁之所以是百万富翁，是因为他们从事高薪工作，而不是因为他们是资产所有者。如果战争相对短暂，他们会留下来。如果战争拖下去，那么人们不可避免地会另寻他处，或者把家人安置到别处、远程工作，直到局势更安全为止。如果你在阿联酋是为了工作，那么在意大利不太可能有那么多同等的职位，”他说。然而，中东战争很可能会让许多原本会迁往那里的富有欧洲人打消迁居阿联酋的念头。根据Henley & Partners的数据，去年迪拜是迄今为止 migrating millionaires 的首选目的地。这一数字在2026年势必大幅下降，而凭借其对极富人群的吸引力以及当然还有“甜蜜生活”的声誉，意大利很可能成为受益者。——欲获取面向董事会及更高层的全球洞察与专家分析，请订阅《World of Business》新闻简报，而《The Essential List》则精选特稿与洞察。欲了解更多商业及更多内容，请在LinkedIn上关注我们。商业 国际商业 特稿 《World of Business》
