readings.title: When AI agents run your life
body: Explain It to Me When AI agents run your life ﻿Muse, organize my life. Make no mistakes. by Jonquilyn Hill Oct 25, 2026, 11:00 AM UTC Gift An advertisement for Meta’s personal AI agent app Muse at a BART station in San Francisco on October 15, 2026. Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images Jonquilyn Hill is the host of Explain It to Me , your hotline for all your unanswered questions. She joined Vox in 2022 as a senior producer and then as host of The Weeds , Vox’s policy podcast. There are some days when there’s so much that needs to get done, I daydream about having a clone of myself. Between paying bills, life admin like renewing my driver’s license, keeping up with doctor’s appointments, and planning meals, it’s a lot. And that doesn’t even begin to touch the work that goes into making a podcast or managing my social life. This feeling of overwhelm resonates with Sari Azout. She’s a mom of three who works in tech. “There is just so much doing,” she told Explain It to Me, Vox’s weekly call-in podcast. “I wake up, and I have to do meal coordination and get my kids up for breakfast, coordinate carpools. Then a lot of work during the day, but there’s the email from the teacher, there’s the 20 group chats asking if you want to participate in this group gift. They don’t call it ‘the invisible load’ for no reason.’” Silicon Valley says it has a fix for this kind of mental overload. They don’t want to clone us — at least not yet. But they do think they have the next best thing: AI agents. Azuot was skeptical when she first got an invite to try an agent, but she says she eventually came around on the technology after back-to-school shopping snuck up on her. She used her agent to get it done. “It blew me away,” she said. “I remember that night coming home just feeling so calm and reading my son a book and feeling present. And I was like, ‘Wow, I actually was very cynical about something that is giving me more time for living.’” Azout’s experience is, more or less, the sales pitch for AI agents: They’ll help you save time with everyday tasks, so you have more of it for what you want to do. But what are agents, exactly? Are they really all that? And what do we gain — and give up — when we use the technology? On this week’s episode of Explain It to Me , I spoke with Reece Rogers, a senior software reporter at Wired, to find out. Rogers says to think of agents as the next evolution of AI chatbots like Claude and ChatGPT. “I’d create this mental model of a tiny digital assistant that’s constantly searching the web, going through your email, and checking your calendar, trying to find ways it could proactively be helpful for you,” he explains. “Agents are more proactive. It’s scanning your email 24/7 and sending you a message, maybe highlighting a potential calendar conflict.” Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Rogers, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545. What agents are out there right now? At the start of this year, there was a tool called OpenClaw that really sparked this with early adopters in San Francisco, but now there are much more consumer-friendly versions, with one of the most notable being Meta’s Muse. There’s also a tool from OpenAI called Dots. But where Meta’s Muse is free to download, OpenAI’s Dots is still behind a $100/month paywall. You tried an AI agent for a recent story you wrote. How was that experience? One personal example, to share something that I’ve actually been using agents for, is our couch. It’s broken, and finding a new couch has been a pain. We want a sleeper bed, but we want these specific colors. We have this specific budget. I’ve been using Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots to try to find a few different options for us. One interesting thing is that Meta’s Muse is connected to Facebook Marketplace. There are these really good integrations where I can give it all these details, and it found a few good couches that are only maybe a couple blocks from me. I really enjoyed OpenAI’s Dots experience as well. I spent about an hour talking to it on the phone, and the AI agent made a packet of all these different options I could find. Just this morning, it flagged that one of them is now 40 percent off. Is that how this tech is typically used? Most people are using this as part of a workflow. I attach it to my email, I attach it to my calendar, and I’m using it as a personal assistant to organize my life. But people have been quite creative. One of the breakout uses for Meta’s Muse is people have been connecting their bank account statements and then using it to scan for subscriptions they might want to cancel. So it can be used in many different ways, though I will say I do not connect it to my own bank account for a myriad of reasons. I’m not going to lie, the idea of giving any third party access to my bank information does not thrill me. I don’t love that concept. That’s one of my biggest concerns about these AI agents: how much personal information we’re handing over to these large companies. When I tested Meta’s Muse, it wanted access to my email, my bank account, even my passport expiration details. The pitch is convenience, but Muse users are automatically opted in to having all of their interactions with Muse used to train Meta’s AI models. I would definitely recommend, if you’re sharing personal details, go into the settings and turn that off because you might be handing over even more information about yourself than you initially realize. What is the privacy situation with all of this? We all have various apps where we don’t read and still click “I agree,” but this feels like it could be more invasive. Yes, especially because it’s all about automation. If you’re automating things and it has access to all of your data, it could make mistakes and embarrass you in ways you might not even be thinking about. There was this one really interesting story of someone who had connected an AI agent to their work Slack in addition to their bank account. And their agent just automatically posted how much money was in their checking account for all of their coworkers to see. Oh no. I would be mortified. So there are these kinds of mistakes that these AI tools can still make. If you’re interested in experimenting with them, I would be really thoughtful with how you’re setting up these tools as well as what kind of information you feel comfortable sharing. “You can see in the marketing that these companies are trying to find some way to entice new users.” How are these AI agents being marketed? AI is not popular right now . Just ask any politician who has a data center coming to their state . People are not loving it. How are they trying to sell this to the average person? The AI backlash really is at a fever pitch right now. You could almost see that in the way that AI companies are trying to market these tools. They’ve really, really leaned into cuteness and into adorable mascots. Muse, if you haven’t seen its agent, looks like a mix between a Labubu and an Ewok. It’s very furry, very cuddly, very cute. OpenAI’s tools also have similar kinds of blobs with large eyes that might be a little endearing. I feel like companies are hearing this kind of feedback that people aren’t trusting AI right now, or maybe they have moral or ethical reasons they don’t want to use these tools. You can see in the marketing that these companies are trying to find some way to entice new users. Do you think AI agents are ultimately going to worm their way into our lives despite how unpopular AI companies are? I do think so. I think in a couple months, maybe when I go home from Christmas, I would not be surprised if my mom had an agent on her phone because it does feel like it’s breaking through to average people in the way that ChatGPT had a moment a few years ago. Even though there’s a lot of distrust for large companies like Meta, I think there are some appealing parts of this that will bring in millions of people. I do see this as the future of the internet. When I think of the dream of the average person working in AI in Silicon Valley, it’s “We’re going to use AI. It’s going to free up the free time of so many people. Work is going to get done faster. You’re going to have more leisure time. ” Has that been the case for the people you’ve spoken with who are using this? Has it given them more free time to enjoy themselves or has it done something else? You would think so, right? You would think that if people are automating these boring aspects of their life, that they would have more time to go touch grass, go see a movie, have some fun. But it does feel like that time just gets filled with other work, other productivity measures. While agents may be able to take some more annoying or tedious things off of your plate, I am not as optimistic that it’s going to give us this utopia or freedom where I’m always at the beach. 冲突。”以下是我与罗杰斯对话的节选，为篇幅和清晰度做了编辑。你可以在 Apple Podcasts、Spotify 或任何获取播客的平台收听完整节目。如果你想提交问题，请发送邮件至 askvox@vox.com 或致电 1-800-618-8545。目前市面上有哪些智能代理？今年年初，有一款名为 OpenClaw 的工具在旧金山的早期用户中真正引发了这股热潮，但现在已经有了更加面向消费者的版本，其中最引人注目的之一是 Meta 的 Muse。OpenAI 还有一款名为 Dots 的工具。不过，Meta 的 Muse 可以免费下载，而 OpenAI 的 Dots 仍需要每月 100 美元的付费墙。你最近为一篇报道试用了一款 AI 智能代理。那次体验如何？分享一个我实际使用智能代理的个人例子——我们的沙发。它坏了，找新沙发一直很头疼。我们想要一张沙发床，但想要特定的颜色，还有特定的预算。我一直在用 Meta 的 Muse 和 OpenAI 的 Dots 试着帮我们找几个不同的选项。有意思的是，Meta 的 Muse 连接了 Facebook Marketplace。这些集成做得非常好，我可以把所有这些细节告诉它，它找到了几张离我只有几个街区远的好沙发。我也很喜欢 OpenAI 的 Dots 的体验。我花了大约一个小时在电话上和它交谈，这个 AI 智能代理为我整理了一份包含各种可选方案的资料包。就在今天早上，它还提醒我其中一个选项现在打六折。这项技术通常是这样用的吗？大多数人把它作为工作流程的一部分来使用。我把它连接到我的电子邮件、我的日历，把它当作个人助理来安排我的生活。但人们一直很有创意。Meta 的 Muse 的一个爆款用法是，人们连接自己的银行账户对账单，然后用它来扫描可能想要取消的订阅服务。所以它可以用在很多不同的方面，不过我要说的是，出于种种原因，我不会把它连接到自己的银行账户。说实话，让任何第三方访问我的银行信息这个想法并不会让我兴奋。我不喜欢这个概念。这是我对这些 AI 智能代理最大的担忧之一：我们把多少个人信息交给了这些大公司。当我测试 Meta 的 Muse 时，它要求访问我的电子邮件、我的银行账户，甚至我的护照到期信息。卖点是便利，但 Muse 用户会被自动选择将其与 Muse 的所有交互用于训练 Meta 的 AI 模型。我强烈建议，如果你要分享个人信息，进入设置把那个选项关掉，因为你可能正在交出更多信息

readings.title: Let’s stop calling them “soft skills” — and call them “real skills” instead
body: Let’s stop calling them “soft skills” — and call them “real skills” instead
We persist in hiring and training as if we’re running a bowling squad, as if easily measured skills are all that matter.

What causes successful organizations to fail ? What makes stocks fade, innovations slow, customers jump ship? We can agree that certain skills are essential. That hiring coders who can’t code, salespeople who can’t sell, or architects who can’t design is a waste. But these skills — let’s call them vocational skills — have become the backbone of the recruitment process.

But how do you explain that similar organizations, with similarly vocationally skilled people, find themselves with very different outcomes? Most of the textbooks that students experience and the tests they take are about vocational skills, the checkboxes that have to be checked to get a job. By misdefining “vocational” and focusing on these allegedly essential skills, we’ve diminished the value of the other skills that matter.

We give too little respect to the other skills when we call them “soft” and imply that they’re optional. What actually separates thriving organizations from struggling ones are the difficult-to-measure attitudes, processes and perceptions of the people who do the work.

Vocational skills can be taught: You’re not born knowing engineering or copywriting or even graphic design, therefore they must be something we can teach. But we let ourselves off the hook when it comes to decision-making, eager participation, dancing with fear, speaking with authority, working in teams , seeing the truth, speaking the truth, inspiring others, doing more than we’re asked, caring and being willing to change things. We underinvest in this training, fearful that these things are innate and can’t be taught. Perhaps they’re talents. And so we downplay them, calling them soft skills, making it easy for us to move on to something seemingly more urgent.

At scale, organizations pay less attention to soft skills when hiring because we’ve persuaded ourselves that vocational skills are impersonal and easier to measure. If it’s easier to test for, it seems more important when selecting our team.
And we fire slowly (and retrain rarely) when these skills are missing, because we’re worried about stepping on toes, being called out for getting personal or possibly wasting time on a lost cause.

But these skills can all be learned, as obvious skills like chess or typing can be learned. We learn them accidentally, by osmosis, by the collisions we have with teachers, parents, bosses and the world. Even though they’re more difficult to measure, that doesn’t mean we can’t improve them, can’t practice them or can’t change the way we do our work.

Let’s stop calling them soft. They’re interpersonal skills. Leadership skills. The skills of charisma and diligence and contribution. But these modifiers, while accurate, somehow edge them away from the vocational skills, the skills that we actually hire for, the skills we measure a graduate degree on.
So let’s uncomfortably call them real skills instead.
Real because they work, because they’re at the heart of what we need today.
Real because even if you’ve got the vocational skills, you’re no help to us without these human skills, the things that we can’t write down or program a computer to do.
Real skills can’t replace vocational skills, of course. What they can do is amplify the things you’ve already been measuring.
Imagine a team member with all the traditional vocational skills: productive, skilled, experienced. A resume that can prove it. That’s a fine baseline.

Now add to it. Perceptive, charismatic, driven, focused, goal-setting, inspiring and motivated. Generous, empathic and consistent. A deep listener , with patience. What happens to your organization when someone like that joins your team?
Writing in the Harvard Business Review , Lou Solomon reports that 69 percent of managers are uncomfortable communicating with their employees. I’d guess that many of the other 31 percent are lying.

Communicating with employees is uncomfortable because we’ve built systems of compliance and dominance that make it difficult. We ask people to leave their humanity at the door, then use authority to change behavior. We overlay corporate greed and short-term thinking with a human desire to create work that matters.

How do we build people-centric organizations while also accepting the fact that two thirds of our managers (presumably well paid, well trained and integral to our success) are so uncomfortable doing an essential part of their job that they admitted it to a stranger?

In a recent survey, the Graduate Management Admission Council reported that although MBAs were strong in analytical aptitude, quantitative expertise and information-gathering ability, they were sorely lacking in other critical areas that employers find equally attractive: strategic thinking, written and oral communication, leadership and adaptability . Are these mutually exclusive? Must we trade one for the other?

The foundation of all real skills is this one: the confidence and permission to talk to one another. Not to manage, belittle, intimidate or control. Simply to seek to be understood and to do the work to understand.

##段落
我们不要再称它们为“软技能”了——而应称之为“真正的技能”。

##段落
2023年6月9日

##段落
塞斯·高汀

##段落
Facebook X LinkedIn Reddit WhatsApp

##段落
黛博拉·什皮尔曼

##段落
我们一直在招人和培训时表现得像是在组建一支保龄球队，仿佛那些容易衡量的技能才是最重要的。

##段落
是什么导致成功的组织走向失败？是什么让股票走弱、创新放缓、客户流失？我们可以认同某些技能是必不可少的。招聘不会编程的程序员、不会销售的销售员，或不会设计的建筑师，是一种浪费。但这些技能——我们姑且称之为职业技能——已经成为招聘流程的支柱。

##段落
但你怎么解释，相似的組織、拥有职业技能相似的人，却得到截然不同的结果？学生接触的大多数教科书和参加的考试都与职业技能有关，也就是找工作时必须勾选的复选框。通过错误地定义“职业”并聚焦于这些所谓的核心技能，我们贬低了其他重要技能的价值。

##段落
当我们把这些技能称为“软”技能并暗示它们是可选的，我们就对其他技能给予了太少的尊重。真正将蓬勃发展的组织与挣扎中的组织区分开来的，是那些从事工作的人难以衡量的态度、流程和认知。

##段落
职业技能是可以传授的：你不是生来就懂工程、文案甚至平面设计，因此它们必然是我们能够教授的东西。但在决策、积极投入、与恐惧共舞、有权威地表达、团队协作、看清真相、说出真相、激励他人、做得比要求更多、关心他人并愿意改变事物这些方面，我们却对自己网开一面。我们在这些培训上投入不足，担心这些东西是天生的、无法传授。也许它们是天赋。于是我们贬低它们，称它们为软技能，让我们更容易转向看似更紧迫的事情。

##段落
在大规模层面上，组织在招聘时对软技能关注较少，因为我们已经说服自己，职业技能是客观的、更容易衡量。如果更容易测试，那么在挑选团队时它似乎就更重要。

##段落
而当这些技能缺失时，我们解雇得很慢（也很少再培训），因为我们担心冒犯他人、被指责针对个人，或者可能在注定失败的事情上浪费时间。

##段落
但这些技能都是可以学习的，就像国际象棋或打字等显而易见的技能可以学习一样。我们通过潜移默化、通过与老师、父母、老板和世界的碰撞而偶然学会它们。尽管它们更难衡量，但这并不意味着我们无法改进它们、无法练习它们。

##段落
他们也不能改变我们的工作方式。
##段落
当然可以。
##段落
我们别再管它们叫软技能了。它们是人际交往能力。是领导能力。是魅力、勤勉和贡献的能力。但这些修饰语虽然准确，却不知怎地把它们与职业技能——我们真正招聘时看重的能力、我们用来衡量研究生学位的能力——拉开了距离。
##段落
所以，让我们别扭地称它们为"真技能"吧。
##段落
说它们"真"，是因为它们管用，因为它们是我们今天所需的核心所在。
##段落
说它们"真"，是因为即便你拥有职业技能，若缺少这些为人处世的能力——那些我们无法写下来、也无法编程让计算机去做的事——你对我们依然毫无助益。
##段落
当然，真技能无法取代职业技能。它们能做的是放大你早已在衡量的那些东西。
##段落
设想一位具备所有传统职业技能的团队成员：高效、娴熟、经验丰富。一份能证明这一切的简历。这是一个不错的基本盘。
##段落
现在，在此基础上再加点什么。敏锐、有魅力、有驱动力、专注、善于设定目标、鼓舞人心且充满动力。慷慨、共情且始终如一。是一位有耐心的深度倾听者。当这样的人加入你的团队，你的组织会发生什么变化？
##段落
卢·所罗门在《哈佛商业评论》上撰文指出，69%的管理者与员工沟通时感到不自在。我猜其余31%里有很多人在撒谎。
##段落
与员工沟通之所以令人不自在，是因为我们建立了一套服从与支配的体系，让沟通变得困难。我们要求人们把人性留在门外，然后用权威去改变行为。我们用企业对利益的贪婪和短视思维，去掩盖那种想要创造有意义工作的人性渴望。
##段落
我们一边想建立以人为本的组织，一边又要接受这样一个事实：三分之二的管理者（想必薪酬优厚、训练有素、对我们的成功不可或缺）在做自己工作中一项 essential 的部分时如此不自在，以至于他们向一个陌生人坦承了这一点——这两者该如何调和？
##段落
在最近的一项调查中，美国研究生入学管理委员会报告称，尽管MBA在分析能力、定量专业知识和信息收集能力方面很强，但他们在雇主同样看重的其他关键领域却严重欠缺：战略思维、书面与口头沟通、领导力和适应力。这些能力是互斥的吗？我们必须以一项换另一项吗？
##段落
所有真技能的根基只有这一条：彼此交谈的信心与许可。不是为了管理、贬低、恐吓或控制。而仅仅是为了寻求被理解，并付出努力去理解。
##段落
摘自塞斯·高汀的《意义的颂歌：团队新宣言》，经Portfolio（企鹅出版集团旗下品牌，企鹅兰登书屋分部）授权。

readings.title: How social media ceased to be social
body: 22 May 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google John Laurenson Social media platforms used to be about communication between friends – now many are increasingly short video entertainment hubs. The business model is to increase the time people spend on their apps and increase ad revenue. But is there already a consumer backlash? Aurélia fixes herself a coffee, sits down in her beautiful garden not far from Paris and goes on Instagram "to relax." First up: "a guy I like a lot who does interior design. He's in Venice at the moment." She's into interior design, and has even just had two bird drawings by the 19th Century English designer William Morris tattooed on her arms. She scrolls down. Two kittens having a fight. "I love animals so I get a lot of animals. That's how it works, social media. You click on bananas and they give you bananas." There are ads too – although they look just like the other posts – for a robot-vacuum cleaner, a diet and bed linen (with Morris-inspired designs). But no friends. She has 198 on Instagram but she says "it's completely changed. I practically don’t see any friends' posts anymore." She’s pretty much given up posting herself. "I don't think anyone sees them anymore anyway."  While there remain committed social, amateur posters on Instagram and especially Facebook, the switch from communicating with people you know to scrolling through professionally made content from people you don't, is even more pronounced among young users. Kylian, 16, is in vocational training to become a chef. He's on TikTok and Youtube a lot, he says. "I like looking at videos more than photos or messages. I watch videos made by people I don't know. I don’t post at all. I'm a rather shy person. I stay in my bubble. I watch and that’s all. I keep my reactions to myself." "I spend a lot of time scrolling through videos made by content-creators," says Lucie, also 16. "They're more interesting than the posts of people I know." She doesn't post except sometimes "stories" which disappear after 24 hours.  Whether it's TikTok, Snapchat, Facebook and Instagram, we are a long way from the "digital town square" of personal interaction that social media was even just a few years ago. In France, annual official Barometre du numerique 2026  shows 49% of social media users are "active only occasionally". In the UK, an Ofcom report   published in April showed a year-on-year drop of users who actively post from 61% to 49%. In the US, a Morning Consult survey of June last year found 28% reported posting less often than the previous year. Just 33% now post daily compared to 57% who use it for entertainment daily. The gap is a lot wider still for Gen Z – 18% active for 74% passive. Vanessa Lalo, a Paris-based clinical psychologist specialising in on-line behaviour, says "users have become more conscious that the traces you leave (on social media) stay there forever and some no longer want to maintain social media relations that can be superficial. Some don’t want the exposure to criticism that might be a risk when you post or the feeling that their post will seem poor alongside all the professional content". However, Lalo adds, people haven’t stopped posting, rather they are posting different things and in different places. "On TikTok, for example, young people publish a lot of content but it's more funny parodies and remixes of existing material. The goal is to make people laugh, not to tell people about their lives." That still happens, she says, but it’s moved from social media platforms like Instagram and Facebook to messaging sites like WhatsApp. There's also been a move towards private groups on Instagram and Snapchat. "These are much more intimate places where you're not bombarded with ads and content made by influencers," she says. "What we're seeing is social media splitting in two," says social media consultant Matt Navarra, author of the Geekout Newsletter. "Big platforms like Instagram and TikTok are becoming more about entertainment and discovery. WhatsApp is becoming the place people go to actually be social. The catch is, those kinds of spaces are harder for companies to make money from." Small business owners are being pushed to become presenters, editors, trend spotters and content creators, on top of actually running the business – Matt Navarra It was TikTok that helped to pioneer an algorithm that figures out from the moment you start scrolling what you like, and then fills your feed with material calculated to keep you on the app for the longest possible time. Now, says Matt Navarra, "Meta has built what it calls an AI system for unconnected content recommendations on Facebook and Instagram, which basically means, they're increasingly showing you stuff from people you don't follow because the machine thinks you're going to like it. It's not biased towards, is it a professional creator? Is it a brand? Is it a friend? If they can see that you've engaged with a friend a lot, you might see a lot more of their content. It's just that who you are friends with, who you follow, has become irrelevant in a way." This all means that small businesses, that have long used social media for free promotion have to up their game.   "There's a real opportunity for some small businesses," says Matt Navarra. "A bakery, florist, salon or local café can still break through if they have a good story, strong visuals or behind-the-scenes content people want to watch. But it also means the job has changed. Small business owners are being pushed to become presenters, editors, trend spotters and content creators, on top of actually running the business." The social platforms continue to be monetised predominantly by ad revenue. That is still the core business model. And ad revenue continues to grow – Matt Navarra Social media is evolving into something passive like television, albeit television that adapts as you zap. Or rather which knows you so well that it doesn't seem to matter that much that it's taken the remote control. You give the platform information about yourself that it uses for commercial gain and, in return, it gives you content tailored to please you for free. The transition from truly social media to entertainment platform does seem to be paying off. "The social platforms continue to be monetised predominantly by ad revenue. That is still the core business model. And ad revenue continues to grow," says Matt Navarra. Global social media ad revenue is expected to reach $317 billion (£236bn) in 2026, up from $277 billion (£206bn) last year. Meta is the biggest winner. Its ad sales already increased 22% year-on-year in 2025.  Ad sales are expected to hit $243 billion (£181bn) this year , enough to overtake Google for the first time. AI powered digital ad targeting is becoming ever more effective and precise. "The social platforms allow companies to put ads amongst the content that you're scrolling through. Every third or fourth scroll is an ad. And they are the world's best ad targeting engines. They know so much about your interests because of what you've looked at, liked, engaged with, what you've chosen to follow, the time you've spent in certain areas of the app, things like that," Navarra says.  "So advertisers will go in and say: 'I want to place an ad next to people in the UK who are between thirty and sixty years old and who are interested in DIY' and the social platforms will have that information and will place the ads accordingly." The price will depend on the number of impressions (clicks) the advertiser wants and how tight the criteria are. It costs more to place ads in the social media feeds of people who buy horses than people who buy ice-cream. More like this: •  TikTok is tracking you, even if you don't use the app. Here's how to stop it •  How to stop AI from turning your brain to mush •  This monkey selfie will protect you from AI slop Might there be a backlash coming? Don't many people go on to social media to see how friends are reacting to their posts or comments before settling down to scroll through professionally made content? Whether it's the shrinking social motivation to get on these apps or something else, the amount of time people spend on social media plateaued at an average of 141 minutes in 2025, down slightly from 143 minutes in 2024 . However, this is only part of the story, as the number of people using social media and the total time humanity spends on these apps continues to rise. For Gen Z it’s higher still. Around five hours a day in the United States where, for this demographic, social media has also become the primary search engine and shopping tool. Meanwhile, for those who miss what are fast becoming the old days when social media enabled you to share a bit of your life, a joke or a point of view with people you more-or-less knew, there are tools within platforms, says Matt Navarra, that allow you to choose to see mainly friends and family content. "People can flick to a feed that gives them that," he says. "But most people don't." -- If you liked this story, sign up for The Essential List newsletter – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.   For more on business and beyond, follow us on  LinkedIn . ##2026年5月22日 分享 收藏 在Google上设为首选 约翰·劳伦森 社交媒体平台过去是关于朋友之间交流的——如今许多平台日益成为短视频娱乐中心。其商业模式是增加人们在应用上花费的时间，从而增加广告收入。但消费者是否已经出现了反弹？奥蕾莉亚给自己冲了杯咖啡，坐在巴黎附近她美丽的花园里，打开Instagram“放松一下”。首先看到的是：“一个我很喜欢的做室内设计的人。他目前在威尼斯。”她热衷室内设计，甚至刚在手臂上纹了两幅19世纪英国设计师威廉·莫里斯的鸟类画作。她继续往下滑。两只小猫在打架。“我喜欢动物，所以会看到很多动物内容。社交媒体就是这样运作的。你点击香蕉，它就给你香蕉。”还有广告——虽然看起来和其他帖子一模一样——推销扫地机器人、减肥方案和床品（带有莫里斯风格的设计）。但没有朋友。她在Instagram上有198个好友，但她说“完全变了。我几乎看不到任何朋友的帖子了。”她基本上已经放弃自己发帖了。“反正我觉得也没人看得到。”虽然Instagram、尤其是Facebook上仍有一些坚持发帖的社交型业余用户，但从与认识的人交流转向浏览不认识的人制作的专业内容，这一转变在年轻用户中更为明显。16岁的基利安正在接受职业培训，准备成为厨师。他说自己经常刷TikTok和YouTube。“我更喜欢看视频，而不是照片或消息。我看不认识的人做的视频。我完全不发帖。我是个比较害羞的人。我待在自己的小世界里。我就看看，仅此而已。我的反应都留给自己。”同样16岁的露西说：“我花很多时间刷内容创作者做的视频。它们比认识的人的帖子更有趣。”她不发帖，只是偶尔发“快拍”，24小时后消失。无论是TikTok、Snapchat、Facebook还是Instagram，我们离几年前社交媒体那个个人互动的“数字城市广场”已经相去甚远。在法国，2026年度官方《数字晴雨表》显示，49%的社交媒体用户“只是偶尔活跃”。在英国，Ofcom今年4月发布的一份报告显示，活跃发帖用户同比从61%降至49%。在美国，晨间咨询去年6月的一项调查发现，28%的人表示发帖频率低于前一年。如今仅33%的人每天发帖，而57%的人每天使用社交媒体是为了娱乐。这一差距在Z世代中更为悬殊——18%主动发帖，74%被动消费。驻巴黎的临床心理学家、专攻网络行为的瓦妮莎·拉洛

##段落
他说：“用户越来越意识到，（在社交媒体上）留下的痕迹会永远存在，有些人不再想维持可能流于表面的社交媒体关系。有些人不想要发帖时可能面临的被批评的风险，也不喜欢自己的帖子在众多专业内容旁边显得逊色的感觉。”然而，拉洛补充说，人们并没有停止发帖，而是发不同的东西、发在不同的地方。“以TikTok为例，年轻人发布大量内容，但更多是搞笑的模仿和对现有素材的混剪。目的是逗人笑，而不是告诉别人自己的生活。”她说，那种情况仍然存在，只是从Instagram和Facebook等社交媒体平台转移到了WhatsApp等即时通讯应用上。此外，人们也在向Instagram和Snapchat上的私密群组迁移。“这些是私密得多的空间，你不会被广告和网红制作的内容狂轰滥炸，”她说。“我们看到的是社交媒体正在一分为二，”社交媒体顾问、《Geekout Newsletter》作者马特·纳瓦拉说。“Instagram和TikTok这样的大平台越来越偏向娱乐和发现。WhatsApp正在成为人们真正进行社交的地方。问题在于，这类空间更难让公司赚钱。”小企业主正被推动着成为主播、编辑、趋势捕捉者和内容创作者，而且还是在经营业务之外——马特·纳瓦拉。正是TikTok率先开创了一种算法，从你开始滑动的那一刻就判断你喜欢什么，然后用精心计算的内容填满你的信息流，尽可能让你留在应用上更长时间。现在，马特·纳瓦拉说，“Meta已经在Facebook和Instagram上构建了所谓的无关联内容推荐AI系统，这基本上意味着，它们越来越多地给你展示你不关注的人的内容，因为机器认为你会喜欢。它不会偏向于——这是专业创作者吗？是品牌吗？是朋友吗？如果它们看到你经常与某位朋友互动，你可能会看到更多对方的内容。只是你与谁是朋友、你关注了谁，在某种程度上已经变得无关紧要了。”这一切都意味着，长期以来利用社交媒体进行免费推广的小企业必须提升水平。“对一些小企业来说确实存在机会，”马特·纳瓦拉说。“一家面包店、花店、美发沙龙或本地咖啡馆，只要有好的故事、强烈的视觉效果或人们想看的幕后内容，仍然可以突围。但这也意味着这份工作变了。小企业主正被推动着成为主播、编辑、趋势捕捉者和内容创作者，而且还是在

“实际上是在经营业务。”社交平台的主要盈利方式仍然是广告收入。这依然是核心商业模式。而且广告收入还在持续增长——马特·纳瓦拉

社交媒体正在演变成某种类似电视的被动媒介，只不过这是一台会随着你换台而自适应调整的电视。或者说，它太了解你了，以至于它夺走了遥控器也显得没那么要紧。你向平台提供关于自己的信息，平台将其用于商业获利；作为回报，它免费给你量身定制、取悦你的内容。从真正的社交媒体向娱乐平台的转变，似乎确实在见效。

“社交平台的主要盈利方式仍然是广告收入。这依然是核心商业模式。而且广告收入还在持续增长，”马特·纳瓦拉说。全球社交媒体广告收入预计将在2026年达到3170亿美元（2360亿英镑），高于去年的2770亿美元（2060亿英镑）。Meta是最大赢家。其广告销售额在2025年已同比增长22%。今年广告销售额预计将达2430亿美元（1810亿英镑），足以首次超越谷歌。AI驱动的数字广告定向投放正变得越来越有效、越来越精准。

“社交平台允许企业把广告放进你正在滑动的信息流里。每滑三四下就有一条广告。而且它们是世界上最好的广告定向引擎。它们对你的兴趣了如指掌，因为你看了什么、点赞了什么、互动了什么、选择关注了谁、在应用某些区域停留了多久，诸如此类，”纳瓦拉说。“所以广告主会进来说：‘我想把广告投给英国30到60岁、对DIY感兴趣的人’，社交平台掌握这些信息，就会相应地投放广告。”价格取决于广告主想要的曝光（点击）次数以及定向条件有多严格。把广告投放到买马的人的信息流里，比投放到买冰淇淋的人的信息流里更贵。

更多类似内容：• TikTok正在追踪你，即使你不使用该应用。以下是阻止它的方法 • 如何阻止AI把你的大脑变成浆糊 • 这张猴子自拍将保护你免受AI垃圾内容的侵扰

会不会出现反弹？难道很多人上社交媒体，不是为了先看看朋友对自己帖子或评论的反应，然后才安下心来刷专业制作的内容吗？无论是因为使用这些应用的社会动机在减弱，还是其他原因，人们在社交媒体上花费的时间在2025年平均停留在141分钟，较2024年的143分钟略有下降。然而，这只是故事的一部分，因为使用社交媒体的人数……

## 人工智能与人类在这些应用上花费的总时间持续上升。对于Z世代来说，这一数字更高。在美国，该人群每天约花费五小时，社交媒体对他们而言也已成为主要的搜索引擎和购物工具。与此同时，对于那些怀念社交媒体昔日时光——那时你可以与或多或少认识的人分享生活点滴、笑话或观点——的人，马特·纳瓦拉表示，平台内部设有工具，允许你选择主要查看朋友和家人的内容。“人们可以切换到能提供这种内容的信息流，”他说，“但大多数人并不会这么做。”——如果你喜欢这个故事，请订阅《精选清单》新闻简报——每周两次将精心挑选的专题、视频和不容错过的新闻发送到你的邮箱。欲了解更多商业及其他内容，请在领英上关注我们。商业 科技 专题 社交媒体 商业世界

readings.title: This test predicts your risk of death
body: 5 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Jasmin Fox-Skelly How quickly your heart rate returns to normal after exercise can reveal a surprising amount about your underlying health. If your heart hammers in your chest when you walk up the stairs, or you need to gasp for air while jogging to catch a bus, it may be a sign that you are not in peak physical shape. Yet what happens after you stop exercising can be just as revealing about the inner workings of your body. Enter the heart rate recovery (HRR) test. This is the difference between your pulse when your heart is pumping hard during exercise, and how fast it beats about a minute after you have finished.  Nieca Golderberg, a cardiologist at New York University Grossman School of Medicine, explains that HRR is a good indicator of your cardiovascular health. It can predict high blood pressure and cardiac events . But your HRR is also so much more than that. A poor result can act as an early warning sign, helping to uncover hidden problems with the rest of the body. Crucially, that includes your overall risk of death. Back in 1999, scientists from the Cleveland Clinic, Ohio, published some striking results . They had tested the HRRs of 2,400 adults, then followed them for six years. The team found that people with low heart rate recovery were around four times more likely to die during the study period.  Other teams around the world have since found similar results . HRR has emerged as a surprisingly strong predictor of death from any cause, whether there seems to be anything wrong with your heart or not . In young adults and the middle aged, HRR is even more closely linked to your risk of death than high blood pressure.  Here's a quick, simple way to calculate your HRR using materials you're already likely to have at home.  *It's important to consult your doctor before starting a new exercise regime. If you experience dizziness, chest pain or tightness, or shortness of breath that's out of proportion to the exercise you're doing, stop immediately. This test is not suitable for people with pre-existing heart conditions without medical supervision. The first step is to make sure you have a way of writing down your data and a timer (most phones have one). If you have a smartwatch or other wearable activity tracker, this will be useful. Then you need to calculate your maximum heart rate. If you have a smartwatch or other wearable device, this will be able to tell you what yours is. If not, this is usually around 220 minus your age. Next, it's time to do some exercise. This should be intense enough to raise your heart rate to between 70 and 85% of its maximum . It could include running, cycling, or rowing, depending on your level of fitness. To calculate your HRR, measure your pulse immediately after you stop exercising, when it is still at its highest. The easiest way to do this is with a smart watch or a fitness tracker.  Alternatively, you can also hold a finger against your neck and count the beats for 10 seconds. Multiply this number by six for an approximate beats-per-minute. Next, rest for one minute by sitting or lying down and re-check your pulse. Then simply subtract the second number from the first. This is your HRR. HRR to aim for You want your heart rate to drop back to normal quickly after you finish exercising. The more quickly it drops, the better. A good recovery rate would be one that goes down by at least 18 beats in the first minute.    The number can also vary between individuals and depends on factors such as age. However, a HRR of fewer than 12 beats could put you at risk of health problems down the line. The link between HRR and a person's risk of death is thought to be down to the vagus nerve . This major nerve is a critical link between the brain and the rest of the body, relaying signals to and from the heart, liver, intestines and other organs . It controls whether you are in the more stressful fight-or-flight mode, or the more relaxed rest-and-digest state.      "We have these two systems that work on the heart, we've got a brake and we've got an accelerator," says Lindsay Bottoms, professor in exercise and health sciences at the University of Hertfordshire, UK. When you exercise, the accelerator – also known as the sympathetic nervous system – activates, causing the body to enter "fight or flight" mode. Your heart beats faster and your blood vessels dilate, allowing oxygen to be pumped to the muscles. When you stop working out, your body needs to clear out all the metabolic "debris" created during exercise, such as lactic acid and other waste products. This process requires oxygen. "You have to get rid of that out of the muscles, so you still need increased blood flow, and you still need your heart rate to keep high," says Bottoms. When this has been done the body applies the brakes and switches to parasympathetic mode. This is the brake, and it puts the body into the rest-and-digest state. As you get fitter, your body gets better at switching between the accelerator and brakes. This is known as higher vagal tone, and it's known to be highly beneficial. It's linked to better mental health and cognitive functioning , as well as higher immune health and lower inflammation, among other things. That includes a lower risk of death .     If you are concerned about your HRR then Golderberg recommends booking an appointment with a doctor who can do a full cardiac risk assessment. The good news is that any problems identified are not set in stone. Research has found that you can improve your HRR with exercise programmes. This can reduce your risk of death back to a normal level. Both Bottoms and Golderberg recommend regular cardiovascular exercise to make sure your cardiovascular system is in tiptop shape. "If you want to improve your heart rate recovery, try moderate pace walking, cycling or, if you can, jogging, running or swimming," says Golderberg. Or you could even try dancing, she says. Once your HRR improves, you'll really have something to dance about. * All content within this article is provided for general information only, and should not be treated as a substitute for the medical advice of health care professionals. -- For trusted insights on health and wellbeing, sign up to the Health Fix newsletter  by senior health correspondent Melissa Hogenboom who also writes the Live Well For Longer and Six Steps to Calm courses. For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on Facebook and Instagram .  Health Human body Science Features

##段落
5天前 分享 收藏 在谷歌上设为首选 Jasmin Fox-Skelly 运动后心率恢复正常的速度能揭示关于你潜在健康的惊人信息。如果你爬楼梯时心脏在胸腔里狂跳，或者追公交车小跑时需要大口喘气，这可能表明你的体能状态并不理想。然而，停止运动后发生的事情，同样能揭示你身体内部的运作状况。这就是心率恢复（HRR）测试的用武之地。它指的是运动时心脏剧烈跳动时的脉搏，与你结束运动约一分钟后心跳速度之间的差值。

##段落
纽约大学格罗斯曼医学院的心脏病学家妮卡·戈尔德伯格解释说，HRR是衡量心血管健康的一个良好指标。它可以预测高血压和心脏事件。但你的HRR远不止于此。较差的结果可以充当早期预警信号，帮助发现身体其他部位的隐藏问题。至关重要的是，这其中包括你的整体死亡风险。早在1999年，俄亥俄州克利夫兰诊所的科学家们发表了一些引人注目的结果。他们测试了2400名成年人的HRR，随后对他们进行了六年的跟踪调查。研究团队发现，心率恢复较慢的人在研究期间死亡的可能性大约高出四倍。

##段落
此后，世界各地的其他研究团队也发现了类似的结果。HRR已成为一个出人意料地强有力的全因死亡预测指标，无论你的心脏看起来是否有任何问题。在年轻人和中年人中，HRR与死亡风险的关联甚至比高血压更为密切。

##段落
这里有一个快速、简单的方法，用你家里可能已经有的材料来计算你的HRR。

##段落
*在开始新的锻炼计划之前，务必咨询你的医生。如果你出现头晕、胸痛或胸闷，或与所做运动不成比例的呼吸急促，请立即停止。本测试不适合有既往心脏疾病的人在没有医疗监督的情况下进行。第一步是确保你有办法记录你的数据，并有一个计时器（大多数手机都有）。如果你有智能手表或其他可穿戴活动追踪器，这会很有用。然后你需要计算你的最大心率。如果你有智能手表或其他可穿戴设备，它可以告诉你你的最大心率是多少。如果没有，最大心率通常约为220减去你的年龄。接下来，该做一些运动了。运动强度应足以将你的心率提升到最大心率的70%至85%之间。可以包括跑步、骑行或划船，取决于你的体能水平。要计算你的HRR，请在运动结束后立即测量你的脉搏

##段落
当你停止锻炼时，趁心率仍处于最高点进行测量。最简单的方法是用智能手表或健身追踪器。或者，你也可以将手指按在脖子上，数10秒内的脉搏跳动次数。将这个数字乘以六，即可得出大约的每分钟心跳次数。接下来，坐着或躺下休息一分钟，再次检查脉搏。然后只需用第一个数字减去第二个数字。这就是你的心率恢复值（HRR）。

##段落
目标心率恢复值 你希望在结束锻炼后心率能迅速恢复正常。下降得越快越好。良好的恢复率是在第一分钟内至少下降18次。这个数值也因人而异，并取决于年龄等因素。然而，心率恢复值低于12次可能使你面临未来健康问题的风险。心率恢复值与死亡风险之间的关联被认为归因于迷走神经。这条重要的神经是大脑与身体其他部位之间的关键连接，负责向心脏、肝脏、肠道和其他器官传递信号。它控制着你处于压力更大的“战斗或逃跑”模式，还是更放松的“休息与消化”状态。

##段落
“我们有两个系统作用于心脏，我们有一个刹车和一个加速器，”英国赫特福德大学运动与健康科学教授林赛·博顿斯说。当你锻炼时，加速器——也称为交感神经系统——被激活，使身体进入“战斗或逃跑”模式。你的心跳加快，血管扩张，使氧气能被泵送到肌肉。当你停止锻炼时，你的身体需要清除运动过程中产生的所有代谢“碎片”，如乳酸和其他废物。这个过程需要氧气。“你必须把这些从肌肉中清除出去，所以你仍然需要增加的血流量，你仍然需要心率保持高位，”博顿斯说。当这一过程完成后，身体踩下刹车，切换到副交感神经模式。这就是刹车，它使身体进入休息与消化状态。随着你变得更健康，你的身体在加速器和刹车之间的切换会变得更好。这被称为更高的迷走神经张力，已知这非常有益。它与更好的心理健康和认知功能，以及更高的免疫健康和更低的炎症等有关。这包括更低的死亡风险。

##段落
如果你担心自己的心率恢复值，戈尔德伯格建议预约医生进行完整的心脏风险评估。好消息是，发现的任何问题都不是一成不变的。研究发现，你可以通过锻炼计划改善心率恢复值。

这可以将你的死亡风险降回正常水平。博特姆斯和戈尔德伯格都建议定期进行心血管锻炼，以确保你的心血管系统处于最佳状态。戈尔德伯格说：“如果你想改善心率恢复，可以尝试适度快走、骑自行车，或者如果可以的话，慢跑、跑步或游泳。”她说，你甚至可以尝试跳舞。一旦你的心率恢复得到改善，你就真的有值得跳舞庆祝的事情了。* 本文中的所有内容仅供一般信息参考，不应被视为医疗保健专业人员医疗建议的替代品。——如需获取关于健康与福祉的可信见解，请订阅由高级健康记者梅丽莎·霍根博姆撰写的《健康修复》新闻简报，她还撰写了《更长久地美好生活》和《平静六步》课程。如需更多来自BBC的科学、技术、环境和健康故事，请在Facebook和Instagram上关注我们。健康 人体 科学 专题

readings.title: What do you do when your love and your life are in two different places?
body: Future Perfect What do you do when your love and your life are in two different places? How to make a huge decision when there’s no perfect choice.﻿ by Shayla Love Oct 25, 2026, 12:30 PM UTC Gift Pete Gamlen for Vox Shayla Love is a science journalist based in Brooklyn who writes about science, health, and the mind. Hi readers! Shayla Love here, science journalist and longtime fan of Your Mileage May Vary. I’m honored to be subbing for Sigal Samuel while she’s out on parental leave. I’m diving into your questions as a way to help understand human nature and our choices through multiple lenses: philosophical, psychological, and beyond. Please send in any emotional, body/brain, sociological, perceptual, or other kind of life quandaries you might have. I am someone who notoriously struggles with big decisions. Over a year ago, I found a wonderful partner, who very much feels like they could be my soulmate. We’ve been dating three time zones apart for a while. Being near our families, communities, and aging parents is a shared value — unfortunately one that makes it hard to compromise on location. Either way, I have to give up something I want and value — a wonderful partner who I can see a life with (the first time I’ve felt this way about someone), or the place I’ve always imagined settling down and that represents the person I am becoming and values I want to live. Two good things are pulling me toward opposite paths and there’s not much room for compromise. How do I make the “right” decision? Dear Fork in the Road, You’ve found a place in the world that you feel connected to and you met a person you envision spending the rest of your life with. Geographically restless and lonely people everywhere are jealous! But with your good fortunes seemingly at odds with one another, it feels that by choosing one, you’ll forsake the other — and doom the choice you did make to feel like a sacrifice. When circumstances have forced me to make a tough decision, I’ve daydreamed about a thought experiment: the Many Worlds Interpretation. In quantum physics, particles behave differently than us mortals. For example, an electron can be in more than one place at once until it’s measured. How can it be in multiple locations and then be observed to be in a single position? In the 1950s, the American physicist Hugh Everett proposed an explanation: The universe splits into alternate versions of itself, one for each place a particle could be measured. To apply this theory to your life, if you chose to move cities, don’t worry, another universe would be created in which you didn’t choose to do this, and you’ll stay right where you are! Fill out this anonymous form ! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does and their questions will be prioritized for future editions. Sign up here! Yes, I know you can’t transport yourself into such a quantum realm, but there is something helpful in thinking about alternative universes. Did you have an immediate reaction to which universe you would be upset not to inhabit? Take that information to heart, because it’s likely you’re not ultimately going to make your choice based on a tidy pro-con list. The psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky won a Nobel Prize for pointing out that most of our decisions are not based on rationality. People use two systems for decision-making: System one is faster and emotionally based, and system two is more logical and slow. But even the slower, more deliberate decision-making can fall prey to any number of cognitive biases. In your case, one called loss aversion may be especially relevant. People have the tendency to worry more about what they’ll lose, even if what they stand to gain is equal in value. For example, it will likely feel worse to lose a $10 bill from your pocket than it would feel good to find a $10 bill on the ground. This bias is relevant in people’s social lives too: They hold onto older, maybe fading, friendships because the thought of losing them is too painful, but don’t seek out new friends with equal effort. Or, they stay in a meh job because it feels scary to let it go, rather than applying that same energy to finding a new one. Once you accept that your decision-making process will be subject to messy feelings and biases, you can let go of trying to make the perfect choice. You opened your question by sharing that you struggle with big decisions, and it makes me wonder if you simply feel anxiety about making a choice at all. This is called analysis paralysis . When outcomes are uncertain, anxiety wakes up, and a voice in your head tells you to avoid taking risks . People with analysis paralysis overthink their options, over-research, and second-guess their first instincts. These actions have more to do with stress over committing to any decision rather than the content of what you’re deciding on. A surprising finding from psychology may ease your paralysis. Researchers told people to make a big life decision — on the order of ending a relationship or quitting their job — by flipping a coin. Heads, they made the change; tails, they didn’t. For those who followed the results of the toss, the people who made the change were overwhelmingly happier, even though their decision to do so was made by pure chance. These random-flip outcomes also show “that people may be excessively cautious when facing life-changing choices,” the authors wrote. The coin helped the participants resist the bias of tending to stick with the status quo, even if it doesn’t make them happier. To begin to loosen your paralysis, something that might assist you, paradoxically, is to introduce more options into the mix. Jacques Derrida, the 20th-century French philosopher, is known for the concept of deconstruction, a way of analyzing texts or ideas more critically, and showing they’re not as stable as they seem. He pointed out that we often think in binaries and false opposites: good vs. evil, man vs. woman, nature vs. culture. This can set up an easy dichotomy in which one of the items is good, and the other, by being its opposite, is bad. You’ve created a binary situation, and you don’t actually have to be in one. What if there’s a third option, or a fourth? What if you and your partner move to a brand-new city, and set out to create new community, together? What if you and your partner find a way to split your time between your respective hometowns? Now you don’t have only two good things pulling you in opposite directions, you would have different options you can be more creative with. You also don’t have to commit to the decision you make now for the rest of your life. You can always move cities again, or try to find another mate. You are with a partner you love, and live in a place that you love. You might reframe your situation as a win-win, rather than a lose-lose. And remember that if you don’t make a choice, you’re not successfully avoiding a decision — it’s a choice of its own. Your partner may get tired of long-distance or end the relationship for another reason. Or, you could start to resent the place you live since you have to travel so much to spend time with your partner. I also want to point out how you describe your partner. Don’t turn your nose up at finding someone who you can see making a life with, especially as you note, if you’ve never felt that way before. Billionaire investor Warren Buffett has said that there were two most important moments in his life: when he came out of the womb, and when he met his wife. “What happened with me would not have happened without her.” Buffett’s view is supported by research that shows that people with supportive spouses tend to take on more rewarding challenges throughout their lives, and end up having more personal growth and happiness. Another quantum idea that might interest you is spooky action at a distance. This is when two particles, even far apart, become connected to one another. Measuring one affects the other, no matter how far apart they are. If your partner feels like your “soulmate,” perhaps you have become entangled already. Don’t fret about making the perfect choice about the next phase of life, but do make a choice (any choice!) that considers your futures as bound up together. For the other details, maybe it’s time to find a coin to flip. I’m currently re-watching The Twilight Zone and recommend the episode Mirror Image , about a young woman who encounters her double from a parallel universe. The show’s creator, Rod Serling, was inspired to write the script when he saw a man at the airport who looked suspiciously like him, and had a similar suitcase and jacket. What if he approached the man, and it turned out to be himself? The dreamy story also inspired the movie Us by Jordan Peele. The 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai for their work on “handedness”: how molecules can have variants that are non-identical mirror images of one another. These variants are their own kind of dark doppelganger; only one can exist in the body. The science writer Ann Finkbender wrote a charming essay about understanding this principle of life in Last Word on Nothing. If you haven’t yet read Stoner by John Williams, just put down whatever you’re currently reading and do it. It’s a cautionary tale about what happens when you don’t act, and let your passivity make choices for you. 未来完成时 当你的爱与你的生活身处两地，你该怎么办？当没有完美选择时，如何做出重大决定。作者：Shayla Love 2026年10月25日 12:30 PM UTC 赠礼 Pete Gamlen 为 Vox 绘制 Shayla Love 是一位驻布鲁克林的科学记者，撰写关于科学、健康和心灵的文章。嗨，读者们！我是 Shayla Love，科学记者，也是《你的体验因人而异》的长期粉丝。很荣幸在 Sigal Samuel 休育儿假期间代班。我深入解答你们的问题，以此借助多重透镜——哲学的、心理学的以及其他视角——来帮助理解人性与我们的选择。请把你们在情感、身体/大脑、社会学、感知或其他方面的生活困境发给我。我是一个众所周知在重大决定上挣扎的人。一年多前，我遇到了一位很棒的伴侣，感觉对方很可能就是我的灵魂伴侣。我们隔着三个时区约会已经有一段时间了。靠近各自的家庭、社区和年迈的父母是我们共同的价值观——不幸的是，这也让在居住地点上妥协变得困难。无论怎样，我都必须放弃一些我想要且珍视的东西——要么是一位很棒的伴侣，我能与之看到共同生活（这是我第一次对某人有这种感觉），要么是我一直想象着定居、并且代表着我正在成为的人和我想要践行的价值观的地方。两件美好的事物把我拉向相反的道路，而妥协的空间并不多。我该如何做出“正确”的决定？亲爱的岔路口，你找到了一个自己觉得与之有联结的地方，也遇到了一个你设想与之共度余生的人。各地在地理上不安分又孤独的人都会羡慕！但你的好运似乎彼此相冲突，感觉选择其中一个，就会舍弃另一个——并让你所做的选择注定感觉像是一种牺牲。当环境迫使我做出艰难决定时，我曾幻想过一个思想实验：多世界诠释。在量子物理中，粒子的行为与我们凡人不同。例如，一个电子在被测量之前可以同时处于不止一个位置。它怎么能处于多个位置，然后又被观测到处于单一位置？20世纪50年代，美国物理学家休·埃弗雷特提出了一个解释：宇宙分裂成自身的替代版本，粒子可能被测量的每个位置各对应一个版本。把这个理论应用到你的生活中，如果你选择搬到城市，别担心，另一个宇宙会被创造出来，在那里你没有选择这样做，而你会留在原地！填写这张匿名表格！简报订阅者会比其他人更早看到我的专栏，他们的问题也会被优先考虑用于fu

真实版本。点此注册！是的，我知道你无法把自己传送进那样的量子领域，但思考替代宇宙这件事确有其助益。对于哪个宇宙是你不愿错过的，你是否立刻有了反应？把这一信息放在心上，因为你最终很可能不会基于一份整齐的利弊清单做出选择。心理学家丹尼尔·卡尼曼和阿莫斯·特沃斯基曾因指出我们大多数决策并非基于理性而获得诺贝尔奖。人们用两套系统做决策：系统一更快、基于情绪，系统二更合逻辑、更缓慢。但即便是更缓慢、更深思熟虑的决策，也可能沦为各种认知偏差的牺牲品。在你的情形中，一种名为“损失厌恶”的偏差可能尤为相关。人们倾向于更担忧自己会失去什么，即便可能获得的东西价值相当。例如，从口袋里丢掉一张10美元钞票，感觉很可能比在地上捡到一张10美元钞票更糟。这种偏差在人们的社交生活中同样相关：他们紧抓着更年长、或许正在褪色的友谊不放，因为想到失去它们太痛苦，却不会以同等努力去结交新朋友。或者，他们留在一份平庸的工作里，因为放手让人害怕，而不是把同样的精力用于寻找新工作。一旦你接受自己的决策过程会受混乱情绪和偏差影响，你就可以放下追求完美选择的执念。你以分享自己在大决定上挣扎来开启提问，这让我好奇，你是否只是对做出任何选择都感到焦虑。这被称为“分析瘫痪”。当结果不确定时，焦虑便会苏醒，你脑中的一个声音告诉你要避免冒险。患有分析瘫痪的人会过度思考选项、过度研究，并质疑自己的第一直觉。这些行为更多与对承诺任何决定感到的压力有关，而非你所决定之事的内容本身。心理学中一个令人惊讶的发现或许能缓解你的瘫痪。研究人员让人们通过抛硬币来做重大人生决定——诸如结束一段关系或辞去工作之类。正面，他们就做出改变；反面，他们就不做。对于那些遵循抛掷结果的人，做出改变的人总体上更快乐，尽管他们这样做的决定纯属偶然。这些随机抛掷的结果也表明，“人们面对改变人生的选择时可能过度谨慎，”作者写道。硬币帮助参与者抵抗了倾向于维持现状的偏差，即便现状并不让他们更快乐。要开始松动你的瘫痪，某种

##段落
矛盾的是，能帮到你的做法，是把更多选项引入其中。20世纪法国哲学家雅克·德里达以“解构”概念闻名，这是一种更具批判性地分析文本或观念的方式，揭示它们并不像看上去那样稳固。他指出，我们常常以二元对立和虚假的对立面来思考：善与恶、男与女、自然与文化。这会制造出一种简单的二分法，其中一项是好的，而另一项因其对立面而是坏的。你制造了一个二元处境，而你其实并不必身处其中。如果有第三个选项，或者第四个呢？如果你和伴侣搬到一个全新的城市，一起着手建立新的社群呢？如果你和伴侣找到一种办法，在各自家乡之间分配时间呢？这样你就不只有两件美好的事物把你拉向相反方向，而是会有不同的选项，可以更有创意地处理。你也不必为余生锁定现在的决定。你随时可以再次搬城市，或者试着另寻伴侣。你与所爱的伴侣在一起，住在你喜爱的地方。你可以把处境重新界定为双赢，而非双输。还要记住，如果你不做选择，你并没有成功避开决定——那本身就是一种选择。你的伴侣可能厌倦异地恋，或因其他原因结束关系。或者，你可能会开始怨恨自己居住的地方，因为你得频繁奔波才能与伴侣相聚。我还想指出你描述伴侣的方式。不要对找到一个你能与之共度一生的人嗤之以鼻，尤其如你所言，如果你从未有过这种感觉。亿万富翁投资者沃伦·巴菲特说过，他一生中最重要的时刻有两个：出生时，以及遇见妻子时。“没有她，我身上发生的一切都不会发生。”巴菲特的观点得到研究支持：有支持型配偶的人往往一生中承担更多有回报的挑战，最终获得更多个人成长与幸福。另一个你可能感兴趣的量子概念是“鬼魅般的超距作用”。这是指两个粒子即使相隔遥远，也彼此相连。测量一个会影响另一个，无论它们相距多远。如果你的伴侣感觉像你的“灵魂伴侣”，也许你们已经纠缠在一起。不必为人生下一阶段做出完美选择而烦恼，但一定要做出一个选择（任何选择！），把你们的未来视为紧密相连。至于其他细节，也许是时候找枚硬币来抛了。我目前正在重看《阴阳魔界》，并推荐那一集——

##塞林（Serling）的《镜子影像》（Mirror Image），讲述一位年轻女子在平行宇宙中遇见另一个自己。该剧创作者罗德·塞林（Rod Serling）的灵感来源于他在机场看到一个人，长得跟他极为相似，连行李箱和夹克都差不多。要是他走上前去，结果发现那人就是他自己呢？这个如梦似幻的故事也启发了乔丹·皮尔（Jordan Peele）的电影《我们》（Us）。2026年诺贝尔化学奖授予亨利·B·卡根（Henri B. Kagan）和曾我健三（Kenso Soai），以表彰他们在“手性”方面的研究：分子如何拥有彼此并非完全相同镜像的变体。这些变体就像是它们自己的暗黑分身；在人体中只能存在其中一种。科学作家安·芬克本德（Ann Finkbender）在《Last Word on Nothing》上写了一篇妙趣横生的文章，讲述如何理解这一生命原理。如果你还没读过约翰·威廉斯（John Williams）的《斯通纳》（Stoner），那就放下你手头正在读的书，去读它。这是一个警示故事，讲的是当你不行事、任由被动替你做出选择时会发生什么。查看更多：建议 未来完美生活 人际关系 你的体验可能因人而异 特朗普正试图推翻一场尚未发生的选举 用最新的Vox填字游戏让大脑休息一下 我该对AI黑客恐慌和“黑色十月”有多担心？ 美国下一场重大医疗改革可能已经在进行中 保守派对阿利托大法官出人意料的强烈反对 电子邮件（必填） 注册 提交你的电子邮件即表示你同意我们的条款和隐私声明。本网站受reCAPTCHA保护，并适用谷歌隐私政策和服

readings.title: How birdwatching slows down brain ageing
body: 2 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Becca Warner Birdwatching can help slow brain ageing and is increasingly being used as therapy for dementia patients. Every week, a group of elderly birders spend hours hunkering down inside a wooden hide in the English countryside, peering through binoculars as they excitedly share what they spot. An oystercatcher's long, bright beak probing the pebbled ground; two great crested grebes bobbing in the water, their plumed heads poised.  Most of these birdwatchers have difficulty recalling what happened earlier that day, and might struggle to follow a conversation. But they become animated when swapping notes on the birds that fill the sky around Forge Mill Lake in the UK's West Midlands. Among them is 78-year-old Harold*. He loved the outdoors when he was younger, but more recently dementia has made him withdrawn and anxious. His daughter Lucy* brought him here, hoping that the change of scenery and peaceful lake might be good for him. After an apprehensive start, Harold began smiling when someone pointed out a robin and enjoyed watching the ducks splashing in the water. Blue tits darted between the nearby trees, and Lucy saw Harold laugh for the first time in a long time. "For that moment in time he was present in the moment, he wasn't worried about his memory or his confidence. That is very powerful, in a gentle way," says Jenny Budinger, a community dementia advisor at Age UK, the non-profit that runs the birdwatching group. Birdwatching is increasingly recognised as a valuable way for elderly people and dementia patients to spend their time, with groups set up in nursing homes in the UK, Germany and the US. Paying attention to birds , even through the window, can help older people feel more connected to others, experience more positive emotions and boost memory skills. Now new research shows that birdwatching can reshape the brain, much like learning an athletic sport or a musical instrument – and may even help slow the brain's ageing. Meanwhile, in the laboratory, neuroscientists are investigating how birdwatching impacts the brain. They tested keen birdwatchers' identification skills to determine who was an expert and who was a novice, then looked at their brains. The scientists found that the very structure of experts' brains was different – and that birdwatching expertise might slow age-related decline by keeping the brain more organised. Erik Wing, who led this research at Baycrest Academy for Research and Education in Toronto, Canada, compared MRI brain scans from bird experts to those of novices while they identified birds. He found that expert brains were wired differently in regions important for functions like attention, visual perception and visual recognition.  Among expert birders, these regions showed more activity – particularly when they were asked to identify birds they weren't already familiar with. The findings don't prove whether structural brain differences are the cause or effect of birdwatching expertise. But, Wing says, one explanation is that the areas of the brain used for birdwatching might undergo "neuroplasticity" – the ability to change shape and function over time. Wing also analysed how organised the birdwatchers' brains were. Organisation in the brain tends to reduce with age, and lower measures of organisation are associated with reduced cognition . In experts' brains, some regions had higher levels of organisation and coherence than novices of the same age. Some of these regions were also the ones that showed more activity during bird identification. This indicates a "kind of preservation of organisation" in the brains of experts as they age, Wing says. More research is needed to understand the nature of this preservation and how it links to wider cognitive function. But for now, the results may indicate that "acquiring this skill earlier in life might produce benefits that continue through to older adults", Wing says. This is good news for the many Gen Z (16 to 29-year-old) birdwatchers who are getting their binoculars out long before old age sets in. Wing's research looked at birdwatching expertise, but other findings suggest that there may be psychological benefits to birdwatching even for those without special knowledge or skills.  In fact, when it comes to experiencing psychological restoration – feelings of calm, freedom and rejuvenation – enthusiasm may be more relevant than expertise . A study of 388 birdwatchers in Poland found that those who say they are more interested in birding than other activities and consider it an important part of their lives are more likely to experience psychological restoration than birdwatchers who are highly skilled but less enthusiastic. Simply choosing to be interested in birds, then, could have its own benefits. Elisabeth Kals, a professor of social and organisational psychology at the Catholic University of Eichstätt-Ingolstadt in Germany, is interested in how our relationship with nature shapes our life experiences and wellbeing. She studied what happened when people living in nursing homes had the chance to watch the local bird life.  Her team installed bird feeding stations outside 65 homes, positioned so that residents could watch the birds from the comfort of the indoor common area, and assessed the residents' cognition, mobility and wellbeing through self-reports and inputs from staff and family. They saw improvements after just a few weeks, and after a month birdwatching explained residents' wellbeing better than their age and care level. "The findings were clearly positive," Kals says. Those who took part in birdwatching became more cognitively agile, she adds – meaning they were more able to follow a conversation and interact with family who visited, remember and recognise birds that had visited before, and show alertness. Nursing home staff were the first to see the difference the birds made. "For weeks, they haven't seen a smile on [a resident's] face, and then they see the smile," Kals says. Some of the memory and concentration improvements are evident after just three to four weeks, Kals says. Her team's findings have prompted German health insurance companies – who, among others, initially funded the research project – to invest in setting up bird feeders and viewing areas in more than 400 nursing homes across Bavaria. "It was so effective, it just economised money," Kals says. In the US, a similar initiative was set up at four care communities in 2013 in Connecticut, and later in Texas and Colorado . Bird Tales is a therapy programme for people living with dementia that involves installing bird feeders in the facilities where they live and giving them stuffed bird animals that make bird-like calls so they can learn about different species. The result has been positive for those taking part: they report finding it cognitively stimulating and say it connects them with the past. A similar programme has seen benefits for survivors of stroke, some of whom experience aphasia – difficulty speaking or understanding spoken language. The University of Montana's Intensive Comprehensive Aphasia Program started with owl spotting in 2021, and now includes guided observations and call identification of Montana's diverse bird population.  Why does watching birds have such a positive impact on how we feel and think? For Kals, it's "not just about birds as such; it is about nature, attention, emotion, meaning, social exchange, and activity coming together in a very simple way. It creates small moments of curiosity – pleasure, anticipation". And, she adds, it is "extremely accessible". This may be why, in a UK survey of dementia patients and their carers, watching birds and other wildlife was the second most popular outdoor activity after simply walking in nature. The same survey found that challenges with transport and access are big considerations for people with dementia – which may not be such a barrier for those who can see birds from their kitchen window. Wing says birdwatching is a means of exploring curiosity, and it is perhaps this curiosity that is so beneficial. "I think there's a lot of benefit to incorporating more novelty in our lives, in midlife and as we continue to age," Wing says. Curiosity plays an important role in maintaining cognitive function later in life, possibly because it activates norepinephrine and dopamine in the brain, which have a positive, anti-inflammatory effect. For Kals, getting to know the birds that call and swoop around us is a way to remember who we are. "We are part of nature as human beings, but we lose that connection, unfortunately, quite early in life. [Birdwatching] is a way to reestablish this connection, and it's so simple." * Names have been changed for privacy reasons.  -- For trusted insights on health and wellbeing, sign up to the Health Fix newsletter by senior health correspondent Melissa Hogenboom who also writes the Live Well For Longer and Six Steps to Calm courses.   For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on Facebook and Instagram . ##段落
2天前 分享 保存 添加为Google首选 贝卡·华纳 观鸟有助于延缓大脑衰老，正越来越多地被用作痴呆症患者的疗法。每周，一群老年观鸟爱好者都会花上数小时，蜷缩在英国乡村一个木制隐蔽观察棚里，透过双筒望远镜凝神张望，兴奋地交流各自的发现。一只蛎鹬用长而鲜亮的喙在碎石地面上探寻；两只凤头䴙䴘在水中起伏，羽冠高耸。这些观鸟者大多难以回忆起当天早些时候发生的事，也可能跟不上对话的思路。但当他们交流英国西米德兰兹郡福奇米尔湖周围天空中鸟类的见闻时，便变得神采奕奕。其中有一位78岁的哈罗德*。他年轻时热爱户外活动，但近来痴呆症让他变得孤僻而焦虑。他的女儿露西*带他来到这里，希望换个环境和宁静的湖泊对他有所裨益。起初哈罗德有些忐忑，但当有人指给他看一只知更鸟时，他露出了笑容，也喜欢看鸭子在水中扑腾。蓝山雀在附近的树间穿梭，露西看到哈罗德笑了——这是很久以来的第一次。“在那一刻，他活在当下，不再担心自己的记忆或信心。这以一种温和的方式，非常有力量，”珍妮·布丁格说，她是英国老年关怀组织（Age UK）的社区痴呆症顾问，该非营利机构运营着这个观鸟小组。观鸟正日益被认可为老年人和痴呆症患者度过时光的一种宝贵方式，英国、德国和美国的养老院都成立了相关小组。关注鸟类——哪怕只是透过窗户——也能帮助老年人感到与他人更紧密相连，体验更多积极情绪，并提升记忆能力。如今新研究表明，观鸟可以重塑大脑，其原理与学习一项体育运动或一种乐器颇为相似——甚至可能有助于延缓大脑衰老。与此同时，在实验室里，神经科学家正在研究观鸟如何影响大脑。他们测试了热衷观鸟者的识别能力，以判定谁是专家、谁是新手，然后观察他们的大脑。科学家发现，专家的大脑结构本身就不一样——而观鸟专长可能通过让大脑保持更有组织性来延缓与年龄相关的衰退。领导这项研究的埃里克·温就职于加拿大多伦多贝克里斯特研究与教育学院，他在鸟类专家和新手识别鸟类时对比了他们的核磁共振脑部扫描。他发现，专家大脑在对注意力、视觉感知和视觉识别等功能至关重要的区域，神经连接方式有所不同。在专家级观鸟者中，这些

##段落
这些区域表现出更多活动——尤其是当他们被要求识别自己不熟悉的鸟类时。这些发现并不能证明大脑结构的差异是观鸟专长的原因还是结果。但Wing表示，一种解释是，用于观鸟的大脑区域可能会经历"神经可塑性"——即随着时间推移改变形状和功能的能力。Wing还分析了观鸟者大脑的有序程度。大脑的有序性 tends to 随着年龄增长而下降，而有序性指标较低与认知能力下降相关。在专家的大脑中，一些区域的有序性和连贯性水平高于同龄新手。其中一些区域也正是鸟类识别过程中表现出更多活动的区域。Wing表示，这表明专家的大脑在衰老过程中存在"某种有序性的保持"。需要更多研究来理解这种保持的本质及其与更广泛认知功能的关联。但就目前而言，Wing表示，结果可能表明"在生命早期习得这项技能可能会产生持续到老年的益处"。这对许多Z世代（16至29岁）观鸟者来说是个好消息，他们在年老到来之前很久就已经拿起了望远镜。Wing的研究关注的是观鸟专长，但其他发现表明，即使对于没有特殊知识或技能的人来说，观鸟也可能带来心理上的益处。事实上，在体验心理恢复——平静、自由和焕新的感受——方面，热情可能比专长更为重要。一项针对波兰388名观鸟者的研究发现，那些表示自己对观鸟比对其他活动更感兴趣、并将其视为生活中重要组成部分的人，比那些技能高超但热情较低的人更有可能体验到心理恢复。因此，仅仅选择对鸟类产生兴趣，本身就可能带来益处。Elisabeth Kals是德国艾希施泰特-因戈尔施塔特天主教大学社会与组织心理学教授，她关注我们与自然的关系如何塑造我们的生活体验和幸福感。她研究了养老院居民有机会观察当地鸟类生活时会发生什么。她的团队在65个住所外安装了喂鸟站，位置安排使居民可以从室内公共区域的舒适环境中观看鸟类，并通过自我报告以及工作人员和家属的反馈来评估居民的认知、活动能力和幸福感。仅仅几周后他们就看到了改善，而一个月后，观鸟对居民幸福感的解释力超过了年龄和护理水平。"这些发现令人……

##段落
“早期效果就很积极，”卡尔斯说。她补充道，参与观鸟的人认知灵活性提高了——也就是说，他们更能跟上对话、与来访的家人互动，能记住并辨认出以前来过的鸟，并表现出警觉性。养老院的工作人员最先看到了这些鸟带来的变化。“好几个星期以来，他们都没在[一位住户]脸上见过笑容，然后他们看到了笑容，”卡尔斯说。卡尔斯表示，有些记忆力和注意力的改善仅在三到四周后就显现出来。她团队的发现促使德国医疗保险公司——它们是最初资助该研究项目的机构之一——投入资金，在巴伐利亚州400多家养老院安装喂鸟器和观鸟区。“效果太好了，还省了钱，”卡尔斯说。在美国，2013年在康涅狄格州的四个照护社区启动了类似项目，后来又推广到得克萨斯州和科罗拉多州。Bird Tales是一个面向痴呆症患者的治疗项目，做法是在他们居住的机构里安装喂鸟器，并给他们发会发出鸟叫般声音的毛绒鸟玩具，让他们了解不同种类的鸟。参与者的反响是积极的：他们表示这能刺激认知，并说自己因此与过去建立了联系。一个类似项目也让中风幸存者受益，其中一些人患有失语症——说话或理解口语有困难。蒙大拿大学的强化综合失语症项目于2021年从观察猫头鹰开始，现在包括在引导下观察蒙大拿州多样的鸟类种群并辨识鸟叫。为什么观鸟对我们的感受和思维有如此积极的影响？在卡尔斯看来，“这不只是关于鸟本身；而是关于自然、注意力、情感、意义、社交互动和活动以一种非常简单的方式结合在一起。它创造出小小的好奇时刻——愉悦、期待”。而且，她补充说，它“极其容易参与”。这或许可以解释，为什么在英国一项针对痴呆症患者及其照护者的调查中，观鸟及其他野生动植物观察是仅次于单纯在自然中散步的第二大受欢迎的户外活动。同一项调查发现，交通和通行方面的困难是痴呆症患者的重要顾虑——而对于那些能从厨房窗户看到鸟的人来说，这可能不算什么障碍。温说，观鸟是探索好奇心的一种方式，而或许正是这种好奇心如此有益。“我认为，在我们的人生中途以及随着我们继续变老，在生活中加入更多新鲜事物有很多好处，”温说。好奇心在晚年维持认知功能方面发挥着重要作用，可能是因为它会激活去甲肾……

## 大脑中的去甲肾上腺素和多巴胺，具有积极的抗炎作用。对卡尔斯来说，了解那些在我们周围鸣叫、盘旋的鸟类，是一种记住我们是谁的方式。“作为人类，我们是自然的一部分，但不幸的是，我们在生命早期就失去了这种联系。〔观鸟〕是重建这种联系的一种方式，而且非常简单。”* 为保护隐私，部分姓名已更改。 -- 欲获取值得信赖的健康与福祉洞察，请订阅由资深健康记者梅丽莎·霍根布姆撰写的《健康修复》通讯，她还撰写了《更长久地美好生活》和《平静六步》课程。 欲了解更多BBC的科学、技术、环境与健康故事，请在Facebook和Instagram上关注我们。 健康 鸟类 动物 自然与户外 环境 大脑 专题
